statement: A.6b (Refuted: uniqueness without the normalization).. The three arithmetic hypotheses do not make an arbitrary transitive, isomorphism-natural system of determinant identifications unique unless the distinguished norm coset is required. If $t_{XY}$ is one such system and $s_X\in\{\pm1\}$ is constant on isomorphism classes, then $t'_{XY}=s_Yt_{XY}s_X^{-1}$ is another. Over $\overline{\mathbb F}_{11}$, the curves with $j=0$ and $j=1728$ have automorphism groups of orders $6$ and $4$ respectively. Taking $s_X=-1$ in the first class and $+1$ in the second gives a distinct system, natural even under equivalences that preserve endomorphism rings. The positive construction in A.6a removes this ambiguity. There is also still a scalar automorphism of the common determinant line; a canonical object is not thereby a uniquely trivialized line.

statement: A.8b (Proved neighboring unit statement; unfinished question unresolved).. For $p>3$, $O^*=\{\pm1\}$ except at $j=0$, where its order is $6$, and $j=1728$, where its order is $4$. These curves are supersingular precisely for $p\equiv2\pmod3$ and $p\equiv3\pmod4$ respectively. At $p=2$ the unique geometric supersingular curve has $24$ automorphisms; at $p=3$ it has $12$. The displayed ``respectively'' in the supplied transcription of 15:70 reverses the orders $4,6$. These statements follow from the standard Weierstrass changes: for odd characteristic greater than three an automorphism scales $(x,y)$ by $(u^2,u^3)$, forcing $u^4=1$ when $j=1728$ and $u^6=1$ when $j=0$. The supersingularity assertions also follow from the Hasse invariant coefficient or the inertness of $p$ in the quadratic CM field. At $2$, use $y^2+y=x^3$: the changes have $u^3=1$, $r=s^2$, $s^4=s$, and $t^2+t=s^6$, giving $3\cdot4\cdot2=24$. At $3$, use $y^2=x^3-x$: one has $s=t=0$, $u^4=1$ and $r^3=r$, giving $4\cdot3=12$. statement: A.8c (Known with derivation: the corrected maximal-order count).. Restrict to geometric trace-zero descents $E/\mathbb F_p$ with $R\hookrightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_p}(E)$ sending $\sqrt{-p}$ to Frobenius. Their number is \[ \#\operatorname{Pic}(R)= \begin{cases}h(-4p),&p\equiv1\pmod4,\\ h(-p),&p\equiv3\pmod4,\\ h(-8)=1,&p=2. \end{cases} \] In particular the answer is $h(-3)=1$ at $p=3$. To derive this, trace zero is an elliptic isogeny class by \citet[Theorem 4.1(5)]{Waterhouse1969}. Its rational endomorphism algebra over $\mathbb F_p$ is $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-p})$. The maximal order is an allowed endomorphism ring by that paper's Theorem 4.2(3). Theorem 4.5 then makes its isomorphism classes a principal homogeneous space under $\operatorname{Pic}(R)$. The embedding is fixed by its prescribed value on $\sqrt{-p}$, so it adds no multiplicity. When $p\equiv3\pmod4$, the other $h(-4p)$ trace-zero curves have the nonmaximal Frobenius order. This also derives the small-prime trace-zero counts independently of the exhaustive enumeration.

statement: Products and the proposed tetrahedral coefficient.. The same argument gives the natural exact sequence in every integer degree. In particular, for $P=\operatorname{Spec}k$ it gives \[ K_{-2}(E)[1/p]\xrightarrow[\sim]{\ \partial\ } K_{-3}(R)[1/p]. \] The sequences are compatible with external products by classes on the fixed parameter scheme. Indeed, each relative $K$-theory fibre is a module over the base $K$-theory spectrum; the connecting map of a fibre sequence of modules is linear, with the usual graded convention. The nonconnective module structure is described in \citet[Section 6.5, pp.~360--361]{D_ThomasonTrobaugh1990}. Thus, if $\kappa\in K_{-2}(E)[1/p]$ and $\xi\in K_2(P)[1/p]$, then \begin{equation} \partial_P(\kappa\boxtimes\xi) = (\partial\kappa)\boxtimes\xi \quad\hbox{in }K_{-1}(\operatorname{Spec}R\times_kP)[1/p]. \tag{FF.3} \end{equation} The degree of $\xi$ is even, so exchanging the displayed factors does not introduce a sign.

statement: Remaining work for C.2.. We have proved affine vanishing, isolated its exact failure to prove cycle localization, and given the correct conditional positivity argument. statement: Outcome for E.3 and Lead E4.. The positive-characteristic direction is proved in E.3e, with its integral premise retained. E.3u refutes the complex converse, even rationally, by the displayed codimension-four family on a sixfold. E.3t proves the stronger necessary condition that the entire Lawson cylinder vanish; the example has a zero singular cylinder and an injective Lawson cylinder. E.3m--p remain exact equivalences for each fixed target, but their universal conditions are false: on the specified sixfold $\langle\mathcal H^{*2}\rangle_0^4(X) \subsetneq(\mathcal A*\mathcal H)^4(X)$, and the corresponding quotient has nontorsion classes. The left side is $N^4(X)$ and needs only surface Albanese kernels as generators; the right side is exactly $\ker\psi_W$. E.3j proves that converse for one-cycles whenever zero-cycles are supported on a curve; E.3l extends it to support on a surface and identifies $P^{n-1}(X)$ integrally with the Walker Jacobian group in that case. E.3q adds codimension two under the same surface-support hypothesis, with the ordinary Jacobian as well. Applied to the Ottem--Suzuki fourfold, this combines with E.3h to refute the unqualified integral biconditional in Lead E4: its family-map assertion is true and its equality of equivalence relations is false on the same variety. statement: Supported higher families (auxiliary proof under review).. Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $p>0$ and let $E=\bigcup_iE_i$ be a projective SNC surface with smooth connected components. No negative exceptional divisor is needed in this lemma. Let $u\in k^*$ and choose a finite tuple \[ z_i\in\operatorname{CH}_0(E_i)^0_{\mathbf Q}. \] Regard these as their canonical top classes in $K_0(E_i)_{\mathbf Q}$. Then there exist a smooth connected projective curve $P$, points $o,t\in P(k)$, and an actual class $\eta\in K_1(E\times P)_{\mathbf Q}$ satisfying \begin{equation} \bigl((\eta_t-\eta_o)|_{E_i}\bigr)_i=(u z_i)_i \quad\hbox{in }\bigoplus_iK_1(E_i)_{\mathbf Q}. \tag{HK.1} \end{equation} In fact the two component endpoint tuples can be chosen to be $(0)_i$ and $(u z_i)_i$ separately. The theorem does not identify the global endpoint difference with $u$ times a selected global $K_0(E)$ lift. It makes no assertion about a proper relation in $K_0(E)$ or about the quotient (UK.7). \emph{1. Represent the component cycles on transverse proper curves.} Clear one common denominator. Move each integral degree-zero representative away from all double curves, using the explicit smooth-curve moving argument of C.3br Step~4. Choose a smooth connected projective curve $A_i\subset E_i$ through its finitely many support points, transverse to every double curve and avoiding all triple points. A sufficiently high very ample system separates these finite values and first jets. The same incidence dimension counts and connectedness argument as in C.3br give the required curve in every characteristic. Put \[ L_i=\mathcal O_{A_i}\left(\sum_x n_{i,x}[x]\right) \in\operatorname{Pic}^0(A_i)(k). \] For $a_i:A_i\hookrightarrow E_i$ the exact sequences of point Cartier divisors on the smooth curve give the integral identity \begin{equation} (a_i)_*([L_i]-1)=\sum_x n_{i,x}[\mathcal O_x] \quad\hbox{in }K_0(E_i). \tag{HK.2} \end{equation} Thus no rational cohomological representative has replaced the specified zero-cycle class. \emph{2. Use the complete marked edge-family lemma.} Apply the integral lemma (VE.2) simultaneously to the curves $A_i$ with line bundles $L_i$ and the fixed unit $u$. Mark every point of $A_i$ on every double curve of E. It yields one actual smooth connected proper parameter $P$ and classes \[ \xi_i\in K_1(A_i\times P),\qquad (\xi_i)_o=0,\qquad(\xi_i)_t=u([L_i]-1), \qquad \xi_i|_{\{q\}\times P}=0 \] for every marking q. The final equality holds in the actual $K_1(P)$, not just at the endpoints or after a norm. \emph{3. Retain supports to remove all triple coherence.} Let $W\subset E$ be the reduced closed union of the finitely many $A_i$. It avoids every triple point. Write $W_i=W\cap E_i$ and $W_e=W\cap C_e$; each $W_e$ is a finite reduced set. Use nonconnective perfect K-theory with the indicated support. The regular closed immersion $A_i\times P\hookrightarrow E_i\times P$ gives a proper perfect pushforward to the supported group \[ \beta_i=(a_i\times1)_*\xi_i \in K_1(E_i\times P\ \mathrm{on}\ W_i\times P)_{\mathbf Q}. \] The support is enlarged from $A_i\times P$ to $W_i\times P$ if necessary. Perfect proper pushforward and its supported form are \citet[Sections 3.16.4--3.16.7]{D_ThomasonTrobaugh1990}. For an incident edge $C_e\subset E_i$, transversality makes the square with $A_i\subset E_i$ Tor-independent. Its derived base-change homotopy, including supports, identifies the restriction of $\beta_i$ with the sum of the pushforwards of $\xi_i|_{\{q\}\times P}$ for $q\in A_i\cap C_e$. Every one is zero. This is zero in $K_1(C_e\times P\ \mathrm{on}\ W_e\times P)$ itself. If $W_e$ includes further points arising from a neighbouring component, enlarging support preserves zero. The exact primary base-change statement and full proof are \citet[Proposition 3.18, pp.~321--322]{D_ThomasonTrobaugh1990}. Consequently the alternating edge restriction of $(\beta_i)_i$ is zero. Apply the rational closed-union descent of (ET.6)--(UK.2) both to $E\times P$ and to its complement of $W\times P$. Finite homotopy limits commute with the fibre defining support K-theory. Hence the supported descent diagram is the actual fibre of those two coherent diagrams, with the canonical geometric nullhomotopies retained. All its vertex support spectra are zero, because W avoids the vertices. It therefore gives the fibre sequence \begin{equation} K(E\times P\ \mathrm{on}\ W\times P)_{\mathbf Q} \longrightarrow \bigoplus_iK(E_i\times P\ \mathrm{on}\ W_i\times P)_{\mathbf Q} \longrightarrow \bigoplus_eK(C_e\times P\ \mathrm{on}\ W_e\times P)_{\mathbf Q}. \tag{HK.3} \end{equation} Its long exact sequence lifts $(\beta_i)_i$ to an actual supported $K_1$ class. Forget its support to obtain $\eta$. There is no use of a perfect pushforward $K(A_i)\to K(E)$, which would be unjustified at the double points. Only the regular component pushforwards and actual supported descent are used. \emph{4. Evaluate the actual proper family.} Both endpoint squares with $a_i\times1$ are Tor-independent. Perfect derived base change and the projection formula give \[ \eta_o|_{E_i}=0,\qquad \eta_t|_{E_i}=u(a_i)_*([L_i]-1)=u z_i. \] The complete projection-formula proof is \citet[Proposition 3.17, pp.~320--321]{D_ThomasonTrobaugh1990}. Divide by the cleared common denominator. This proves (HK.1). No Adams decomposition or semisimplicity of $K_1$ has been used. The construction lives on the fixed proper product $E\times P$. \emph{Why this is not yet a solution of the component gate.} The statement raises the K-degree by multiplication with u. A valuation of u over an auxiliary function field may recover the component zero-cycle tuple, but compatibility of that residue with ordinary proper $K_0$ relations is an additional theorem. A regular semistable parameter model can have a special dual graph with cycles; its support Mayer--Vietoris boundary has node coefficients in $K_{-1}(E)$. Their vanishing after point pushforward is not the vanishing of the abstract Picard tensor in (PL.5). C.3bt removes global endpoint ambiguities with zero component image, but does not by itself supply this missing specialization theorem. The previously retained negative-K valuation counterexample remains valid and rules out an unrestricted residue principle.

statement: The scope of the available comparison theorems.. The opened results impose the following precise limits. The converse from the integral Hodge conjecture for curves on $A$ to the direct-summand property requires a unimodular line bundle in \citet[Theorem 1.1 and the paragraph immediately following it]{cyBeckmannFortman2023} and \citet[Theorem 1.1 and the paragraph following it]{cyScaviaSuzuki2025}. Without that hypothesis the applicable complex criterion is on $A\times\widehat A$ \citep[Theorem 1.4]{cyVoisin2024}. statement: Auxiliary lemma (proved and independently audited): divisibility of the relevant $K_2$-cohomology.. statement: Auxiliary Hodge calculation for a quartic containing a line.. Fix a line $D_0\subset\mathbb P^3_{\mathbb C}$ and let $B\subset\mathbb P H^0(\mathcal I_{D_0}(4))$ be the nonempty open subset parametrizing smooth quartics. We choose a \emph{Hodge-generic complex point} $b\in B$ as part of the data, in the precise sense described below. Write $W=W_b$, $H=c_1(\mathcal O_W(1))$, and $D=D_0\subset W$. We can and do choose $b$ so that \[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{NS}(W)=\mathbb ZH\oplus\mathbb ZD, \qquad \begin{pmatrix}H^2&H\cdot D\\H\cdot D&D^2\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix},\\ T=\operatorname{NS}(W)_{\mathbb Q}^{\perp} \subset H^2(W,\mathbb Q), \qquad \operatorname{End}_{\mathrm{Hdg}}(T)=\mathbb Q. \end{gathered} \] Let $C$ be the Fermat plane quartic and put $S=W\times C$. Then the largest rational sub-Hodge structure of $H^3(S,\mathbb Q)$ whose Hodge types are contained in $\{(2,1),(1,2)\}$ is \begin{equation} \operatorname{NS}(W)_{\mathbb Q}\otimes H^1(C,\mathbb Q). \end{equation} In particular, for every smooth projective complex curve $P$ and every $z\in\mathrm{CH}^2(W\times C\times P)$, the component of its rational cycle class in $H^3(S,\mathbb Q)\otimes H^1(P,\mathbb Q)$ belongs to \[ \operatorname{NS}(W)_{\mathbb Q}\otimes H^1(C,\mathbb Q)\otimes H^1(P,\mathbb Q). \] \emph{Choice of the quartic and its Hodge-generic complex point.}\par Theorem~1.1 and Corollary~1.3(c) of \citet[p.~2 of the opened author version]{frBrevikNollet2011} apply to $D_0$ with $d=4$: $\mathcal I_{D_0}(3)$ is globally generated and $H^0(\mathcal I_{D_0}(2))\ne0$. They give the asserted Picard group for a very general member of $B$. A smooth quartic is a K3 surface, and adjunction gives the displayed intersection matrix. For completeness, we also justify the endomorphism condition rather than inferring it solely from the Picard rank. Locally mark the second cohomology. The Local Torelli Theorem and its line-bundle formulation in \citet[Proposition~6.2.8 and Section~6.2.4, pp.~107--108 of the opened author version]{frHuybrechtsK3Book} identify the local deformations preserving $H,D$ with an open subset of the period quadric in $(\mathbb QH+\mathbb QD)^\perp_{\mathbb C}$. It has dimension $18$. These are locally realized by quartics containing a line: very ampleness of $H$ persists; Riemann--Roch, $D^2=-2$, and $H\cdot D=1$ make $D$ effective, and an effective divisor of hyperplane degree one is a line. A projective coordinate change puts that line back at $D_0$. For every nonscalar $a\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q}(T)$, the condition that $a$ is a Hodge endomorphism implies that the period line is an eigenline of $a$. The eigenlines form a finite union of proper linear subspaces. They cannot contain the nondegenerate irreducible period quadric, which spans the ambient projective space. Thus each such Hodge-endomorphism locus is proper. There are countably many rational endomorphisms. Applied to the polarized weight-zero variation $\operatorname{End}(T)$, the Hodge-locus theorem of \citet[Theorem~1.1 and Corollary~1.3, p.~2]{frCDK1994} shows that these loci are algebraic (with their monodromy translates). Avoiding their countable union, together with the extra Picard loci, produces the stipulated complex point. This is the meaning of the Hodge-generic choice. We do not assert that every embedding of a field with coefficientwise algebraically independent quartic parameters has this property. \emph{The product Hodge group and its representations.} By \citet[Theorem~2.2.1 and Example~2.2.3, p.~211]{frZarhin1983}, \[ \operatorname{Hg}(T)=\operatorname{SO}(T). \] The exact original theorem and its proof in Section~2.5, pp.~212--213, have been inspected. By \citet[Lemma~2, p.~106, and Example~3, pp.~106--107]{frBeauville2014}, the Jacobian of $C$ is isogenous to $E^3$, where $E=\mathbb C/\mathbb Z[i]$. Hence, for $V=H^1(E,\mathbb Q)$, we have $H^1(C,\mathbb Q)\simeq V^{\oplus3}$ and $\operatorname{Hg}(V)=\operatorname{Res}^{1}_{\mathbb Q(i)/\mathbb Q} \mathbb G_m=:U$. Let $G=\operatorname{Hg}(T\oplus V)$. Its two projections are surjective, and $G$ is connected. The image of $G^{\mathrm{der}}$ on $\operatorname{SO}(T)$ is the full group, while its image on the torus $U$ is trivial. Therefore $\operatorname{SO}(T)\times1\subset G$; surjectivity on $U$ then gives \[ G=\operatorname{SO}(T)\times U. \] This argument uses only that the special orthogonal group in rank $20$ is connected and semisimple; no independence assumption on periods of $W$ and $E$ is being inserted. Over $\mathbb Q(i)$, the representation $T\otimes V$ is the direct sum of the two twists of the standard $\operatorname{SO}(T)$ representation by the two opposite nontrivial characters of $U$. Both summands are absolutely irreducible, they are nonisomorphic, and complex conjugation exchanges them. A rational invariant subspace therefore contains both or neither. Thus $T\otimes V$ is a simple rational Hodge structure. Moreover \[ (T\otimes V)^{3,0}=T^{2,0}\otimes V^{1,0}\ne0. \] It consequently has level three. Semisimplicity of polarizable rational Hodge structures implies that every nonzero sub-Hodge structure of $(T\otimes V)^{\oplus3}$ has a simple constituent isomorphic to $T\otimes V$; in particular none has level at most one. Since $H^1(W)=H^3(W)=0$, Kunneth gives \[ H^3(S,\mathbb Q)= \bigl(\operatorname{NS}(W)_{\mathbb Q}\otimes H^1(C,\mathbb Q)\bigr) \oplus\bigl(T\otimes H^1(C,\mathbb Q)\bigr). \] The first summand has exactly the two indicated Hodge types and the second has no nonzero sub-Hodge structure with those types. This proves \eqref{eq:N6-level-one}. Finally, the indicated Kunneth component of the class of $z$ is a rational Hodge class of type $(2,2)$. Poincare duality on $P$ turns it into a morphism of Hodge structures $H^1(P,\mathbb Q)(-1)\to H^3(S,\mathbb Q)$. The source has types $(2,1),(1,2)$, so its image lies in \eqref{eq:N6-level-one}, proving the claimed consequence for every such cycle and parameter curve.

statement: The nearby integral Hodge and Tate theorems.. The distinction in C.4q matters even though integral curve classes on the original variety $A$ are understood in these dimensions. In characteristic zero, Grabowski's theorem applies to every abelian threefold, with no principal-polarization hypothesis. Its proof transforms integral divisor classes, expresses them as differences of ample classes, and principalizes each ample class; this produces curves on the dual threefold. It does not assert the algebraicity of the Poincar\'e curve class on the sixfold $A\times\widehat A$. Likewise, \citet[Theorem 7.1 and Proposition 7.2, pp.~17--19 of the opened author version]{frC4Totaro2021} proves the integral Tate conjecture for abelian threefolds over the separable closure of a finitely generated field. The formulation uses $\ell$-adic cohomology for $\ell\ne\operatorname{char}(k)$, as specified in its Section 1; it does not itself supply the crystalline statement at the characteristic prime. Nor does it assert the required integral curve theorem on $A\times\widehat A$. C.4q identifies an explicit limitation of trying to obtain that cross class only by pushing curves forward from its proper abelian subvarieties.

statement: Square-zero $K_2$ and the first normal-motion symbol.. Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic $p>2$, let $V/k$ be smooth, and let $L$ be a line bundle. For the split thickening $V_2=\operatorname{Spec}_V(\mathcal O_V\oplus L)$, with $L^2=0$, there is a natural isomorphism of relative Zariski $K$-sheaves \[ \mathcal K_2(V_2,V)\simeq L\otimes\Omega^1_{V/k}. \] We choose the sign normalization \[ \{1+tc,u\}\longmapsto tc\,d\log u. \] This is the negative of the map in \citet[Chapter III, Exercise 5.14, pp.~46--47]{frWeibelKbookIII} with his modern Dennis--Stein convention. Indeed his Definition 5.11, p.~43, gives $\langle r,s\rangle=\{r,1-rs\}$ when $r$ is a unit, and his exercise sends $\langle m,r\rangle$ to $m\,dr$. Our normalization therefore sends $\langle m,r\rangle$ to $-m\,dr$. The isomorphism for a ring $R$ with $1/2\in R$ is the unnumbered theorem and corollary of \citet[p.~A1204, proof pp.~A1205--A1207] {frVanDerKallen1971}; it has no characteristic-zero hypothesis. The construction is natural in $R$ and homogeneous in the square-zero coordinate, so it glues for $L$. Since $k$ is perfect of positive characteristic, $\Omega^1_{k/\mathbb Z}=0$, and absolute differentials on $V$ agree with $\Omega^1_{V/k}$. Locally let $x,y$ be regular parameters on $V$, and let $t$ generate $L$. The difference of the two Koszul symbols for a first normal motion is \[ \{x-at,y-bt\}-\{x,y\} \longmapsto t\frac{b\,dx-a\,dy}{xy}. \] The term with two infinitesimal units has zero image. If $\eta=t^{-1}(\eta_x\,dx+\eta_y\,dy)$ is a local section of $\Omega^1_V\otimes L^{-1}$, wedging the displayed form with $\eta$ in that order and taking the local residue gives \[ a\eta_x+b\eta_y. \] The simultaneous sign of the Koszul orientation and the chosen $K_2$ map is thus fixed. This is a local symbol computation; the global Chow-to-$K$-cohomology comparison needed in C.3an is a separate argument in that statement.

An explicit ordered small resolution of a tetrahedral fibre.. Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $p>0$. In four variables we put  egin{equation} Q=x_0x_1x_2x_3,\qquad G= egin{cases} \sum_{i=0}^3x_i^5,&p
e5,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i^5+\sum_{0\le i<j\le3}x_i^4x_j,&p=5, \end{cases} \qquad F=Q-G. 	ag{TG.1} \end{equation} Let $R$ be the local ring of $F=0$ at the origin, or its strict henselization. We construct a projective morphism $Z	o\operatorname{Spec}R$ which is an isomorphism off the closed point and whose source is regular. Its reduced closed fibre $E$ is an effective Cartier simple normal crossings divisor with four components. In the order $0,1,2,3$, these components are respectively blowups of $\mathbf P^2_k$ at $15,10,5,0$ distinct points on their coordinate edges. Every double curve is $\mathbf P^1_k$, the four triple intersections are single points, and there is no quadruple intersection. Thus its dual complex is the boundary of a tetrahedron. \emph{Step 1: the isolated local hypersurface and the first blowup.} Every coordinate-plane section of $G=0$ is smooth, every coordinate edge meets it in five distinct nonvertex points, and $G$ is nonzero at the four coordinate vertices. For $p
e5$ these assertions follow directly from the Fermat equation. For $p=5$, the plane polynomial is \[ g=a^5+b^5+c^5+a^4b+a^4c+b^4c. \] At a common zero of $g$ and its three derivatives, $a=0$ would imply $b=0$ and then $g=c^5
e0$. If $a
e0$, the first derivative gives $c=-b$, and the third gives $a^4+b^4=0$. Substitution in $g=0$ gives $a^5=b^5$, hence $a=b$. This contradicts $2a^4=0$ in characteristic $5$. On an edge the polynomial is $a^5+b^5+a^4b$; in the chart $b=1$ its derivative is $4a^3$ and its value at $a=0$ is $1$. There are therefore five distinct roots, none at a coordinate vertex. Euler's homogeneous identities give \[ \sum_i x_iF_{x_i}=4Q-5G. \] At a singular point of $F=0$ we consequently have $Q=G=0$, in every characteristic. A nonzero such point lies on a coordinate face. The restriction of $Q$ to that face is identically zero, so the tangential derivatives of $G$ there would all vanish. The smooth plane and edge sections just checked exclude this, and the vertices have $G
e0$. Thus the affine hypersurface is smooth away from the origin. At the origin its local ring is a domain: a factorization into two nonunits in the ambient regular local UFD would make their intersection, of dimension at least two, singular. Repeated factors are excluded for the same reason. The hypersurface is Cohen--Macaulay and regular in codimension one, hence normal. The blowup $Z_0$ of the origin is the strict transform inside $\operatorname{Tot}(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^3}(-1))$. With $t$ the fibre coordinate and $w_i$ homogeneous base coordinates, its equation is  egin{equation} w_0w_1w_2w_3=tG(w_0,w_1,w_2,w_3). 	ag{TG.2} \end{equation} This description is the actual Rees blowup, obtained on each chart by cancelling the common fourth power in the domain. Its Cartier closed fibre $E_0=(t=0)$ is the reduced union of the four coordinate planes. At a triple vertex $G$ is a unit, so $t$ is a unit times the product of three regular parameters. Away from the vertices and double edges the source is regular. On a double edge it is regular unless $G=0$. At each of the thirty zeros of $G$ on the six edges, its simple zero permits an etale change of coordinates putting (TG.2) into the form  egin{equation} uv=tw,\qquad E_0=(t=0),\qquad (E_i,E_j)=((u,t),(v,t)). 	ag{TG.3} \end{equation} Indeed, after dividing by the two nonzero homogeneous coordinates, we may use the edge parameter $G$ as one of the local coordinates. There are no other singularities of $Z_0$. \emph{Step 2: the two actual blowup charts.} For the domain in (TG.3), blow up the ideal $(u,t)$. The two affine Rees charts are  egin{equation}  egin{array}{c|c|c} 	ext{chart}&	ext{independent coordinates}&	ext{map to (TG.3)}\ \hline u&u,a,w&t=ua,\quad v=aw,\ t&t,b,v&u=tb,\quad w=bv. \end{array} 	ag{TG.4} \end{equation} Here $a=t/u$ and $b=u/t$, with $ab=1$ on the overlap. statement: Actual curve germs, without an irreducibility assumption.. In a trivialization of $L$ with fibre coordinate $t$, the equations \[ s=0,\quad T=at,\quad z=-a^{p+1}t^{p+1},\quad y^n-y=z^{n-1} \] define a curve smooth at $(y,t)=(0,0)$ because the derivative with respect to $y$ is $-1$. We take the unique irreducible component through that smooth point. We make no claim that the entire displayed polynomial is irreducible. Its closure meets the exceptional surface in finitely many points; normalization over its cone image is finite. After strict henselization, the chosen branch is a finite local factor and is already normal at its selected closed point. This produces an actual integral curve on the fixed strict-local resolution. The symbol calculation of the preceding lemma gives residue $a$, up to the fixed simultaneous orientation convention. The global Chow construction and the quotient by ordinary algebraic equivalence are proved separately in C.3aq.

statement: Consequence for a proposed direct detector (conditional only on the stated relative-sheaf data).. Let $E$ be a square-zero thickening of the smooth variety $V$ above, and suppose there is an exact sequence of Zariski sheaves \[ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal J\longrightarrow\mathcal K_2(E) \longrightarrow\mathcal K_2(V)\longrightarrow0, \qquad p\mathcal J=0 \] in characteristic $p$. statement: Application to the ordered tetrahedral germ (proved application).. For the exact TG construction, TS gives a fixed natural summand $\kappa K_2(P)_{\mathbf Q}$ on $E\times P$, where $\kappa\in K_{-2}(E_0)_{\mathbf Q}$ has weight zero. Let $\xi\in K_2(P)$ and put $a=\kappa\xi\in K_0(E\times P)_{\mathbf Q}$. The class $a$ has rank zero, since $\kappa$ restricts to zero in negative $K$-theory at every point. Lift $a$ to $K_0(D\times P)_{\mathbf Q}$ by nilpotent invariance after inverting $p$\citep[Theorem A]{rootGeisserHesselholt2011}. For either endpoint $u$, its restriction $a_u$ is square-zero and has Adams weight two: $\kappa^2=0$ by TS over $k_0$, and field $K_2$ has weight two. Choose a positive integer $N$ such that the lift $Na$ is integral, necessarily of rank zero. In the special lambda-ring, \[ \gamma^2(Na_u) =\frac{(Na_u)^2+2Na_u-\psi^2(Na_u)}2=-Na_u. \] Apply (EL.1) to $-\gamma^2(Na)/N$. It yields an actual perfect family on $Z\times P$ whose endpoint restrictions to $E$ are exactly $a_o,a_t$. No global weight decomposition for $K_2(P)$ has been used. By FF.4, restriction $K_0(Z)_{\mathbf Q}\to K_0(E)_{\mathbf Q}$ is an isomorphism. Its endpoint lifts are therefore precisely the unique weight-two lifts used in TC. The second Chern-character component of the actual family, defined on finite-type smooth etale models and then pulled back, proves that their difference is ordinarily algebraically trivial in $\mathrm{CH}^2(Z)_{\mathbf Q}$. Ordinary here means an actual fixed product with the smooth proper curve $P$, as required. Every field symbol $\{a,b\}\in K_2(k)$ is such an endpoint difference on a smooth proper curve, by the explicitly proved proper-curve symbol lemma retained in the top-quotient research: normalize a component of $(f-1)^2(g-1)^2=c f g$, use the unramified symbol $\{f,g\}$, and compare $(a,b)$ with $(0,1)$. The exact localization and Gersten inputs are \citet[Section 7, Proposition 3.2 and equation (3.3), p.~127; Theorem 5.11, pp.~133--134]{rootQuillen1973}. Finite sums of these symbols generate $K_2(k)$. TC identifies $\mathrm{CH}^2(X)_{\mathbf Q}$ with precisely this coefficient group and kills the four degree coordinates by exceptional curves. Consequently \[ B^2(X)_{\mathbf Q}=0 \] for this specified tetrahedral family in every positive characteristic and over every algebraically closed extension of $\overline{\mathbf F}_p$. The endpoint theorem and this application have full independent root and two-peer proof audits. The conclusion is specific to this tetrahedral family; it does not assert the same result for every isolated threefold singularity.

statement: Uniform smooth surface data for every prime.. Fix a prime $p$, put \[ e=p+1,\qquad n=p(p+1),\qquad d=n-3>0, \] and work over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p$. Consider the smooth plane curve \[ C:\quad Y^n-YW^{n-1}=Z^{n-1}W. \] It has the unique point $\infty=(0:1:0)$ at infinity, and for $y=Y/W$, $z=Z/W$ we have $\operatorname{div}(dz)=n(n-3)\infty$. Set $D_1=ed\,\infty$, so that $\operatorname{div}(dz)=pD_1$. To verify the exact local normalization, put $q=Y/Z$ and $h=W/Z$. Then \[ h=q^n-qh^{n-1},\qquad z-q^{-n}=q^{n(n-3)}c,\qquad c=q(h/q^n)^{n-2}. \] The quotient $h/q^n$ is a unit with residue one, and $c$ is a uniformizer. In particular $dc$ is a unit differential. The Frobenius-killed extension constructed from $dz$ is $0\to\mathcal O_C(-D_1)\to E\to\mathcal O_C\to0$. Use the lines convention for $\mathbb P(E)$; its section $S_\infty$ has normal bundle $\mathcal O_C(D_1)$. The inseparable curve $G$ is locally $s^p=z$, is smooth and disjoint from $S_\infty$, and satisfies \[ G\sim pS_\infty-pg^*D_1. \] This minus sign is obtained from the local equations and the normal bundle, rather than from the conflicting display in RIMS1736, p.~5. The cyclic cover of degree $e=p+1$ has inverse-root line bundle \[ M=\mathcal O(-S_\infty+pd\,g^*\infty) \] and branch divisor $G+S_\infty$. Affinely it is $T^{p+1}=s^p-z$. The branch components are smooth and disjoint, and $e$ is prime to $p$, so the cover is smooth. Valuation one at a branch component proves that it is connected even when $e$ is composite. Let $S$ be the reduced section above $S_\infty$. Then $N_{S/V}=\mathcal O_C(d\infty)$ and $S^2=d$. Put \[ D=pS+d\,g^*\infty, \qquad L=pD. \] We have $D^2=(e^2-1)d$, $D\cdot S=ed$ and $D\cdot F=p$. Each fibre is integral (its cusp has coprime exponents $p$ and $p+1$). Every horizontal curve other than $S$ has nonnegative intersection with $S$ and positive intersection with a fibre. Thus Nakai--Moishezon proves that $D$, and therefore $L$, is ample. The local change at base infinity is $s=q^{ed}s_i+q^{-e}$ and $T=q^{pd}T_i$. At $S$, set $x=1/s_i$ and $w=T_i/s_i$. The cover equation becomes \[ w^{p+1}=x-cx^{p+1}, \qquad dT_i=-\frac{x^p}{w^p}\,dc. \] Consequently the order of $dT_i$ at $S$ is $p^2$; the base-infinity factor contributes $pd$. The local unit calculation also checks the intersection point of these divisors. We obtain \[ \operatorname{div}(dT)=pD, \qquad 0\ne\eta=dT\in H^0(V,\Omega^1_V\otimes L^{-1}). \] These are the uniform surface ingredients used in C.3aq. They specialize to valid data in characteristics two and three; C.3an uses a smaller separate characteristic-five example.

statement: Remaining work for C.4 and status of Lead C1.. The degree-one theorem, its independence of $\ell$, the corrected integral form and denominator, both proposed equivalences in their stated settings, and the conditional reduction are proved above. Lead C1 is correct with the stated coefficient and principal- polarization qualifications. The full requested C.4 remains incomplete in the residual nonprincipal cases isolated in the supplements. C.4h--l supply an exact scalar-factorization ideal, factorial bounds, simultaneous-polarization criteria, and the specific limitation of the divisor-product method. The Prym argument improves the surface bound to two and settles all surfaces with odd $\delta(A)$, including type $(1,3)$; the remaining surface cases have even $\delta(A)$. C.4o--p improve the threefold bound to $\gcd(6,\delta(A))$, leaving only primes two and three in that dimension. C.4r gives one exact all-characteristic residual test: the specified rational numerical surface class on $A\times\widehat A$ must belong to the integral numerical cycle lattice. C.4s settles every supersingular abelian surface, including characteristic two. C.4u settles every supersingular abelian threefold in characteristic at least five; only the indicated factors two and three remain for supersingular threefolds in those respective characteristics. C.4v settles the full totally real multiplication cases in characteristic zero, including its stated maximal-order CM case, and their good reductions. C.4w settles ordinary abelian varieties with the stated full real multiplication and Rosati hypotheses in every positive characteristic, including two. These families are removed from the residual unresolved cases; no nonmaximal-order extension at an obstruction prime is asserted. The refined order-index criterion covers real multiplication locally maximal at two for surfaces, or at two and three for threefolds, including the corresponding ordinary and good-reduction cases. C.4x removes the ordinary hypothesis for full real multiplication in positive characteristic: its polarization index is a power of the characteristic, and is one under the stated determinant condition, in particular under total ramification. Thus all such surfaces in characteristic other than two and all such threefolds in characteristic at least five split; the determinant condition also settles their remaining small characteristics. C.4ab identifies the remaining Mumford--Tate general type-$(1,2)$ surface case with the existence of an integral correspondence whose two specified scalar actions have opposite parity. Its partial Fourier construction is integral, but the existence of such a correspondence remains undecided. The semihomogeneous and residual-surface exclusions and the abstract graph calculation do not decide that existence question; C.4aa expressly refutes an unrestricted geometric transfer from the abstract graph condition. No general integral splitting in dimensions two and three is asserted.

statement: The corresponding presentation of the ordinary top quotient (proved consequence in the same resolved scope).. Define \[ S_d(E)=F_\gamma^dK_0(E)_{\mathbf Q}, \] and let $J_K^d(E)$ be the subgroup generated by endpoint differences of classes in $F_\gamma^dK_0(E\times P)_{\mathbf Q}$, with $P$ smooth connected projective and with actual product sections. Restriction and the rational Chern character give an isomorphism \begin{equation} \rho_d:\mathrm{CH}^d(Z)_{\mathbf Q} \xrightarrow{\sim}S_d(E). \tag{AE.11} \end{equation} Indeed FF.4 gives $K_0(Z)_{\mathbf Q}\simeq K_0(E)_{\mathbf Q}$ by restriction, using KST, levelwise nilpotent invariance and Drinfeld's $K_{-1}(R)=0$ for henselian local rings \citep[Theorem 3.7 and Remark (ii), p.~8]{frDrinfeld2004Tate}. No normal-crossing hypothesis is used in that argument. On $E$, $F_\gamma^{d+1}=0$ and $\psi^2$ acts by $2^j$ on the $j$th associated graded piece. Hence the projector onto $S_d(E)$ is \begin{equation} \prod_{j=0}^{d-1} \frac{\psi^2-2^j}{2^d-2^j}. \tag{AE.12} \end{equation} For the regular algebraizable $Z$, rational Chern character identifies this weight-$d$ subgroup with $\mathrm{CH}^d(Z)_{\mathbf Q}$ \citep[Chapter II, Proposition 4.9 and Corollary 8.9.1] {D_Weibel2013KbookII}. The finite bundles, cycles, relations and operations descend to smooth finite-type pointed etale models as in EP, and the isomorphism passes to their filtered limit. The same assertion applies to $Z\times P$. Let $\theta_d$ be proper cycle pushforward $\mathrm{CH}_1(E)_{\mathbf Q}\to\mathrm{CH}^d(Z)_{\mathbf Q}$ followed by $\rho_d$. Then \begin{align} \rho_d\bigl(\mathrm{CH}^d(Z)_{\mathrm{alg},\mathbf Q}\bigr) &=J_K^d(E), \tag{AE.13}\\ B^d(X)_{\mathbf Q} &\simeq S_d(E)\big/ \bigl(J_K^d(E)+\theta_d\mathrm{CH}_1(E)_{\mathbf Q}\bigr). \tag{AE.14} \end{align} Here is a proof of both inclusions, without a family-lifting assumption. Nilpotent invariance in characteristic $p$ makes \[ K_0(D\times P)_{\mathbf Q}\longrightarrow K_0(E\times P)_{\mathbf Q} \] an isomorphism of rational lambda rings \citep[Theorem A]{rootGeisserHesselholt2011}; its inverse preserves the rational gamma filtration, by the universal operations after clearing denominators. Lift an exceptional family in that filtration and apply (AE.1). Its two endpoint classes on $Z$ are forced by the point isomorphism to have pure weight $d$. The actual cycle $\operatorname{ch}_d(b)$ therefore realizes their difference as ordinary algebraic equivalence. This proves the inclusion of $J_K^d(E)$ in the left side of (AE.13). Conversely a cycle family on $Z\times P$ has, on a smooth finite-type model, an inverse rational Chern-character class with that codimension-$d$ component and all others zero. Its pullback is an actual pure-weight-$d$ class in $F_\gamma^dK_0(Z\times P)_{\mathbf Q}$. Restricting it to $E\times P$ gives the required exceptional perfect-family relation. This proves the opposite inclusion. A smooth nonproper parameter curve can be compactified and its finitely many horizontal cycle components closed in the fixed product; their torsion-free local coordinate rings over the regular curve give flatness and preserve the two fibres. Thus proper curves generate exactly the ordinary relation group. Finally the same closure in $Z\times P$ lifts relations from $X$, and localization for Chow groups gives (AE.14). This comparison removes the ambient endpoint-lifting problem in every dimension in the displayed resolved scope. It neither asserts the existence of these resolutions in arbitrary positive characteristic dimension nor computes $J_K^d(E)$ for a general singular exceptional scheme. In particular it does not replace actual perfect families on $E\times P$ by independently moving classes on its strata, and it does not assert that the full negative-$K$ family obstruction vanishes.

statement: A fixed-node correction for a two-component exceptional surface (intrinsic auxiliary lemma).. Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $p>0$ and let $E=S\cup R$ be a projective SNC surface with two smooth connected components and smooth connected double curve $C$. Suppose that $S$ is a smooth projective surface, that $R$ is a blow-up of $\mathbf P^2$ at distinct points of a smooth plane model of $C$, and that $C\subset R$ is its strict transform. Write these points as $z_1,\ldots,z_v$, where $v>0$, and the corresponding exceptional curves as $e_1,\ldots,e_v$. Thus \[ \mathcal O_R(e_j)|_C=\mathcal O_C(z_j). \] Assume that there are an ample line bundle $A$ on $S$, an integer $a>0$, a section $h\in H^0(S,A^a)$ cutting out $C$, and a section $g\in H^0(S,A^b)$ such that \[ \operatorname{div}(g|_C)=z_1+\cdots+z_v \tag{FN.1} \] is reduced. Let $S(E)=F_\gamma^2K_0(E)_{\mathbf Q}$ and define $J_K(E)$ by actual smooth projective curve families as in EP. Then component degrees induce an isomorphism \begin{equation} S(E)/J_K(E)\simeq\mathbf Q^2. \tag{FN.2} \end{equation} Consequently, if this $E$ is the full exceptional surface of data satisfying EP and has a positive exceptional Cartier combination with ample negative restriction, then $B^2(X)_{\mathbf Q}=0$. The last implication is conditional on that geometric realization. \emph{1. Move on the first component with fixed boundary support.} Fix $x,y\in(S\setminus C)(k)$. Choose $m$ so large that the sections of $A^{mb-a}$ separate the prescribed values and first jets at $x,y$, and supply all required first jets away from $C$. In the affine linear system \begin{equation} T=\{g^m+hq=0\},\qquad q\in H^0(S,A^{mb-a}), \tag{FN.3} \end{equation} impose the two linear conditions that $T$ contain $x$ and $y$. Choose $q(z_j)\ne0$ for every $j$. A general such section defines a smooth connected curve $T$. Here is the precise elementary Bertini argument. Away from $C$, multiplication by the nonzero section $h$ preserves first-jet generation, so the incidence of a singular point has codimension three over a two-dimensional surface. The same estimate after imposing the two values, and the remaining free derivative choices at $x,y$, avoids all singularities there. On $C$ the only zeroes are $z_j$. For $m>1$ the differential there is $q(z_j)\,dh$, which is nonzero, since $C$ is smooth. For $m=1$ its restriction to the tangent of $C$ is $dg|_C\ne0$. Finally, a sufficiently ample smooth divisor on a connected smooth projective surface is connected, for example by Serre duality and Serre vanishing applied to $0\to A^{-mb}\to\mathcal O_S\to\mathcal O_T\to0$. The chosen curve satisfies the exact scheme-theoretic intersection \begin{equation} T\cap C=m\sum_jz_j. \tag{FN.4} \end{equation} Denote its parameter points over $z_j$ by $t_j\in T(k)$. The points $x,y$ are different from all the $t_j$. The graph of the inclusion $T\hookrightarrow S$ gives a perfect class on $S\times T$. Replace it by its rational Adams-weight-two projection, denoted $\alpha_S$. Its restrictions at $x,y$ are $[\mathcal O_x]$ and $[\mathcal O_y]$. On the smooth surface $C\times T$, refined intersection and (FN.4) give \begin{equation} \alpha_S|_{C\times T} =m\sum_j[\mathcal O_{z_j}]\boxtimes [\mathcal O_{t_j}]. \tag{FN.5} \end{equation} The length-$m$ local intersection is a zero-dimensional sheaf on the regular surface $C\times T$, so its perfect $K_0$ class is exactly $m$ times the residue-field class. On $R\times T$ take the weight-two projection of \[ m\sum_j[\mathcal O_{e_j}]\boxtimes [\mathcal O_{t_j}], \] and call it $\alpha_R$. Transversality of $e_j$ and $C$ shows that its restriction is the right side of (FN.5), and its restrictions at $x,y$ are zero. Rational closed-union descent in positive characteristic, as used in FF and TS, gives the exact Mayer--Vietoris sequence \begin{equation} K_1(C\times T)_{\mathbf Q}\longrightarrow K_0(E\times T)_{\mathbf Q} \longrightarrow K_0(S\times T)_{\mathbf Q}\oplus K_0(R\times T)_{\mathbf Q} \longrightarrow K_0(C\times T)_{\mathbf Q}. \tag{FN.6} \end{equation} Thus $(\alpha_S,\alpha_R)$ has an actual lift. Apply the rational weight-two projector on the projective threefold $E\times T$ to that lift. The gamma dimension bound and the distinct Adams eigenvalues make this a class in $F_\gamma^2K_0(E\times T)_{\mathbf Q}$, with the same component restrictions. Its two fibres therefore give a relation in $J_K(E)$ whose component image is $([x]-[y],0)$. Every degree-zero class on $S$ is generated by such differences with $x,y$ outside $C$. To justify moving the support, take a smooth projective curve through any unwanted point and not contained in $C$, then use Riemann--Roch on that curve to replace its point divisor by a divisor supported in the complementary open set. This uses cycle representatives, not a nonexistent pushforward from the Chow group of an open immersion. \emph{2. Kill the entire double-curve ambiguity by proper families.} At a point parameter, the weight-two part of (FN.6) gives \begin{equation} K_1(C)_{\mathbf Q}^{(2)}\xrightarrow{\delta}S(E) \longrightarrow\mathrm{CH}_0(S)_{\mathbf Q}\oplus \mathrm{CH}_0(R)_{\mathbf Q} \longrightarrow0. \tag{FN.7} \end{equation} The last zero follows from $F_\gamma^2K_0(C)=0$; rational weight projection makes the preceding sequence exact in this weight. We check that the first image is contained in $J_K(E)$. The Gersten sequence on the smooth curve shows that $K_1(C)^{(2)}$ is generated, rationally, by $u[\mathcal O_c]$ with $u\in k^*$ and $c\in C(k)$. Indeed the generic-point $K_1(k(C))$ has weight one, so a weight-two class lies in the point-pushforward subgroup. Write \[ u[\mathcal O_c] =u\bigl([\mathcal O_c]-[\mathcal O_{z_1}]\bigr) +u[\mathcal O_{z_1}]. \] The first summand is the difference of two fibres of an actual Poincare line-bundle family on $C$ with a smooth proper curve parameter. Multiply its rank-zero $K_0$ class by the constant $K_1$ unit $u$, apply the natural Mayer--Vietoris boundary on the whole product, and then apply the weight-two projector on $K_0$ of the product. This produces exactly its boundary as a relation in $J_K(E)$. One may use $C$ itself with the normalized diagonal Poincare line bundle, or a smooth curve in its Jacobian. The second summand is already in the restriction image from $K_1(R)$. In fact the rank-zero line-bundle class $[\mathcal O_R(e_1)]-1$ restricts to $[\mathcal O_C(z_1)]-1=[\mathcal O_{z_1}]$, and multiplying by the constant unit gives the asserted lift. Its boundary in (FN.7) is zero. There are no triple strata in this two-component argument, so no additional compatibility is being suppressed. \emph{3. Take the quotient.} The blow-up formula gives $\mathrm{CH}_0(R)=\mathbf Z$. Step~1 supplies every degree-zero relation on the first component, while Step~2 removes the full kernel of the component map. Degrees themselves are constant in all proper perfect families. Thus (FN.7) proves (FN.2). For an actual exceptional realization satisfying EP, the negative-definite degree matrix in C.3bm makes exceptional pushforwards span both remaining coordinates. EP then gives $B^2(X)_{\mathbf Q}=0$. \emph{Application and limit.} This applies intrinsically to the proposed plane--degree-$q$ surface test whenever its asserted regular resolution has exactly $S$ and $R=\operatorname{Bl}_{C\cap G}\mathbf P^2$ as components: take $A=\mathcal O_S(1)$, $h=H$, and $g=G|_S$, of degree $q+2$. In particular the quintic test has $35$ such points. The argument settles the intrinsic family obstruction for those data. It does not by itself certify the proposed hypersurface resolution or its ampleness, and it is not a proof for arbitrary SNC exceptional surfaces. Blowing up a general double-curve point creates an additional plane component and a triple point; the above two-component Mayer--Vietoris argument cannot simply be reused without checking that new global compatibility.

statement: A quotient of relative $K_2$ in every characteristic.. Let $S=R\oplus I$ be a split square-zero extension of commutative rings. There is a natural surjection \[ \tau:K_2(S,I)\longrightarrow I\otimes_R\Omega^1_{R/\mathbb Z} \] specified, in Weibel's modern Dennis--Stein convention, by \[ \tau\langle m,r\rangle=-m\,d\bar r,\qquad \tau\langle r,m\rangle=m\,d\bar r\qquad(m\in I). \] In particular symbols with both entries in $I$ have zero image. The relative presentation is \citet[Chapter III, Theorem 5.11.1(b), p.~44]{frWeibelKbookIII}. Its hypothesis that $I$ is a radical ideal means that $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical, as in that chapter; a square-zero ideal qualifies. The relation (D1) gives skew symmetry. In (D2), the correction term $rst$ disappears after multiplication by the entry in $I$, or after reduction to $R$, because $I^2=0$. Relation (D3) is the Leibniz rule. For example, if its middle entry is $m\in I$, its two sides map to $mt\,dr$ and $-rm\,dt+m\,d(tr)$, respectively. The cases with the first or third entry in $I$ give the same rule; multiple entries in $I$ give zero. Thus all relations hold, and the elements $m\,dr$ show surjectivity. This is the negative of the map in Weibel's Exercise 5.14(a). It gives the positive Steinberg normalization \[ \tau\{1+tc,u\}=tc\,d\log u. \] In characteristic two we claim a quotient, not an isomorphism. No surjectivity on sheaf cohomology follows merely from this local surjection. Naturality and homogeneity in $I$ make the map glue when $I=L$ is a line bundle. For a perfect field of positive characteristic, the resulting target is $L\otimes\Omega^1_{V/k}$.

statement: Auxiliary lemma (proved here): the codimension-three exceptional boundary in dimension seven.. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of arbitrary characteristic, let $W_1,W_2$ be smooth cubic surfaces over $k$, and put $a=c_1(\mathcal O_{W_1}(1))$ and $b=c_1(\mathcal O_{W_2}(1))$. statement: Endpoint lifting through regular surface families (audited auxiliary theorem).. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>0$. Let $R$ be an excellent henselian local $k$-algebra with residue field $k$, obtained by strict localization of a finite-type $k$-scheme. Let $Z\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ be a regular projective threefold, an isomorphism outside the closed point. Suppose its reduced closed fibre $E$ is a simple normal crossing divisor, and that there is an effective Cartier divisor $D$ supported on all of $E$ such that $\mathcal O_D(-D)$ is ample. The scheme $D$ may be nonreduced. Let $P/k$ be a smooth connected projective curve, and fix two points $o,t\in P(k)$. Put $T=D\times P$. For every $\beta\in F_\gamma^2K_0(T)_{\mathbf Q}$ there is an actual class $b\in K_0(Z\times P)_{\mathbf Q}$ satisfying \begin{equation} (b|_{Z\times\{u\}})|_E =(\beta|_{D\times\{u\}})|_E\quad(u=o,t). \tag{EL.1} \end{equation} Here $K_0$ is the group of perfect complexes, and $F_\gamma$ is its vector-bundle gamma filtration. No equality over the entire family $E\times P$ is asserted. This is an endpoint theorem on a fixed proper parameter curve, not a general specialization theorem for vector bundles or $K$-theory. \emph{1. Perfect classes modulo the third gamma filtration.} The schemes $D$, $E$, and $T$ are projective over $k$, so they have the resolution property. To justify this also for the nonreduced $D$, some power $\mathfrak m^M$ annihilates $\mathcal O_D$; the Artinian local ring $R/\mathfrak m^M$ is finite-dimensional over the given coefficient field $k$. Projectivity over this finite $k$-algebra gives projectivity over $k$. Their perfect $K_0$ is the vector-bundle $K_0$, with its special lambda-ring structure. For a noetherian quasi-projective scheme of dimension $d$, the dimension theorem is \begin{equation} F_\gamma^{d+1}K_0=0. \tag{EL.2} \end{equation} We use its actual singular-scheme scope, not a regular-scheme substitute: see \citet[Chapter II, Remark 8.8.5, p.~83] {D_Weibel2013KbookII}, which cites SGA~6, VI.6.6. In particular $F_\gamma^3K_0(E)=0$. A representation of $\beta$ modulo $F_\gamma^3K_0(T)_{\mathbf Q}$ therefore gives its exact restrictions at both endpoints after further pullback to $E$. We give a perfect-complex representation retaining classes in the kernel of the Cartan map. Modulo $F_\gamma^3$, $F_\gamma^2$ is generated by $\gamma^2(v)$ and products $v w$, for rank-zero classes $v,w$. Every such $v$ can be written $[A]-[B]$, with $A,B$ of the same rank and sufficiently generated first jets on every smooth stratum used below. Indeed, if $L$ is very ample and $V$ is any vector bundle, choose $m$ with $V^\vee\otimes L^m$ globally generated. Dualizing a generating surjection and tensoring by $L^m$ gives \[ 0\longrightarrow V\longrightarrow (L^m)^N \longrightarrow Q\otimes L^m\longrightarrow0, \] where $Q$ is globally generated. Taking $m$ still larger supplies first jets: products of generating sections of $Q$ and first-jet generators of $L^m$ generate all first jets of $Q\otimes L^m$. Apply this to finitely many bundles and add the same positive bundle to both sides if necessary. Their determinants can likewise be made very ample. The universal identities give, modulo $F_\gamma^3$, \[ \gamma^2([A]-[B]) =\gamma^2([A]-n)-\gamma^2([B]-n) -(\det A-1)(\det B-1)+(\det B-1)^2. \] Here a line bundle denotes its $K_0$ class. The equality follows from the special lambda-ring identities and $([A]-n)\equiv\det A-1\pmod {F_\gamma^2}$; it is valid in every characteristic. Products of arbitrary line differences can be written, modulo $F_\gamma^3$, using differences of positive line bundles. Thus it suffices to treat second gamma classes of these generated bundles and products of two positive line differences. For a rank-$n$ bundle $A$ choose a general homomorphism $\mathcal O_T^{n-1}\to A$. The locus of rank at most $n-3$ has expected codimension six and is empty. The rank-$n-2$ locus $C$ has codimension two and is a regular immersion. Locally an invertible $(n-2)$-minor reduces the map to an identity block and a column $(a,b)$; the pair $a,b$ is a regular sequence. Its Koszul sequence is the local verification of the global exact sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_T^{n-1}\longrightarrow A \longrightarrow I_C\otimes\det A\longrightarrow0. \] Consequently \begin{equation} [\mathcal O_C] =1-[A\otimes(\det A)^{-1}]+(n-1)[(\det A)^{-1}] \equiv\gamma^2([A]-n)\pmod {F_\gamma^3}. \tag{EL.3} \end{equation} The equality is in perfect $K_0(T)$. It is not merely an equality of ordinary cycles on the singular threefold $T$. The congruence also follows from the exact universal identity $\det A-[A]+n-1=\sum_{j=2}^n\gamma^j([A]-n)$: divide by $\det A$, whose difference from $1$ belongs to $F_\gamma^1$. The identity itself follows after the injective flag-bundle splitting principle by expanding the product of line roots. Products of positive line differences are represented modulo $F_\gamma^3$ by the perfect Koszul classes of general complete intersections of two sections. Hence $\beta$, modulo $F_\gamma^3$, is a finite rational linear combination of such $[\mathcal O_C]$. The choices can satisfy all the following additional conditions simultaneously. The reduced curve meets each component stratum $E_i\times P$ transversely; it meets each double stratum in finitely many transverse points; it avoids all triple strata; and its fibres over $o,t$ are finite regular immersions of codimension two in $D$. The full curve $C$ need not be flat over every point of $P$; only these two selected fibres will be used in the endpoint identity. These are characteristic-free first-jet incidence conditions. On a smooth stratum of dimension $d$, rank drop by one has codimension two, and failure of transversality at that rank has total codimension at least $d+1$. Deeper rank drop has codimension six. First-jet generation makes these the actual incidence codimensions. Apply this also to the component and intersection strata in the two endpoint fibres. The corresponding bad sets have images whose closures are proper in the finite-dimensional parameter space, so their finite union is avoidable over the infinite field $k$. The same argument for two sections handles complete intersections. Since $D$ is Cartier in a regular scheme, it is Cohen--Macaulay; transversality on its reduced strata makes the two local equations a regular sequence also on $D$, with its given multiplicities. \emph{2. Put each perfect curve on an actual regular surface family.} Fix one of these curves $C\subset T$. Choose a sufficiently high power $\mathcal A$ of a line bundle on $Z\times P$ ample relative to $\operatorname{Spec}R$. It can be taken as an exterior product of a relatively ample bundle on $Z$ and an ample bundle on $P$. Serre vanishing makes $I_C\mathcal A|_T$ generated, and makes its global sections surject onto the sections of $(I_C/I_C^2)\mathcal A|_C$. The latter is a rank-two bundle on the one-dimensional scheme $C$. A general section is nowhere zero on $C_{\mathrm{red}}$: the zero condition has codimension two over a space of dimension one. Choose such a section, general also away from $C$, and let $H$ be its zero scheme in $T$. Then $C$ is an effective Cartier divisor on $H$. Locally, the chosen equation is a linear combination of the regular-sequence generators $a,b$ with one coefficient a unit, so the complementary generator defines $C$ in $H$. Choose the section transverse to every reduced normal-crossing stratum away from $C$. Along $C$, the first-jet transversality in Step~1 and the nowhere-zero conormal combination give a nonzero ambient differential. This includes the finitely many double stratum intersections; triple strata were avoided by $C$. In addition, the section can be required not to vanish identically on any surface $E_i\times\{v\}$, for every $v\in P$. For a high twist the space of its restrictions on each such surface has dimension at least two, uniformly in $v$: take a generator of a first twisted ideal that is nonzero on the surface and multiply it by two independent restrictions from a further very ample factor. The condition of being zero on that surface has codimension at least two; the parameter $v$ contributes only one dimension. The incidence union is therefore a proper subset. This makes $H\to P$ a projective flat family of curves, with the indicated multiplicities allowed. Flatness follows from the fibrewise nonzerodivisor criterion for the Cartier equation on the Cohen--Macaulay scheme $D\times P$. Relative Serre vanishing on $Z\times P$ gives the surjection \[ H^0(Z\times P,\mathcal A)\longrightarrow H^0(T,\mathcal A|_T) \] from $H^1(\mathcal A(-D\times P))=0$. Lift the chosen equation, and let $W\subset Z\times P$ be its zero divisor. The source $W$ is regular along its closed fibre: this is exactly the nonzero ambient differential just imposed on every reduced stratum of $E\times P$. It is regular everywhere. Indeed its nonregular locus is closed, since the schemes are excellent, and its proper image in the local scheme $\operatorname{Spec}R$ would contain the closed point if it were nonempty. Its intersection with that fibre is empty. The same fibrewise nonzerodivisor criterion gives $W\to P$ flat: on every parameter fibre its equation is nonzero on every regular component of $Z$. Every such component meets the closed fibre by properness, and the equation was required not to vanish identically on any of its exceptional surface components. Thus it is a nonzerodivisor on every fibre of the flat morphism $Z\times P\to P$. We have constructed the actual fixed subscheme \[ W\subset Z\times P,\qquad H=W\cap(D\times P), \] proper over $R$, with $C$ Cartier on $H$. All finite first-jet and section choices may equivalently be made after descending to one pointed etale finite-type model of $Z$ and then pulling back; no Bertini statement for an unspecified non-finite-type variety is being assumed. The only use of relative Serre vanishing here is its usual projective form \citep[Lemma 30.17.1]{frC3azStacksSerre}. \emph{3. One finite power lifts the whole line bundle on $H$.} Put $J=\mathcal O_W(-D\times P)$ and $L=J|_H$. This is ample on every fibre of the projective morphism $H\to P$, since $\mathcal O_D(-D)$ is ample. Relative Serre vanishing therefore gives $R^i(H\to P)_*L^n=0$ for $i>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$. As $P$ is a curve, the Leray sequence gives \begin{equation} H^2(H,L^n)=0\quad(n\gg0). \tag{EL.4} \end{equation} We do not assert that $H^1(H,L^n)$ vanishes. Start with $Q_0=\mathcal O_H(-C)$. For the thickenings $H_n=V(J^n)\subset W$, the obstruction to extending a line bundle from $H_n$ to $H_{n+1}$ lies in $H^2(H,L^n)$, by the square-zero unit sequence\citep[Lemma 37.4.1]{frC3azStacksPicThickening}. These groups are killed by $p$. At each of the finitely many steps before (EL.4) applies, raise the current partial bundle and all its preceding restrictions to the $p$th tensor power before extending. After a finite number $e$ of such steps, there is a compatible system on every $H_n$ restricting to $Q_0^{p^e}$ on $H$. Subsequent obstruction groups vanish, so the exponent never increases again. No uniform Frobenius bound for arbitrary vector bundles is used. The ideals $J$ and $\mathfrak m\mathcal O_W$ have the same radical and cofinal powers. Projective Grothendieck existence algebraizes this formal line bundle on $W_{\widehat R}$ \citep[Lemma 30.24.3]{frC3azStacksExistence}; algebraizing its inverse and using full faithfulness verifies invertibility. The regular completion map $R\to\widehat R$ is a filtered colimit of smooth $R$-algebras by Popescu \citep[Lemma 15.51.14; Theorem 16.12.1] {frC3azStacksCompletion,frC3azStacksPopescu}. The algebraized bundle descends to one such algebra by finite presentation\citep[Lemma 32.10.3(2)]{frC3azStacksLimitBundles}. Choose $M$ with $\mathfrak m^M\mathcal O_W\subset J$. The descended algebra's map to $\widehat R/\mathfrak m^M=R/\mathfrak m^M$ lifts to $R$, since $(R,\mathfrak m^M)$ is a henselian pair and the algebra is smooth\citep[Lemma 15.13.3]{frC3azStacksHenselSmooth}. The resulting actual line bundle $Q$ on the fixed $W$ satisfies \begin{equation} Q|_H\simeq Q_0^{p^e}. \tag{EL.5} \end{equation} Matching this finite quotient preserves the whole proper parameter curve and the entire first thickening $H$, not just two pointwise Picard classes. \emph{4. Exact endpoint equality, without a filtration pushforward.} Let $j:W\hookrightarrow Z\times P$. This is a regular Cartier immersion, so \[ b_C=j_*(1-[Q]) \] is an actual perfect class. Fix $u=o$ or $t$. All intersections with the parameter fibre and with $D$ are Tor independent by the flatness and regular-sequence conditions already imposed. Thus restriction to $D\times\{u\}$ is \[ (j_{H_u})_*\bigl(1-[\mathcal O_{H_u}(-p^e C_u)]\bigr). \] The scheme $C_u$ is finite over $k$. Every line bundle on a finite Artinian $k$-scheme is trivial. The Cartier sequence and the geometric-series identity therefore give, in perfect $K_0(D)$, \begin{align*} (j_{H_u})_*(1-[Q_{0,u}]^{p^e}) &=\sum_{a=0}^{p^e-1}(j_{H_u})_* \bigl([\mathcal O_{C_u}]\,[Q_{0,u}]^a\bigr)\\ &=p^e[\mathcal O_{C_u}]. \end{align*} This is exact; no compatibility of a singular pushforward with the gamma filtration has been assumed. Pull back further to $E$. Dividing $b_C$ by $p^e$ and adding the finite rational combination of Step~1 gives (EL.1), since the omitted $F_\gamma^3$ part vanishes on both copies of $E$ by (EL.2). This proves the endpoint theorem.

statement: Remaining work for C.1.. We have rigorously deduced the quintic refutations from the opened Clemens theorem, proved the exact divisor criterion, and classified the universal truth of $A$ in every $(n,i)$ over $\mathbb C$ by C.1f. C.1g supplies the full line argument and a specified geometric generic counterexample, also sufficient for C.1f without the stronger infinite-dimensional input. C.1h--i give the exact geometric-generic Gysin image and classify all the universal $A',A''$ cases in their stated range, with explicit complete-intersection counterexamples. C.1j identifies the exact primitive Griffiths-kernel obstruction to $B$; C.1k classifies universal cycle-class injectivity, equality with numerical equivalence, and finite generation. C.1l--m give explicit nonzero radicals, including a specified geometric generic plane-quartic surface example, and classify universal finite semisimplicity of the correspondence algebra: precisely dimensions zero and one. C.1n identifies the remaining endpoint image criterion with the universal standard conjecture $D_{\mathbb C}$, even if the target is restricted to projective space. C.1o identifies universal $B$ with the precise shifted Lefschetz injectivity on Griffiths groups, and gives unconditional threefold stabilizations. C.1p identifies the corresponding abelian test with vanishing of the nonpositive Beauville pieces of the Griffiths quotient, including the exact first fourfold and fivefold tests. Its image therefore lies in $K_{\leq1}$, proving the stated consequence for every parameter $P$.

statement: Henselian point parameters and the remaining family obstruction.. If $R$ is henselian, then \begin{equation} K_0(Z)[1/p]\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }K_0(E)[1/p]. \tag{FF.4} \end{equation} Indeed, \citet[Theorem 3.7 and Remark (ii), author p.~8] {frDrinfeld2004Tate} proves $K_{-1}(R)=0$ for every commutative henselian local ring. This gives surjectivity by (FF.1). For injectivity, we use the preceding exact sequence with $P=\operatorname{Spec}k$. The homomorphism $K_0(R)\to K_0(k)$ is the rank isomorphism $\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Z$, so the image of $K_0(R)[1/p]$ in $K_0(Z)[1/p]\oplus\mathbf Z[1/p]$ is the diagonal graph of the unit class. Its intersection with $K_0(Z)[1/p]\oplus0$ is zero. This proves injectivity directly from exactness. In particular every individual proposed coefficient class $\kappa\cdot u$ in $K_0(E)[1/p]$ lifts. The scheme $\operatorname{Spec}R\times_kP$ for a positive-dimensional proper parameter $P$ is not henselian local; Drinfeld's theorem does not dispose of its group in (FF.1). For the tetrahedral regular modification constructed separately in (TG.1)--(TG.5), the whole-diagram calculation (TS.1)--(TS.4) identifies the dual-complex coefficient in the indicated ordinary $K$-group. Formula (FF.3) gives the exact obstruction for lifting its entire proper-curve family. Neither the nonvanishing of $\partial\kappa$ nor the existence of a proper-curve $K_2$ relation proves that its product in (FF.3) is nonzero or zero. We assert neither outcome. In particular (FF.1) does not imply family surjectivity merely from nilinvariance on every finite thickening. The pointwise isomorphism (FF.4) does not settle a rational ordinary-Chow gate. A separate endpoint argument may produce an actual family with the same two endpoint restrictions without lifting the originally prescribed class over the whole parameter; that conclusion would not assert the vanishing of (FF.3).

statement: Auxiliary lemma (proved here; awaiting independent audit): the relative Milnor differential quotient in every characteristic.. Let $k$ be a field, let $V/k$ be smooth, and let $V\hookrightarrow E$ be a square-zero thickening over $k$ whose ideal $I$ is an invertible $\mathcal O_V$-module. We use the Zariski sheaf of ordinary Milnor symbols: on a ring it is the tensor algebra of the group of units, modulo the two-sided ideal generated by $u\otimes(1-u)$ whenever both entries are units. Write \[ \mathcal J_r=\ker\bigl(\mathcal K_r^M(E)\longrightarrow \mathcal K_r^M(V)\bigr),\qquad r\geq1. \] Then this map is surjective, and there is a canonical surjective homomorphism of sheaves of abelian groups \[ \tau_r:\mathcal J_r\longrightarrow I\otimes_{\mathcal O_V}\Omega^{r-1}_{V/k}. \tag{RM.1} \] Its normalization is \[ \tau_r\{1+i,u_2,\ldots,u_r\} =i\otimes d\log\bar u_2\wedge\cdots\wedge d\log\bar u_r. \tag{RM.2} \] It is independent of a local algebra splitting or a local generator of $I$. If $k$ has characteristic $p>0$, then $p\mathcal J_r=0$, including when $p=2$. We assert a quotient, not an isomorphism.

statement: Auxiliary proposition (proved here; pending independent audit): the primitive relative Milnor invariant kills the entire exceptional image.. Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $p>0$, let $s\geq1$ and $m\geq0$, and put $r=s+1$. Let $W_1,\ldots,W_s$ be smooth cubic surfaces, $A_i=\mathcal O_{W_i}(1)=-K_{W_i}$, and let $C/k$ be a smooth projective connected curve of genus at least two. Set \[ \begin{gathered} T=\mathbb P^m\times\prod_{i=1}^sW_i, \qquad L_T=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^m}(1)\boxtimes A_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes A_s, \qquad b=c_1(L_T),\\ V=T\times C,\qquad L=L_T\boxtimes K_C. \end{gathered} \tag{PB.1} \] Suppose $R$ is an excellent henselian local $k$-algebra obtained by strict henselization from an algebraic local $k$-scheme, and $\mathcal Z\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is projective and regular. Suppose that its closed fibre is the smooth Cartier divisor $i:V\hookrightarrow\mathcal Z$, that \[ \mathfrak m_R\mathcal O_{\mathcal Z}=I_V, \qquad I_V/I_V^2=L, \qquad q:\mathcal Z\longrightarrow T, \quad q|_V=\operatorname{pr}_T. \tag{PB.2} \] Write $E=V_2$ and $X=\mathcal Z\setminus V$. We require the given scheme and morphism to descend to the algebraic local model, as they do in the total-line construction of C.3bj. Every finite list of line bundles and Chow relations used below can then be considered on one smooth finite-type model after a pointed etale base change. Define the following direct K\"unneth summand: \[ \mathcal M_k= H^0(\mathbb P^m,\mathcal O(1))\otimes_k \bigotimes_{i=1}^s H^1(W_i,A_i\otimes\Omega^1_{W_i/k}) \otimes_k H^1(C,K_C) \subset H^r(V,L\otimes\Omega^s_{V/k}). \tag{PB.3} \] Let $P$ be the projection onto this summand, with the indicated order of the cubic factors. If $\mathcal A$ is a line bundle on $\mathcal Z$ trivialized on $V$, write $a\in H^1(V,L)$ for its first relative jet. For $D_i\in\operatorname{Pic}(W_i)$ form the actual Chow class \[ \beta=c_1(\mathcal A)\prod_{i=1}^s c_1(q^*D_i) \in\mathrm{CH}^{r}(\mathcal Z). \tag{PB.4} \] Here $q^*D_i$ abbreviates pullback through the $i$th projection of $T$. If \[ P\left(a\smile\prod_i d\log D_i\right)\ne0, \tag{PB.5} \] then $\beta|_X\ne0$ integrally. More precisely, the projected relative Milnor invariant in (PB.5) vanishes on every exceptional class $i_*\gamma$ whose restriction to $V$ is zero. We do not assert that all Hodge components of every exceptional class vanish.

statement: Auxiliary reduction (proved here): the exact Smith-lattice kernel.. Let $s\ge1$, $m\ge0$ and \[ T=\mathbb P^m\times\prod_{i=1}^sW_i, \qquad A_q=\mathrm{CH}^q(T),\qquad b=h+\sum_i a_i, \] where the $W_i$ are smooth cubic surfaces and $a_i$ their anticanonical classes. statement: Independent degree-two Dennis--Stein check.. There is also a direct degree-two check in relative Quillen $K$-theory. For $I^2=0$, the Dennis--Stein presentation of \citet[Chapter III, Definition 5.11, p.~43, and Theorem 5.11.1(b), p.~44]{frWeibelKbookIII} gives \[ \langle i,r\rangle+\langle j,r\rangle =\langle i+j,r\rangle \quad(i,j\in I). \] Here (D1) changes the entries and (D2) adds them; its correction term $rij$ is zero. Thus $pK_2(B,I)=0$ when $pI=0$. The natural homomorphism \[ \langle i,r\rangle\longmapsto-i\otimes d\bar r, \qquad \langle r,i\rangle\longmapsto+i\otimes d\bar r \tag{RM.6} \] respects (D1)--(D3), including all possible placements of an entry in $I$: (D2) is additivity and (D3) is the Leibniz identity. For example, with $s\in I$, (D3) becomes \[ st\,d\bar r=-rs\,d\bar t+s\,d(\bar t\bar r). \] This is the negative of the Dennis--Stein map in Weibel's Exercise 5.14(a), pp.~46--47; the sign makes $\{1+i,u\}\mapsto i\,d\log\bar u$, agreeing with (RM.2). Nilpotent ideals are contained in the Jacobson radical, as required by the term ``radical ideal'' in that presentation. This check is separate from the Milnor proof and is not needed to infer the nonreduced sheaf comparison.

statement: Compatibility with an actual product of line bundles.. Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal D$ be line bundles on $E$, and fix an isomorphism $\mathcal A|_V\simeq\mathcal O_V$. Choose local trivializations respecting it. The transition functions of $\mathcal A$ are $1+a_{ij}$, defining $a\in H^1(V,I)$, and let $g_{ij}$ be those of $\mathcal D$. The symbol cocycle \[ \{1+a_{ij},g_{jk}\} \] defines a relative class $\xi\in H^2(V,\mathcal J_2)$. Its image in $H^2(E,\mathcal K_2^M)$ is the ordinary cup product of the two line-bundle classes. Applying (RM.2) gives exactly \[ H^2(\tau_2)(\xi) =a\smile d\log(\mathcal D|_V) \quad\text{in }H^2(V,I\otimes\Omega^1_{V/k}). \tag{RM.5} \] This follows on the displayed cocycles and is independent of their trivializations. In characteristic $p$, if $H^1(V,\mathcal K_2^M)$ is $p$-divisible, the exact sheaf sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal J_2\longrightarrow\mathcal K_2^M(E) \longrightarrow\mathcal K_2^M(V)\longrightarrow0 \] shows that $H^2(V,\mathcal J_2)\to H^2(E,\mathcal K_2^M)$ is injective: its kernel is the image of a $p$-divisible group in a group killed by $p$. A nonzero right side of (RM.5) therefore detects the nonzero absolute product. This statement uses no comparison between Milnor and Quillen $K$-theory on the nonreduced $E$. The same calculation applies to an actual product of $r$ line bundles, with the first one trivialized on $V$. If the remaining bundles are $\mathcal D_2,\ldots,\mathcal D_r$, their transition symbols give $\xi_r\in H^r(V,\mathcal J_r)$ with \[ H^r(\tau_r)(\xi_r)= a\smile d\log(\mathcal D_2|_V)\smile\cdots\smile d\log(\mathcal D_r|_V) \quad\text{in }H^r(V,I\otimes\Omega^{r-1}_{V/k}). \tag{RM.7} \] If $H^{r-1}(V,\mathcal K_r^M)$ is $p$-divisible, then $H^r(V,\mathcal J_r)\to H^r(E,\mathcal K_r^M)$ is injective by the identical long-exact-sequence argument. No acyclicity of the chosen cover for $\mathcal J_r$ is required: the symbol cocycle maps canonically from \v Cech cohomology to sheaf cohomology, and its image under $H^r(\tau_r)$ is the displayed coherent cup product.

statement: The remaining low-dimensional cases.. The strongest bounds established in this contribution are now \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c} \dim A & \text{proved bound for }s_J(A) &\text{possible residual primes here}\\\hline 2 & \gcd(2,\delta(A)) & 2\\ 3 & \gcd(6,\delta(A)) & 2,3. \end{array} \] Thus the earlier possible prime three for surfaces and prime five for threefolds have been removed. Likewise, the evenness theorem for very general principally polarized fourfolds does not decide the remaining nonprincipal surface cases. These distinctions are essential to the exact integral question.
