statement: C.3ae (Refuted, with an explicit counterexample): ordinary $J^2$ restriction is not surjective in every dimension at least seven.. For every $N\ge7$ we specify an excellent normal strictly henselian local complex ring $R$ of dimension $N$, with regular puncture $X$ and regular punctured principal divisor $Y$, for which there is a surjection \begin{equation} \operatorname{coker}\!\left( \mathrm{CH}^2(X)_{\mathrm{alg}} \longrightarrow\mathrm{CH}^2(Y)_{\mathrm{alg}}\right) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}^0(C)(\mathbb C), \qquad C:\ z_0^4+z_1^4+z_2^4=0. \end{equation} Here the algebraically trivial groups use actual families on the fixed scheme times a smooth connected parameter curve. Consequently the ordinary rational map $J^2(X)\to J^2(Y)$ is not surjective. The argument concerns these ordinary groups; it does not assert that every cycle on $X$ is annihilated by the invariant constructed below. \emph{1. The coefficients and the algebraic local scheme.} Put $m=N-4\ge3$, and let \[ W=V(w_0^4+w_1^4+w_2^4+w_3^4)\subset\mathbb P^3, \qquad S=W\times C, \qquad M=\mathcal O_W(1)\boxtimes K_C. \] Write $A_i=(a_{ijk})_{0\le j\le3,\,0\le k\le2}$ for the following four integer matrices: \[ \begin{aligned} A_0&=\begin{pmatrix}-3&-5&5\\-3&-5&-2\\-5&3&-3\\5&1&-3\end{pmatrix},& A_1&=\begin{pmatrix}-4&4&-1\\3&5&2\\-5&0&-1\\0&2&-5\end{pmatrix},\\[2mm] A_2&=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&-1\\0&-2&4\\-1&1&-4\\-5&-1&-3\end{pmatrix},& A_3&=\begin{pmatrix}0&-4&1\\-5&-4&-4\\-1&5&1\\4&2&5\end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} \] Define \[ s_i(w,z)=\sum_{j=0}^3\sum_{k=0}^2a_{ijk}w_jz_k, \qquad \ell(x,w,z)=\sum_{i=0}^3x_i s_i(w,z), \qquad G(z)=z_0^2z_1^2+z_0^2z_2^2+z_1^2z_2^2. \] For $i>3$ we set $s_i=0$. The four $s_i$ have no common zero on $S$. This is an exact finite verification: over $\mathbb F_{101}$, in each of the twelve affine charts $w_j=z_k=1$, the ideal generated by the two Fermat equations and the four $s_i$ has Groebner basis $[1]$. The common-zero scheme is projective over $\mathbb Z$, so its image in $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ is closed. A nonempty generic fibre would force that image to contain every prime, contrary to the computation at $101$. Thus this particular integer tuple, without a generic-coefficient qualification, is base point free over $\mathbb C$. Set \[ B=\mathbb P^m_x\times W\times\mathbb P^2_z, \qquad \mathcal N=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^m}(-1) \boxtimes\mathcal O_W(-1)\boxtimes\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(-1), \qquad T_B=\operatorname{Tot}(\mathcal N). \] If $t$ is the tautological fibre vector, define the hypersurface \[ Z=V(F+t\ell G)\subset T_B, \qquad F=z_0^4+z_1^4+z_2^4. \] Its zero-section divisor is \[ V=\mathbb P^m\times W\times C, \qquad N_{V/Z}=L^{-1}, \qquad L=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^m}(1)\boxtimes M. \] The expression defining $Z$ is a section of the pullback of $\mathcal O_B(0,0,4)$, so the definition is independent of trivializations. The nonzero differential $dF$ makes $Z$ smooth near $V$. On $\ell G\ne0$ it is the graph $t=-F/(\ell G)$. The locus $F=\ell G=0$ has codimension two in $B$ and produces no additional component of the hypersurface. It is a Cartier hypersurface in a regular scheme, hence Cohen--Macaulay, and it is generically reduced on the graph. It follows that $Z$ is integral. Contract the zero section of $T_B$ by the Segre coordinates \[ y_{ijk}=t x_iw_jz_k. \] This is a proper morphism to the affine cone of the indicated Segre embedding, and it is an isomorphism off the zero section. Let $Q$ be the reduced closed image of $Z$, let $Q^{\mathrm n}$ be its finite normalization, and let $v^{\mathrm n}$ be the point over the cone vertex. This point is unique: after shrinking around the vertex, the smooth proper birational model $Z$ factors through the normalization and is surjective; its connected exceptional fibre $V$ cannot map onto more than one point of the finite normalization fibre. Define \[ R=\mathcal O_{Q^{\mathrm n},v^{\mathrm n}}^{\mathrm{sh}}. \] This specifies $R$ by the displayed integer equations, closed image, normalization, and strict henselization. As in C.3m, properness allows us to shrink only to prove regularity of the model; this shrinking makes no change to $R$. Write $\mathcal Z\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ for the resulting projective regular model. Its exceptional fibre is $V$, and $X=\mathcal Z\setminus V$ is the regular puncture of $\operatorname{Spec}R$. The ring has dimension $m+4=N$ and is excellent and normal. Pointed etale base change and its limit preserve these assertions and the first infinitesimal neighbourhood of $V$. More explicitly, the $y_{ijk}$ generate $(t)$ on each Segre chart, while every extra normalization function in the maximal ideal vanishes on the reduced fibre. Thus $\mathfrak m_R\mathcal O_{\mathcal Z}=\mathcal I_V$, as in C.3m; the quotients by the squares of these ideals are unchanged by a pointed etale extension with the same residue field. The nonzero nonunit \[ f=\sum_{i,j,k}a_{ijk}y_{ijk} \] pulls back to $t\ell$. Its strict transform is $D=V(F,\ell)\subset T_B$, the total space of $L_H^{-1}$ over \[ H=V(\ell)\subset V, \qquad L_H=L|_H. \] The surjection $\mathcal O_S^{m+1}\to M$ with entries $s_i$ has a rank-$m$ vector-bundle kernel $E$, and \[ H=\mathbb P_{\mathrm{lines}}(E), \qquad c_1(L_H)=h+a, \qquad a=c_1(M),\quad h=c_1(\mathcal O_H(1)). \] Thus $H$ and $D$ are smooth. Their corresponding base change $\mathcal D\subset\mathcal Z$ is regular, and $Y=\mathcal D\setminus H=X\cap V(f)$ is the required regular punctured divisor. The divisors $V$ and $\mathcal D$ intersect transversely in $H$. \emph{2. A cycle invariant, with its family compatibility.} Fix $\eta\in\overline{\mathbb Q}$ with $\eta^4=-1$ and the line \[ D_W=V(w_0-\eta w_1,\,w_2-\eta w_3)\subset W. \] Writing $H_W=c_1(\mathcal O_W(1))$, put $\tau=4[D_W]-H_W$. Adjunction and the degree of the line give \begin{equation} H_W^2=4,\qquad H_W[D_W]=1,\qquad [D_W]^2=-2, \qquad \tau H_W=0,\qquad \tau[D_W]=-9. \end{equation} For a smooth projective parameter $P$, Chow localization and refined pullback along $H\times P\subset\mathcal D\times P$ define a homomorphism \[ \sigma_P:\mathrm{CH}^2(Y\times P) \longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{CH}^2(H\times P)} {(h+a)\mathrm{CH}^1(H\times P)}. \] Indeed we lift a class to $\mathrm{CH}^2(\mathcal D\times P)$ and pull back. Two lifts differ by the pushforward of a class in $\mathrm{CH}^1(H\times P)$, and the self-intersection formula makes their pullbacks differ by $c_1(N_{H/\mathcal D})=-(h+a)$ times that class. This proves independence, including for rational-equivalence witnesses. These are the same localization and self-intersection operations used in C.3e. Since $\operatorname{rank}E=m\ge3$, the first projective-bundle relation has degree at least three. Consequently evaluation at $h=-a$ gives an integral isomorphism \begin{equation} \frac{\mathrm{CH}^2(H\times P)} {(h+a)\mathrm{CH}^1(H\times P)} \simeq \mathrm{CH}^2(S\times P). \end{equation} Intersect the right side with $\operatorname{pr}_W^*\tau$ and push forward along $W$. We obtain \begin{equation} \rho_P:\mathrm{CH}^2(Y\times P) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}^1(C\times P) =\operatorname{Pic}(C\times P). \end{equation} All the operations commute with refined pullback to a point of $P$. For example, a lift chosen before taking the fibre is still a valid lift after taking it, and refined pullbacks commute. Hence $\rho=\rho_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C}$ sends ordinary algebraic-equivalence differences to $\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)(\mathbb C)$. If $\Gamma\in\mathrm{CH}^2(X\times P)$ and $\widetilde\Gamma$ is a closure on $\mathcal Z\times P$, write its refined restriction to $V\times P$ as \[ b=b_0+h b_1+h^2 b_2, \qquad b_i\in\mathrm{CH}^{2-i}(S\times P). \] Transverse refined pullback to $H$ and \eqref{eq:C3ae-evaluation} give the exact formula \begin{equation} \rho_P(\Gamma|_{Y\times P}) =\operatorname{pr}_{C\times P,*} \bigl(\tau(b_0-a b_1+a^2b_2)\bigr). \end{equation} There is no presumed extension of a cycle over a varying etale neighbourhood in this formula: the parameter $P$ is fixed, and the closure is on the fixed proper model $\mathcal Z\times P$. \emph{3. The first-neighbourhood obstruction for a cycle class.} We give the required Chern-class argument explicitly. All differential sheaves in this argument are relative to $\mathbb C$. Let $V_2\subset\mathcal Z$ be defined by $\mathcal I_V^2$. Its square-zero ideal is $L$, and its class is $\kappa\in H^1(V,T_V\otimes L)$. For any smooth projective $P$, the conormal sequence of $V\times P$ in $\mathcal Z\times P$ and its second exterior power are \[ \begin{gathered} 0\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow \Omega^1_{\mathcal Z\times P}|_{V\times P} \longrightarrow\Omega^1_{V\times P}\longrightarrow0,\\ 0\longrightarrow L\otimes\Omega^1_{V\times P} \longrightarrow\Omega^2_{\mathcal Z\times P}|_{V\times P} \longrightarrow\Omega^2_{V\times P}\longrightarrow0. \end{gathered} \] The second sequence is exact because the kernel of the first has rank one. Its cohomology boundary is contraction with $\kappa$. This can be checked by taking local splittings of the first sequence: their differences are derivations representing $\kappa$, and the induced difference on a two-form is contraction in either factor with the usual alternating sign. For a vector bundle on $\mathcal Z\times P$, its Hodge Chern character restricts through the middle term of the second sequence. Concretely, on a trivializing cover the matrices $g_{uv}^{-1}dg_{uv}$ represent the Atiyah class, and $\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{At}^2)$ represents its degree-two Chern character. These matrices are defined before restriction, so their trace cup products give the asserted lift. The formula is compatible with direct sums and exact sequences; on a flag bundle it reduces to $\tfrac12\sum c_1(L_i)^2$, which identifies it with the usual Hodge realization of the Chow Chern character. Thus it also applies to virtual vector bundles and rational combinations. For our closure class we may choose such a rational virtual bundle whose degree-two Chow Chern character is $\widetilde\Gamma$. Precisely, the regular scheme $\mathcal Z\times P$ is finite dimensional, has affine diagonal and an ample invertible sheaf, and the rational Chern character is an isomorphism onto its Chow group \citep[Lemma 42.58.1, Tag 0FEY]{cyStacksChernObstruction}. One may equally descend this finite collection of cycles, bundles and maps to a pointed etale neighbourhood and work on a smooth finite-type complex model; its restriction to $V_2\times P$ is the same. Naturality of Chern classes under refined pullback \citep[Remark 42.59.9, Tag 0FF8]{cyStacksChernObstruction} therefore gives \begin{equation} \kappa\mathbin{\lrcorner}\operatorname{cl}_{\mathrm{Hdg}}(b) =0 \quad\hbox{in }H^3(V\times P,L\otimes\Omega^1_{V\times P}). \end{equation} Only this necessary vanishing is used. We make no converse assertion about deforming cycles from their Hodge classes. The class $\kappa$ has only a curve-tangent component, since the construction has a morphism to $\mathbb P^m\times W$. The normal sequence calculation from C.3m gives \begin{equation} \kappa=\sum_{i,j,k}a_{ijk}x_iw_j\otimes\delta(z_kG), \qquad \delta:H^0(C,\mathcal O_C(5))\longrightarrow H^1(C,\mathcal O_C). \end{equation} Up to the same harmless overall sign, the three values $\delta(z_kG)$ are a basis. In the Fermat Jacobian ring they are respectively $z_0z_1^2z_2^2$, $z_0^2z_1z_2^2$, and $z_0^2z_1^2z_2$. The source basis of $H^0(C,K_C)$ used below is the Serre-dual basis to these three values; it need not be identified with a chosen coordinate basis of that space. \emph{4. The exact rank calculation and the Hodge projection.} Put \[ \mathcal R=\mathbb C[w_0,w_1,w_2,w_3]/(w_0^3,w_1^3,w_2^3), \qquad \dim\mathcal R_3=16,\quad\dim\mathcal R_4=19. \] The Euler and normal sequences on the quartic give \[ H^1(W,T_W(-1))\simeq\mathcal R_3, \qquad H^1(W,T_W)_{\mathrm{pol}}\simeq\mathcal R_4. \] For completeness, $H^1(T_{\mathbb P^3}(-1)|_W)=0$, and quotienting $H^0(\mathcal O_W(3))$ by the four partial derivatives gives the first equality. In degree zero, quotienting $H^0(\mathcal O_W(4))$ by linear vector fields gives the $19$-dimensional kernel of \[ H^1(T_W)\longrightarrow H^1(T_{\mathbb P^3}|_W). \] The latter target has dimension one by the Euler sequence. The K3 equalities $K_W\simeq\mathcal O_W$ and $h^{1,1}(W)=20$ identify this kernel with the polarized deformation space. Its Serre-dual annihilator in $H^1(W,\Omega^1_W)$ is exactly $\mathbb C H_W$: the polarization extends to every embedded deformation, and its class is nonzero since $H_W^2=4$. Serre duality makes \[ \frac{H^1(W,\Omega^1_W)}{\mathbb C H_W} \simeq\mathcal R_4^*, \qquad H^1(W,\Omega^1_W(1))\simeq\mathcal R_3^*. \] Multiplication by $w_j$ on these Hodge groups is dual to multiplication $w_j:\mathcal R_3\to\mathcal R_4$. In particular every such multiplication kills $H_W$. The displayed identifications use dual vector spaces, not an unmentioned self-dual monomial basis. Order the degree-three and degree-four monomials lexicographically by their exponent tuples in $\{0,1,2\}^4$. In the dual bases, the map \begin{equation} \mathcal R_4^*\otimes\mathbb C^3 \longrightarrow\mathbb C^4\otimes\mathcal R_3^* \end{equation} induced by \eqref{eq:C3ae-kappa} has rows $(i,u)$, columns $(k,v)$, and entry \[ M_{(i,u),(k,v)} =\sum_{\{j:\,u+e_j=v\}} a_{ijk}. \] It is a $64$ by $57$ integer matrix. The determinant of the submatrix consisting of its first $57$ rows is $47$ modulo $101$. Hence \eqref{eq:C3ae-rank-map} is injective over $\mathbb C$. The retained code records the monomial order, matrices and exact finite-field elimination, and independent implementations reproduce both this minor and full column rank. Now project \eqref{eq:C3ae-obstruction-zero} to \begin{equation} \begin{split} H^0(\mathbb P^m,\mathcal O(1)) \otimes H^1(W,\Omega^1_W(1)) \otimes H^1(C,K_C) \otimes H^1(P,\mathcal O_P). \end{split} \end{equation} Because $\kappa$ contracts only a curve differential, the relevant source component of $\operatorname{cl}(b_0)$ is \begin{equation} H^1(W,\Omega^1_W)\otimes H^0(C,K_C) \otimes H^1(P,\mathcal O_P). \end{equation} Terms with a projective-space differential cannot contribute to \eqref{eq:C3ae-target-component}. They also vanish by the Euler-sequence equality \[ H^1(\mathbb P^m,\Omega^1(1))=0. \] The action on \eqref{eq:C3ae-source-component}, modulo $\mathbb C H_W$ in the first factor, is exactly the injective map \eqref{eq:C3ae-rank-map} tensored with $H^1(P,\mathcal O_P)$. Thus the primitive part of \eqref{eq:C3ae-source-component} is zero. Pairing its first factor with $\tau$ annihilates the remaining $H_W$ part by \eqref{eq:C3ae-intersections}. It follows that the line bundle $\operatorname{pr}_{C\times P,*}(\tau b_0)$ has zero mixed component in $H^0(C,K_C)\otimes H^1(P,\mathcal O_P)$. The correction $-a b_1+a^2b_2$ in \eqref{eq:C3ae-source-invariant} has no effect on this conclusion. Indeed $H^1(W,\mathcal O_W)=0$ and $H^0(W,\Omega_W^1)=0$, so the only varying mixed component of a divisor on $S\times P$ comes from $C\times P$. Multiplication by $a$ supplies the $H_W$ factor, which pairs to zero with $\tau$. All other divisor components are constant in $P$; $b_2$ has codimension zero and is constant as well. This verifies the boundary correction rather than assuming that a chosen lift is unique. \emph{5. Actual ordinary families and the nonzero target.} Every generator of $\mathrm{CH}^2(X)_{\mathrm{alg}}$ is a difference of fibres of a cycle on $X$ times a smooth connected curve. Compactify the curve smoothly and close that cycle in the product. The fibres at the original points are unchanged. Thus it suffices to take the parameter $P$ above to be a smooth projective connected curve and a fixed actual cycle on $X\times P$. The line bundle in \eqref{eq:C3ae-source-invariant} defines, after subtracting its value at a base point, a morphism $P\to\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)$. Its mixed Hodge component is zero by step 4. statement: C.3bc. Top Chow groups for SNC resolutions over \(\overline{\mathbb F}_p\) (Proved).. Let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_p\), and let \(R\) be the strict henselization of a normal local ring essentially of finite type over \(k\), at a closed point with residue field \(k\). Write \(\dim R=d+1\), where \(d\geq1\). Suppose that \(f:Z\to\operatorname{Spec}R\) is projective and birational, that \(Z\) is regular, and that \(f\) is an isomorphism away from the closed point. Suppose that its reduced exceptional fibre is a simple normal crossing divisor \[ E=\bigcup_{i=1}^{c}E_i. \] Assume that there are positive rational numbers \(a_i\) such that the exceptional \(\mathbb Q\)-Cartier divisor \[ D=\sum_i a_iE_i \] satisfies \(-D|_E\) ample. Put \(X=Z\setminus E\), and let \(i_i:E_i\hookrightarrow Z\) denote the inclusions. Then \begin{equation} \mathrm{CH}^{d}(Z)_{\mathbb Q} \xrightarrow[\alpha\mapsto(\deg i_i^!\alpha)_i]{\ \sim\ } \mathbb Q^{c}, \qquad \mathrm{CH}^{d}(X)_{\mathbb Q}=0. \end{equation} In particular the ordinary quotient \(B^d(X)_{\mathbb Q}\) is zero. The statement assumes the indicated resolution and ample exceptional combination; it does not assume their existence in arbitrary dimension. No lifting of algebraic families from the reducible exceptional fibre is used.

statement: C.3be. Rational top Chow vanishing with residue field \(\overline{\mathbb F}_p\) in every local dimension (Proved).. Let \((R,\mathfrak m,k)\) be an excellent local domain with \(k\simeq\overline{\mathbb F}_p\) and \(N=\dim R\geq2\). Put \(S=\operatorname{Spec}R\) and \(X=S\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}\). Then \begin{equation} \mathrm{CH}_1(S)_{\mathbb Q}=0, \qquad \mathrm{CH}^{N-1}(X)_{\mathbb Q}=0. \end{equation} The dimension-indexed group uses \(\delta(\mathfrak p)=\dim(R/\mathfrak p)\), and the puncture inherits this dimension function. Thus \(\mathrm{CH}_1(X)=\mathrm{CH}^{N-1}(X)\); we do not reindex using the smaller Krull dimension of the puncture. The ring need not be henselian, normal, algebraizable over a field, or of equal characteristic, and its puncture need not be regular. In the setting where the ordinary algebraic-equivalence quotient \(B^{N-1}(X)\) is defined, that quotient also vanishes rationally. In particular this gives the ordinary top quotient for the strict-local \(\overline{\mathbb F}_p\)-algebra germs in the manuscript. We impose no coefficient-field family convention on a mixed-characteristic ring.

The proper Segre contraction is an isomorphism away from the zero section. Shrinking around the vertex proves that the normalization is regular away from that vertex; it does not change the specified local ring. Its unique closed preimage follows from the connected zero-section fibre. Denote the resulting regular projective resolution over $R$ by $\mathcal Z$. Its closed fibre is \[ V=\mathbb P^m\times C,\qquad L=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^m}(1)\boxtimes K_C, \qquad I_V=\mathcal O_{\mathcal Z}(-V),\quad I_V/I_V^2=L. \] In fact $\mathfrak m_R\mathcal O_{\mathcal Z}=I_V$: the Segre coordinates generate $I_V$ locally, while every function vanishing at the normalized vertex vanishes on $V$. The compatible unit systems have surjective transition maps from the second stage onward, because the same $H^1(V,L^n)$ vanish. Hence no inverse-limit unit obstruction occurs. The analogous sequence with $L^n$ gives $H^1(H_0,L^n|_{H_0})=0$ for $n\ge2$; also $H^2(H_0,L^n|_{H_0})=0$ for $n\ge1$, since the corresponding $H^2(V,L^n)$ and $H^3(V,L^{n-1})$ vanish. The split projection identifies the compatible formal target Picard identity component with \[ J\times(U_0/U). \] Restriction induces the identity on $J$, and on vector kernels it is the quotient $U_0\to U_0/U$. In particular it annihilates $U$ as a group scheme. The full formal unit calculation, rather than only its tangent map, justifies this last assertion. \emph{3. The extension class has rank three.} The class of $V_2$ is the boundary of $\ell H$ in the twisted normal sequence. The off-diagonal coefficients vanish and each diagonal coefficient is $4!/(2!1!1!)=12=2$ in $k$. Frobenius is therefore bijective. The Abel map identifies $H^1(J,\mathcal O_J)$ with $H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$ compatibly with Frobenius \citep[Lemma9.5]{D_MilneJacobians2021}. Coherent cohomology of an abelian variety is the exterior algebra on $H^1$ \citep[Theorem1.1, p.~1]{D_BrionCoherent2012}, so Frobenius is bijective in every degree. By \citet[Lemma2.3.1 and Proposition2.3.2, p.~12]{D_HaconPatakfalvi2014v2}, $J$ is ordinary and Verschiebung \[ v:J^{(5)}\longrightarrow J \] has étale kernel $K\simeq(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z)^3$. Its pullback on $H^1(\mathcal O)$ is zero: the composite with the bijective Frobenius pullback is $[5]^*=0$. Using the bifunctorial identification $\operatorname{Ext}^1(J,\mathbb G_a)=H^1(J,\mathcal O_J)$ \citep[equation(3.8), Section3.2.3, p.~23, before the characteristic-zero restriction]{D_BrionIsogenyII}, the extension $v^*G$ splits. The Hom--Ext sequence of $0\to K\to J^{(5)}\to J\to0$ therefore identifies \[ \operatorname{Hom}(K,\mathbb G_a) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Ext}^1(J,\mathbb G_a), \] because $v^*$ on the latter Ext group is zero. The three independent classes in Step~3 imply that $b|_K:K\to U$ has rank three and is an injection. As $\ker b\subseteq K$, the whole morphism $b$ is a closed immersion. Its image $B$ is therefore a proper abelian subgroup isomorphic to $J^{(5)}$, and \[ B\cap U=b(K),\qquad b(K)\simeq(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z)^3. \] Under target restriction, $B\to J\times(U_0/U)$ is $(v,0)$: the first component is $v$ and the second is zero because a proper connected group has no nonconstant morphism to an affine group. Choose a smooth connected proper curve $P\subset B$ through $0$ and $\alpha$, by successive sufficiently ample smooth sections through these two points. Its obstruction to extension to $V_2\times P$ is the contraction of its mixed Atiyah class with $\kappa$. The only possible component is in $H^1(V,L)\otimes H^1(P,\mathcal O_P)$: both $H^2(V,L)$ and $H^2(P,\mathcal O_P)$ vanish. Proper formal existence algebraizes the system to a line bundle there. The regular completion map $R\to\widehat R$ is a filtered colimit of smooth $R$-algebras. Descend the line bundle, its inverse, and the specified identification of its first-jet restriction with $\mathcal Q_2$ to one smooth $R$-algebra. The same argument applied to tensor differences proves injectivity on all the distinct elements of $b(K)(k)$; uniqueness of the individual formal Picard lift makes this assignment a homomorphism. Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $p>0$ and let $E=\bigcup_{i=1}^cE_i$ be a projective SNC surface with smooth connected components. Assume that there are no triple intersections. Put \begin{align} \rho:\bigoplus_i\operatorname{Pic}(E_i)_{\mathbf Q} &\longrightarrow\bigoplus_e\operatorname{Pic}(C_e)_{\mathbf Q}, & (L_i)_i&\longmapsto (L_i|_{C_e}-L_j|_{C_e})_{e=(i,j)}, \tag{TF.1}\\ S(E)&=F_\gamma^2K_0(E)_{\mathbf Q}. \notag \end{align} As in EP, $J_K(E)$ denotes the subgroup generated by endpoint differences of actual classes in $F_\gamma^2K_0(E\times P)_{\mathbf Q}$ with $P$ a smooth connected projective curve. If $\rho$ is surjective, then the component Chern-character map is an isomorphism \begin{equation} \varphi:S(E)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \bigoplus_i\operatorname{CH}_0(E_i)_{\mathbf Q}, \qquad \varphi(J_K(E))=\bigoplus_i\operatorname{CH}_0(E_i)^0_{\mathbf Q}. \tag{TF.2} \end{equation} Consequently, \begin{equation} S(E)/J_K(E)\simeq\mathbf Q^c. \tag{TF.3} \end{equation} In particular, for two components $E=S\cup_C T$, the hypothesis holds if the sum of the restrictions \begin{equation} \operatorname{Pic}^0(S)_{\mathrm{red}}\times \operatorname{Pic}^0(T)_{\mathrm{red}}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}^0(C) \tag{TF.4} \end{equation} is surjective. It suffices that either factor already surject. It also holds whenever $C\simeq\mathbf P^1$. Now assume the exact threefold resolution hypotheses of C.3bm: $R$ is the strict henselization at a closed $k$-point of a normal local ring essentially of finite type over $k$, with $\dim R=3$ and regular puncture; $Z\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is projective, its source is regular of pure dimension three, and it is an isomorphism off the closed point; $E$ is its full reduced closed fibre. statement: C.3bt. Proper edge families (Proved).. Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $p>0$. Assume that $D=\sum a_iE_i$, $a_i>0$, satisfies $\mathcal O_E(-D)$ ample. Put $S(E)=F_\gamma^2K_0(E)_{\mathbf Q}$, and let $J_K(E)$ be the actual fixed smooth-proper-curve endpoint relation group of EP. Then \begin{equation} \ker\left(S(E)\longrightarrow \bigoplus_i\operatorname{CH}_0(E_i)_{\mathbf Q}\right) \subseteq J_K(E). \tag{VE.1} \end{equation} There is no hypothesis on second dual cohomology, triple-point Picard periods, or joint Picard restriction. In the exact resolved threefold scope of C.3bm this removes the edge and triple-point kernel. After C.3bo the remaining restrictions lie in the component Albanese kernels, with their induced proper-family and exceptional relations. If all component Albanese kernels vanish rationally, the ordinary rational top quotient of the puncture is zero. The general component kernel quotient is not computed here. The new input is the following actual-family lemma. Its marked restrictions are literally zero in $K_1$, not merely norm-zero. \emph{Marked edge-family lemma.} Let $C_1,\ldots,C_s$ be smooth connected proper curves over $k$, with base points $c_e$ and finitely many marked points on each. For $L_e\in\operatorname{Pic}^0(C_e)(k)$ and $u\in k^*$ there are a smooth connected proper curve $P$, points $o,t\in P(k)$, and actual classes $\xi_e\in K_1(C_e\times P)$ such that \begin{align} \xi_e|_{C_e\times\{o\}}&=0,& \xi_e|_{C_e\times\{t\}}&=u([L_e]-1),\nonumber\\ \xi_e|_{\{q\}\times P}&=0 &&\text{for every marked point }q. \tag{VE.2} \end{align} The construction on smooth products is integral; the singular-scheme application below uses rational coefficients. \emph{1. A proper base and normalized divisors.} If $u=1$ or every $L_e$ is trivial, take zero classes. Otherwise choose a smooth connected projective curve $A\subset\prod_e\operatorname{Pic}^0(C_e)$ through $0$ and the nonzero tuple $(L_e)_e$. In dimension one use the whole abelian variety; otherwise successive sufficiently high complete intersections with prescribed points and first jets give such a curve in every characteristic. The smoothness incidence estimate and connectedness by duality and Serre vanishing are the same ones used in C.3bq \citep[Lemma 33.47.3 and proof]{D_StacksBertiniUniformHigher}. Denote its two points by $a_0,a_1$. The normalized Poincare bundles $\mathcal M_e$ on $C_e\times A$ are trivialized along $c_e\times A$ and $C_e\times\{a_0\}$, and have fibres $L_e$ at $a_1$. For every marked point $q$, put $N_{e,q}=\mathcal M_e|_{\{q\}\times A}$, with its fixed trivialization at $a_0$. Choose a rational section $r_{e,q}$ having value $1$ in that trivialization at $a_0$, and divisor $B_{e,q}=\operatorname{div}(r_{e,q})$ disjoint from $a_0,a_1$. To do this, twist by a large effective divisor supported away from the two points. Vanishing of $H^1$ after subtracting both points makes evaluation onto, so prescribe value $1$ at $a_0$ and a nonzero value at $a_1$, then divide by the twisting section. Only finitely many divisors are involved. \emph{2. Interpolate the covering function at their supports.} Let $F$ be the union of all their supports. Choose a rational function $h$ on $A$, with its only pole at $a_0$, satisfying \begin{equation} h(a_1)=\frac{(u-1)^2}{u},\qquad h(x)=0\quad(x\in F), \tag{VE.3} \end{equation} and having at least one simple zero away from $a_0,a_1$. For the finite prescribed jet scheme $T$, choose $n$ large enough that \[ H^1(A,\mathcal O_A(na_0)(-T))=0. \] This makes all the conditions compatible. A nonzero leading polar coefficient at $a_0$ can be prescribed too. One may impose simple zeros at every point of $F$ and at one further point. This is the curve Riemann--Roch evaluation argument; there is no bound on the characteristic. The value at $a_1$ is nonzero because $u\ne1$. Normalize the double cover with function-field equation \begin{equation} (g-1)^2=h g,\qquad g^2-(h+2)g+1=0. \tag{VE.4} \end{equation} In odd characteristic its discriminant $h(h+4)$ has odd valuation at a simple zero of $h$, proving irreducibility and separability. In characteristic two, $y=(g+1)/h$ satisfies $y^2+y=1/h$. The right side has a simple pole, whereas any pole of $z^2+z$ has even order, so this equation is again irreducible and separable. Thus the normalization $f:P\to A$ is a finite separable degree-two map of smooth connected proper curves. Both $g$ and $g^{-1}$ are integral wherever $h$ is regular. Every zero or pole of $g$ therefore lies above $a_0$. Conversely $g+g^{-1}=h+2$ shows that $g$ is not a unit at any point above that pole. Write $B=f^{-1}(a_0)_{\rm red}$. Choose $o\in B$ and a point $t$ above $a_1$ with $g(t)=u$. Such a point exists by (VE.4), including when it is ramified. For every point $y$ above $F$, the same equation gives \begin{equation} g(y)=1. \tag{VE.5} \end{equation} This holds also in characteristic two and with ramification. \emph{3. An actual Cech $K_2$ class across zeros and poles.} Fix an edge and write $X=C_e\times P$, $\mathcal M=(1\times f)^*\mathcal M_e$ and $V=C_e\times B$. The bundle has its specified trivialization on $V$. Choose a finite Zariski cover trivializing $\mathcal M$, using local frames lifting that trivialization wherever an open meets $V$. Such frames exist by locally lifting a basis of the invertible module modulo the ideal of $V$ and shrinking. Let $b_{ij}$ be the transition units, with the convention that their Cech class is $c_1(\mathcal M)$. Off $V$ take the symbols $\{g,b_{ij}\}$ in the Zariski sheaf $\mathcal K_2$ of Quillen $K$-groups. Near a point above $a_0$, choose a parameter $z$ on $P$ and write $g=z^m v$, $b_{ij}=1+z b'_{ij}$, where $v,b_{ij}$ are units and $m$ may be negative. In additive notation the extension is \begin{equation} m\langle z,-b'_{ij}\rangle+\{v,1+z b'_{ij}\}. \tag{VE.6} \end{equation} Indeed the Dennis--Stein convention is $\langle r,s\rangle=\{r,1-rs\}$ when $r$ is invertible \citep[Chapter III, Definition 5.11 and identities D1--D3, pp.~43--44]{frWeibelKbookIII}. Regular local Gersten injectivity identifies the sheaf $\mathcal K_2$ with its unramified subsheaf in the function-field group \citep[Section 7, Theorem 5.11 and the preceding Gersten complex] {rootQuillen1973}. Thus the extensions glue uniquely and satisfy the Cech cocycle identity, since they do so in the function field. Marked restrictions, including the boundary scalar.} At a marked $q$, the restricted relative-trivialized bundle is $f^*N_{e,q}$. The section $f^*r_{e,q}$ has value $1$ at every point of $B$, and divisor \[ \sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}B_{e,q}}\ \sum_{y\mid x} e(y/x)n_x[y], \qquad B_{e,q}=\sum_x n_x[x]. \] Use this section as frame away from its divisor. It is compatible with the specified boundary trivialization. All remaining transition calculations occur where $g$ is a unit. The Gersten divisor formula for the restricted cup is consequently \begin{equation} \sum_x\sum_{y\mid x} e(y/x)n_x\,g(y)[\mathcal O_y] \quad\text{in }H^1(P,\mathcal K_2). \tag{VE.8} \end{equation} A unit is here written additively as its $K_1(k)$ class. This is also the proper point-pushforward projection formula \citep[Section 7, Propositions 2.10 and 3.2]{rootQuillen1973}. No boundary point-unit term is omitted: the comparison frame has value $1$ at the boundary, so its comparison symbols extend by (VE.6), with zero specializations. This explains the normalization of the rational sections in Step~1. Every $g(y)$ in (VE.8) equals $1$ by (VE.5), hence is zero in $K_1(k)$. Ramification multiplicities, including wild ones in characteristic two, make no difference. Every marked restriction of $c_e$ is literally zero. No norm map is used. \emph{5. Lift to the actual $K_1$ group by sheaf descent.} For a noetherian finite-dimensional scheme there is the natural strongly convergent descent spectral sequence \begin{equation} E_2^{a,b}=H^a(X,\mathcal K_b)\Longrightarrow K_{b-a}(X), \qquad d_r:(a,b)\longmapsto(a+r,b+r-1). \tag{VE.9} \end{equation} Use \citet[Theorem 10.3 and proof, pp.~383--386; Appendix D.4--D.5 and proofs, pp.~424--426]{D_ThomasonTrobaugh1990}. The filtration is the sheaf hypercohomology/Postnikov filtration, not an assertion about pullback preserving codimension of supports. Derived pullback of perfect complexes induces the map of $K$-presheaves \citep[Sections 3.14--3.15, pp.~317--319]{D_ThomasonTrobaugh1990}. The natural augmentation and functorial Postnikov construction give the compatible descent-filtration maps for the horizontal and vertical regular Cartier curves at issue. As $\dim X=2$, no differential of order $r\ge2$ can enter or leave $(a,b)=(1,2)$: its source would have negative cohomological degree or its target would have degree at least three. Hence \begin{equation} F^1_{\rm des}K_1(X)/F^2_{\rm des}K_1(X) \simeq H^1(X,\mathcal K_2). \tag{VE.10} \end{equation} Choose a lift $\xi_e\in F^1_{\rm des}K_1(X)$ of $c_e$. For a regular curve the same descent filtration has $F^2_{\rm des}=0$ and $F^1_{\rm des}K_1\simeq H^1(\mathcal K_2)$. Naturality makes the required restrictions of $\xi_e$ independent of its choice and equal to the sheaf classes computed above. The possible degree-two surface filtration ambiguity restricts to zero on these Cartier curves, while choosing $F^1_{\rm des}$ excludes a determinant/unit term. The ordinary cup on a smooth curve sends $u\,c_1(L_e)$ to $u([L_e]-1)$. Thus (VE.2) holds for actual classes on the fixed proper products. Thus $k$ is algebraically closed of characteristic $p>0$, $R$ is an excellent henselian algebraizable local coefficient-$k$ algebra with residue field $k$, and $Z\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is projective, with $Z$ regular of pure dimension $d+1$, $d\geq1$, and an isomorphism off the closed point. An effective Cartier divisor $D\subset Z$ has the reduced closed fibre $E$ as its full support, and $\mathcal O_D(-D)$ is ample. Let $P/k$ be a fixed smooth connected projective curve and put $T=D\times_kP$. Then \begin{equation} F_\gamma^dK_0(T)_{\mathbf Q}\ \subseteq\ \operatorname{im}\!\left(K_0(Z\times_kP)_{\mathbf Q} \longrightarrow K_0(T)_{\mathbf Q}\right). \tag{WP.1} \end{equation} This is equality with the prescribed perfect class on the entire fixed exceptional product. It does not assert extension of a prescribed vector bundle as an object. In exceptional dimensions $d\leq2$, restriction on the whole rational $K_0$ group is surjective, and \begin{equation} K_{-1}(\operatorname{Spec}R\times_kP)_{\mathbf Q}=0. \tag{WP.8} \end{equation} The latter assertion uses these geometric hypotheses; it is not an application of henselian-local negative-$K$ vanishing to a product. \emph{1. Exact lifting of finite perfect corrections.} Call a finite scheme $F\subset T$ admissible if it is regularly immersed with codimension $d+1$, its support lies in the smooth top-dimensional strata of $E\times P$, and a defining regular sequence has independent differentials on those strata. The nilpotent structure inherited from $D$ is retained. We first prove that \begin{equation} [\mathcal O_F]\in\operatorname{im}\!\left( K_0(Z\times P)\longrightarrow K_0(T)\right) \qquad(F\text{ admissible}), \tag{WP.2} \end{equation} without taking a tensor power or rationalizing. Choose $d$ sufficiently high relatively ample line bundles on $Z\times P$, also ample in the $P$ direction, and sections on $T$ vanishing on $F$. Serre vanishing gives surjectivity onto their twisted conormal sections. A general $(d+1)\times d$ conormal matrix has full rank everywhere on $F$: rank drop has codimension two and $F$ is finite. The condition on $F_{\mathrm{red}}$ gives a locally split injection on $F$ by Nakayama's lemma. Away from $F$, impose transversality to a finite smooth stratification of $E\times P$, for every prefix of the flag. The finite first-jet incidence argument in AE.5--AE.7 supplies all these open conditions. Sufficiently high twists also have \[ H^1\bigl(Z\times P,\mathcal A_j(-D\times P)\bigr)=0, \] so the sections lift to the actual fixed product \citep[Lemma 30.17.1]{frC3azStacksSerre}. Let $j:W\hookrightarrow Z\times P$ be their intersection, and put $H=W\cap T$. Independent ambient differentials make $W$ regular of pure dimension two along the full closed fibre. Its nonregular locus is closed by excellence; a nonempty proper image in the local scheme $\operatorname{Spec}R$ would contain the closed point. It follows that $W$ is regular everywhere. The same argument excludes components of an unintended dimension. Thus $j$ is a regular immersion of codimension $d$. The flag meets the reduced closed fibre in the expected dimension one, so $H$ is Cartier on $W$ and has the full closed fibre as support. The conormal condition identifies the flag equations with the first $d$ members of a regular-sequence generating set of $I_F$. The remaining generator cuts out $F$ as an effective Cartier divisor on the possibly nonreduced Cohen--Macaulay curve $H$. Set $Q_0=\mathcal O_H(-F)$ and $J=\mathcal O_W(-H)$. For every $n\geq1$, \[ H^2(H,J^n/J^{n+1})=0, \] because $H$ has dimension one \citep[Proposition 20.20.7]{frWPStacksDimensionVanishing}. The square-zero unit sequence therefore extends $Q_0$ through all thickenings of $H$, without a power \citep[Lemma 37.4.1]{frC3azStacksPicThickening}. The powers of $J$ and $\mathfrak m\mathcal O_W$ are cofinal. Proper Grothendieck existence algebraizes this formal line bundle and its inverse on $W_{\widehat R}$; full faithfulness verifies invertibility \citep[Lemma 30.24.3]{frC3azStacksExistence}. Regularity of completion and Popescu express $\widehat R$ as a filtered colimit of smooth $R$-algebras \citep[Lemma 15.51.14; Theorem 16.12.1] {frC3azStacksCompletion,frC3azStacksPopescu}. The bundle descends to one such algebra \citep[Lemma 32.10.3(2)]{frC3azStacksLimitBundles}. For $\mathfrak m^M\mathcal O_W\subset J$, preserve the specified $R/\mathfrak m^M$ point by henselian smooth lifting \citep[Lemma 15.13.3]{frC3azStacksHenselSmooth}. This gives a line bundle $Q$ on the fixed $W$ with $Q|_H\simeq Q_0$. This is the actual finite-jet descent of AE.9, rather than a retained formal or etale replacement of the product. The square formed by $j$ and $T\hookrightarrow Z\times P$ is Tor-independent, because $H$ is Cartier on $W$. Writing $i:H\hookrightarrow T$, perfect pushforward and derived base change give \begin{equation} \bigl(j_*(1-[Q])\bigr)|_T =i_*\bigl(1-[\mathcal O_H(-F)]\bigr) =[\mathcal O_F]\quad\hbox{in }K_0(T). \tag{WP.2a} \end{equation} The last equality is the Cartier exact sequence. This proves (WP.2) in perfect $K_0$, without a Cartan injectivity or gamma pushforward assertion. \emph{2. The top gamma tail.} Apply the perfect determinantal construction AE.2--AE.6 with total gamma degree $n=d+1=\dim T$. Modulo $F_\gamma^{n+1}$, any element of $F_\gamma^n$ is a sum of products of gamma operations of total degree $n$ on sufficiently generated bundles. The exact Eagon--Northcott identity AE.3 replaces each factor by its perfect maximal-minor class modulo the next filtration; its resolution and grade statements are \citet[Section 2.C; Theorems 2.1 and 2.16] {D_BrunsVetter1988Determinantal}. The resulting general intersection has dimension zero, misses all lower-dimensional strata, and avoids every deeper rank locus: for a factor of degree $i_a$, that incidence has codimension \[ 2(i_a+1)+\sum_{b\ne a}i_b=n+i_a+2>n. \] Row and column reduction at the intersection gives $n$ defining functions with independent differentials on its top smooth stratum. Cohen--Macaulayness makes them a regular sequence. The tensor product of the perfect determinantal resolutions is therefore exactly $[\mathcal O_F]$ for an admissible finite $F$. The dimension theorem gives $F_\gamma^{n+1}K_0(T)_{\mathbf Q}=0$ \citep[Chapter II, Remark 8.8.5]{D_Weibel2013KbookII}. Consequently \begin{equation} F_\gamma^{d+1}K_0(T)_{\mathbf Q} \text{ is spanned by admissible }[\mathcal O_F]. \tag{WP.3} \end{equation} Only the rational filtration bound is needed here. By (WP.2) the whole tail lifts. \emph{3. Line-bundle differences on the curve representatives.} Let $C\subset T$ be a curve produced in AE.5--AE.6. It is a projective Cohen--Macaulay curve, possibly nonreduced, regularly immersed with codimension $d$. It meets the lower-dimensional strata of $E\times P$ only in a finite set. Off that set, its reduction is smooth and its $d$ defining differentials are independent on the top stratum. For every line bundle $M$ on $C$, choose an ample $A$ and an integer $N$ so large that $M\otimes A^N$ and $A^N$ have the required generated first jets. General sections avoid the associated points and the finite bad set, and have simple zeros on the smooth reduction. Their zero schemes $F_+$ and $F_-$ are finite effective Cartier divisors. The composite immersions into $T$ are admissible: the additional transverse section supplies the last independent differential. The Cartier sequences give \[ [M\otimes A^N]-[A^N] =[\mathcal O_{F_+}(F_+)]-[\mathcal O_{F_-}(F_-)]. \] Every line bundle on a finite $k$-scheme is trivial. Indeed its ring is Artinian semilocal; choose simultaneous residue-field bases by the Chinese remainder theorem and apply Nakayama at every maximal ideal to obtain a single basis \citep[Lemma 10.78.7 and proof hints]{frWPStacksSemilocal}. Multiplication by $[A^{-N}]$ leaves both finite classes unchanged. Hence \begin{equation} [M]-1=[\mathcal O_{F_+}]-[\mathcal O_{F_-}] \quad\hbox{in perfect }K_0(C). \tag{WP.4} \end{equation} This argument retains the finite nonreduced schemes, rather than replacing their perfect classes by cycles. \emph{4. Correct the entire curve class.} Perform the AE.7 flag for $C$. Its $W$ is a regular threefold, $H=W\cap T$ is Cartier on $W$, and $C$ is Cartier on $H$. The conormal $\mathcal O_H(-H)$ is ample relative to $H\to P$. Relative Serre vanishing and coherent cohomological dimension one of $P$ give \[ H^2(H,\mathcal O_H(-nH))=0 \qquad(n\gg0). \] The finitely many earlier Picard obstruction groups are killed by $p$. Successively taking $p$th tensor powers at those stages, then using the finite-jet algebraization just recalled, gives a finite $a=p^e$ and an actual line bundle $Q$ on $W$ satisfying $Q|_H\simeq\mathcal O_H(-aC)$. This is AE.8--AE.9. Put $b_C=j_*(1-[Q])$ for $j:W\hookrightarrow Z\times P$. The whole square with $T$, not just its endpoint squares, is Tor-independent: the flag is regular and the equation of $D$ is a nonzerodivisor on $W$. Successive Cartier sequences give \begin{equation} b_C|_T=\sum_{r=0}^{a-1} [\mathcal O_C\otimes\mathcal O_H(-rC)|_C]. \tag{WP.5} \end{equation} Subtracting $a[\mathcal O_C]$ expresses the difference as perfect pushforwards of line-bundle differences on $C$. By (WP.4) it is a finite integral combination of admissible finite classes on $T$. Lift each by (WP.2), and let $c_C$ be their integral sum on $Z\times P$. We obtain \begin{equation} (b_C-c_C)|_T=a[\mathcal O_C]. \tag{WP.6} \end{equation} Thus the entire prescribed curve class lifts rationally. AE.2--AE.6 express any class in $F_\gamma^d$ as a finite rational sum of these curves modulo $F_\gamma^{d+1}$; (WP.3) lifts the remainder. This proves (WP.1). \emph{5. Full rational $K_0$ in exceptional dimensions at most two.} Nilpotent invariance in characteristic $p$ identifies $K_0(T)_{\mathbf Q}$ with $K_0(E\times P)_{\mathbf Q}$ as rational lambda rings, as in AE.13 \citep[Theorem A]{rootGeisserHesselholt2011}. For $d=2$, start with a prescribed class on $T$. Its componentwise ranks lift by the point isomorphism FF.4 and pullback to the product. After subtraction the class has rank zero. Its determinant is a rational Picard class. For each line-bundle representative $M$ on $T$, a finite power $M^{p^e}$ lifts to $Z\times P$ by AE.8--AE.9 with $W=Z\times P$ and $H=T$: the conormal is ample relative to $P$, so the same eventual $H^2$ vanishing applies. If $Q$ is that lift, then $p^{-e}([Q]-1)$ has the required determinant modulo $F_\gamma^2$ after restriction. The rank-and-determinant description of $K_0/F_\gamma^2$ leaves precisely a class in $F_\gamma^2$, which (WP.1) lifts. Therefore \begin{equation} K_0(Z\times P)_{\mathbf Q}\longrightarrow K_0(E\times P)_{\mathbf Q} \quad\text{is surjective}\qquad(d\leq2). \tag{WP.7} \end{equation} For $d=1$ ranks and (WP.1), applied to $F_\gamma^1$, suffice. Finally FF.1 identifies the cokernel in (WP.7) with the group in (WP.8). This proves the negative-$K$ consequence by the exact fixed-product blow-up sequence, not by a locality assertion. \qed \emph{Scope.} Every flag and every parameter product above is proper over the original local ring $R$. After a transcendental scalar extension, $R\otimes_k k(u)$ is generally not local or henselian, and these arguments do not apply without further proof. Localizing or henselizing would change the prescribed product. The result gives no affine-parameter compactification and no valuation descent of a proper $K_1$ family constructed only after that replacement. It also does not construct a global exceptional family from independent component families. Thus the remaining component Albanese-kernel quotient in C.3bt is unchanged.

statement: C.3bv. Whole proper $K_1$-family lifting (Proved).. Let $k$ be algebraically closed, let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a noetherian local coefficient-$k$ algebra with residue field $k$, and let $P/k$ be a smooth connected projective curve. Write $B=\operatorname{Spec}R\times_kP$. Rank and determinant give an integral isomorphism \begin{equation} K_0(B)\xrightarrow[\sim]{\ (\operatorname{rk},\det)\ } \mathbf Z\oplus\operatorname{Pic}(B). \tag{NK.1} \end{equation} If $I$ is its rank-zero ideal, then \begin{equation} I^2=F_\gamma^2K_0(B)=0,\qquad (\psi^q-1)(\psi^q-q)=0\quad(q\geq1). \tag{NK.2} \end{equation} These assertions require no normality, regularity, henselian property, or characteristic hypothesis on $R$. Suppose further that $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$, $R$ is a normal domain, and $g:Z\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is a proper birational map from a regular integral noetherian scheme, and an isomorphism away from the closed point. Put $E=(Z\times_Rk)_{\mathrm{red}}$. Then restriction is surjective on the entire fixed-product group: \begin{equation} K_1(Z\times_kP)[1/p]\longrightarrow K_1(E\times_kP)[1/p] \quad\text{is surjective}. \tag{NK.7} \end{equation} This conclusion is dimension-independent and requires neither henselianity nor an ample exceptional conormal. It concerns classes in perfect $K$-theory, not extension of specified automorphisms as objects. The pointwise kernel and exact-endpoint consequence are given in (NK.9a)--(NK.10) below. \emph{1. Generation by line bundles on the actual proper product.} Choose an ample line bundle $H$ on $P$ and use the same letter for its pullback to $B$. Let $V$ be a vector bundle of rank $r\geq2$. For $n$ sufficiently large, relative Serre generation gives finitely many global sections generating $V\otimes H^n$ \citep[Lemma 30.17.1]{frC3azStacksSerre}. Their restrictions generate the bundle on the closed fibre $P$. In their finite-dimensional coefficient space, vanishing at a specified point imposes $r$ independent linear conditions. The incidence over the one-dimensional $P$ therefore has dimension at most the dimension of the coefficient space plus $1-r$, strictly smaller than that dimension. Its image is closed because $P$ is proper. A general $k$-linear combination is consequently nowhere zero on $P$. The coefficient field $k\subset R$ lifts this combination to an actual section on $B$. Its zero scheme is closed and proper over the local scheme $\operatorname{Spec}R$. A nonempty image would be closed and contain the closed point, contradicting the closed-fibre choice. Thus the section is nowhere zero on all of $B$. It gives a line subbundle $H^{-n}\hookrightarrow V$ with locally free quotient. Induction gives a filtration with line-bundle quotients. Since $B$ has an ample line bundle over an affine base, perfect $K_0(B)$ is the vector-bundle Grothendieck group \citep[Corollary 3.9 and Proposition 3.10]{D_ThomasonTrobaugh1990}. It follows that line-bundle classes generate $K_0(B)$ additively. The argument does not assert that the filtration splits. \emph{2. Finite Cartier supports and the square-zero ideal.} Given a line bundle $M$ on $B$, take $n$ so large that $M\otimes H^n$ and $H^n$ are generated. Choose sections whose restrictions to the integral closed curve are nonzero. Their closed-fibre zeros are finite effective Cartier divisors, possibly empty. Let $D_+$ and $D_-$ be the actual zero schemes on $B$. They are locally principal. The fibrewise Cartier criterion \citep[Lemma 31.19.9(3)]{frNKStacksRelativeCartier} makes each an effective Cartier divisor flat over $R$ in a neighbourhood of every closed-fibre point. At a point where the section is a unit, the assertion is immediate. These neighbourhoods cover $B$: their closed complement is proper over $R$ and misses its closed fibre. statement: C.3c (Refuted: the unrestricted $J$ and punctured-cone claims).. Let $S/\mathbb C$ be the Fermat quartic surface $x_0^4+x_1^4+x_2^4+x_3^4=0$. Its partial derivatives have no common projective zero, so it is smooth; adjunction gives $K_S\simeq\mathcal O_S$, and the hypersurface cohomology sequence gives $H^1(S,\mathcal O_S)=0$. Thus $S$ is a K3 surface with $\operatorname{Pic}^0(S)=\operatorname{Alb}(S)=0$ and $H^{2,0}(S)\ne0$. Mumford's theorem gives an infinite-dimensional degree-zero Chow group \citep[Section 2, main theorem, p.~200]{cyMumford1969}. This refutes the surjectivity of $J^1(S)\to J^2(S)$. Let $E$ be the complement of the zero section in $\mathcal O_S(-1)$. It is the punctured affine cone over this projectively normal quartic, and has dimension $3$, not $5$. Vector-bundle invariance and localization for the zero section give \begin{equation} \mathrm{CH}^r(E)= \mathrm{CH}^r(S)/\bigl(h\,\mathrm{CH}^{r-1}(S)\bigr). \end{equation} For $r=2$, the denominator is the image of the finitely generated group $\mathrm{Pic}(S)=\mathrm{NS}(S)$, while the rational degree-zero numerator is not finite dimensional. Consequently $\mathrm{CH}^2(E)\otimes\mathbb Q$ is not finite dimensional. This is a counterexample to the global punctured-cone finiteness reading of $\text{\textcircled{3}}'$. We have checked the codimension shift in \eqref{eq:punctured-line-bundle}; writing $\mathrm{CH}^r(Y)$ in place of $\mathrm{CH}^{r-1}(Y)$ in divisor localization is incorrect. A result for this punctured cone does not automatically pass to the punctured spectrum of the strict henselization at its vertex. C.3e below proves the needed separate injection, and C.3f--g give strict local counterexamples with all the required hypotheses. The primitive exponents compatible with the two proposed Lefschetz strings are $n-2i+1$ on $A^i_{\mathrm{alg}}$ and $n-2i+2$ on $J^i$.

statement: C.3h (Known mechanism and proved exact graded gates on abelian varieties).. Let $A$ be a $g$-dimensional abelian variety, $g\ge1$, over an algebraically closed field, of arbitrary characteristic. All groups in this paragraph have rational coefficients. Write \[ B^r(A)=\mathrm{CH}^r(A)_{\mathbb Q}/ \mathrm{CH}^r(A)_{\mathrm{alg},\mathbb Q}, \qquad J^r(A)=\mathrm{CH}^r(A)_{\mathrm{alg},\mathbb Q}. \] Both inherit the Beauville grading, with index $s$ characterized by $[m]^*x=m^{2r-s}x$. For an ample divisor class $h$, the following are exact equivalences for this fixed abelian variety: \begin{equation} \begin{gathered} h^{g-2r}:B^r(A)\longrightarrow B^{g-r}(A) \text{ injective for every }2r\le g\\ \Longleftrightarrow\quad B^*(A)_{(s)}=0\quad(s<0). \end{gathered} \end{equation} \begin{equation} \begin{gathered} h^{g-2r+1}:J^r(A)\longrightarrow J^{g-r+1}(A) \text{ injective for every }2r\le g+1\\ \Longleftrightarrow\quad J^*(A)_{(s)}=0\quad(s\le0). \end{gathered} \end{equation} The displayed implications do not assert these vanishing conditions in general. The first is the adequate-equivalence version of \citet[Proposition 5.11; footnote 1, p.~254]{rootBeauville2010}; the second applies the same representation to its invariant algebraically trivial subgroup.

statement: C.3j (Proved in the stated algebraizable characteristic-zero scope): ordinary algebraically trivial line bundles restrict injectively.. Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic zero, let $(A,\mathfrak m,k)$ be a normal local ring essentially of finite type over $k$, and put $R=A^{\mathrm{sh}}$. Assume $N=\dim A\ge4$ and that the punctured spectrum \[ X=\operatorname{Spec}R\setminus\{\mathfrak m_R\} \] is regular. Let $0\ne f\in\mathfrak m_R$ and assume that $Y=X\cap V(f)$ is regular. For ordinary algebraic equivalence, defined by line-bundle families on the fixed scheme times a connected smooth parameter curve, the restriction \begin{equation} \operatorname{Pic}(X)_{\mathrm{alg}} \longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(Y)_{\mathrm{alg}} \end{equation} is injective integrally. We do not assert surjectivity, the case $N=3$, mixed characteristic, or the same theorem for every nonalgebraizable excellent local ring.

statement: C.3m (Refuted, with an explicit counterexample): ordinary $J^1$ surjectivity fails in every dimension at least four.. For every $N\ge4$ we construct an excellent normal strictly henselian local complex ring $R$ of dimension $N$, with regular puncture $X$ and a regular punctured principal divisor $Y$, such that \begin{equation} \operatorname{Pic}(X)_{\mathrm{alg}}=0, \qquad \operatorname{Pic}^0(C)(\mathbb C) \lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(Y)_{\mathrm{alg}}, \end{equation} where $C$ is the explicitly specified Fermat plane quartic. The right-hand injection has nontorsion image. Thus ordinary $J^1(X)\to J^1(Y)$ is not surjective, even with rational coefficients. All algebraic equivalences here use families on the fixed scheme times a smooth connected parameter curve. The argument below works with actual line bundles throughout. \emph{1. The algebraic contraction and its divisor.} Put $m=N-2\ge2$, and define \[ \begin{aligned} F(z)&=z_0^4+z_1^4+z_2^4, & C&=V(F)\subset\mathbb P^2_{\mathbb C},\\ H(z)&=z_0^2z_1^2+z_0^2z_2^2+z_1^2z_2^2,& \ell(x,z)&=x_0z_0+x_1z_1+x_2z_2. \end{aligned} \] Here $x_0,\ldots,x_m$ are homogeneous coordinates on $\mathbb P^m$. Set \[ B=\mathbb P^m_x\times\mathbb P^2_z, \qquad \mathcal N=\mathcal O_B(-1,-1), \qquad T=\operatorname{Tot}(\mathcal N). \] If $t$ denotes the tautological fibre vector, the expression \[ F+t\ell H \] is a well-defined section of the pullback of $\mathcal O_B(0,4)$ to $T$. Define $Z$ as its zero scheme. Its zero-section divisor is \[ V=\mathbb P^m\times C, \qquad \mathcal N|_V=L^{-1}, \qquad L=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^m}(1)\boxtimes K_C. \] The curve $C$ is smooth, and $Z$ is smooth in a neighbourhood of $V$, since its differential there has the nonzero $dF$ component. The projection of $Z$ onto $B$ is the graph $t=-F/(\ell H)$ on the dense open $\ell H\ne0$. The locus $F=\ell H=0$ has codimension two in $B$, so its inverse image cannot be another component of $Z$. Thus $Z$ is integral. The standard Segre cone contraction \[ T\longrightarrow\mathbb A^{3(m+1)}, \qquad w_{ij}=t x_i z_j \] is proper, contracts the zero section, and is an isomorphism outside it. Let $W$ be the reduced closed image of $Z$, and write $v$ for the vertex. This gives a completely algebraic finite-type construction. Explicit equations for $W$ are the radical of the following ideal: all $2$ by $2$ minors of $(w_{ij})$, together with, for every ordered quadruple $I=(i_1,i_2,i_3,i_4)$, \begin{equation} \sum_{j=0}^{2}\prod_{r=1}^{4}w_{i_rj} +f\sum_{0\le a<b\le2} w_{i_1a}w_{i_2a}w_{i_3b}w_{i_4b}=0, \qquad f=w_{00}+w_{11}+w_{22}. \end{equation} Indeed on the rank-one locus the left side is $t^4x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_4}(F+t\ell H)$; choosing a nonzero row proves the converse away from $v$. The vertex lies in the closure of this integral open, so the reduced image is integral. Let $W^{\mathrm n}$ be the normalization of the original reduced affine scheme $W$; it is finite. For the proof of its local properties choose an open neighbourhood $W^\circ$ of $v$ such that $Z^\circ=Z\times_W W^\circ$ is smooth. Such a neighbourhood exists: the image of the complement of the smooth locus is closed by properness and does not contain $v$. The normal smooth scheme $Z^\circ$ factors through $(W^{\mathrm n})^\circ$, the inverse image of $W^\circ$; the factor is proper, birational and an isomorphism away from the vertex. There is only one point $v^{\mathrm n}$ above $v$. In fact the factorization is surjective, and the connected fibre $V$ cannot map onto more than one point in the finite fibre of the normalization. Its residue field is $\mathbb C$. Define \[ A=\mathcal O_{W^{\mathrm n},v^{\mathrm n}}, \qquad R=A^{\mathrm{sh}}, \qquad \mathcal Z=Z^\circ\times_{(W^{\mathrm n})^\circ} \operatorname{Spec}R. \] In particular $R$ is specified by the original polynomial equations and normalization, followed by localization at its unique vertex and strict henselization. The auxiliary shrinking only proves regularity and introduces no choice in $R$. Then $R$ has all the asserted excellence, normality and dimension properties. The regular scheme $\mathcal Z$ is proper over $R$, its exceptional fibre is the irreducible smooth divisor $V$, and its complement is the regular puncture $X$. These statements are preserved under the pointed etale limit defining the strict henselization. The displayed $f$ is a nonzero nonunit in $R$, and on $Z$ it equals $t\ell$. The global equation of the strict transform of its divisor is \[ D=V(\ell,F)\subset T, \] the total space of $L_H^{-1}$ over \[ H_0=V(\ell)\subset V, \qquad L_H=L|_{H_0}. \] Indeed setting $\ell=0$ in the equation of $Z$ leaves $F=0$. The surjection \[ \mathcal O_C^{m+1}\longrightarrow K_C, \qquad (a_i)\longmapsto a_0z_0+a_1z_1+a_2z_2 \] identifies $H_0$ with the projective bundle of lines in its rank-$m$ kernel. In particular $H_0$ and $D$ are smooth. Set $D^\circ=D\cap Z^\circ$; its morphism to $(W^{\mathrm n})^\circ$ is the restriction of the factorization already constructed. The base change \[ \mathcal D=D^\circ\times_{(W^{\mathrm n})^\circ} \operatorname{Spec}R \] is regular and proper over $R$. Its exceptional divisor is $H_0$, with normal bundle $L_H^{-1}$, and \[ \mathcal D\setminus H_0=Y=X\cap V(f). \] This proves regularity of the required punctured divisor, without asserting any projective-normality property of its section ring. \emph{2. A full-rank first-neighbourhood deformation.} Let $V_2\subset\mathcal Z$ be defined by the square of the ideal of $V$. It is a square-zero thickening of $V$ by $L$. Its class \[ \kappa\in H^1(V,T_V\otimes L) \] is obtained by taking the boundary of $\ell H$ in the normal sequence of $V\subset B$, twisted by $L$. Its curve component is \begin{equation} \kappa=\sum_{i=0}^{2}x_i\otimes\delta(z_iH), \qquad \delta:H^0(C,\mathcal O_C(5))\longrightarrow H^1(C,\mathcal O_C), \end{equation} where $\delta$ is the boundary of \[ 0\longrightarrow T_C\otimes K_C=\mathcal O_C \longrightarrow T_{\mathbb P^2}|_C\otimes K_C \longrightarrow\mathcal O_C(5)\longrightarrow0. \] To verify the class directly, choose local vector fields lifting the normal displacement $\ell H$. Their differences on overlaps are the derivations which identify the local retractions of $V_2$ onto $V$; this is precisely the boundary cocycle. The sign depends on the choice of retraction and does not affect the injectivity below. The Euler sequence twisted by $K_C=\mathcal O_C(1)$ and Serre duality give $H^1(C,T_{\mathbb P^2}|_C\otimes K_C)=0$. Thus $\delta$ is surjective. More explicitly its cokernel description is the degree-five part of the Fermat Jacobian ring: \[ H^1(C,\mathcal O_C) \simeq \left(\frac{\mathbb C[z_0,z_1,z_2]} {(z_0^3,z_1^3,z_2^3)}\right)_5. \] Here the image of quadratic vector fields consists of the degree-five Jacobian ideal, modulo the three multiples $z_iF$ already zero on $C$. statement: C.3n (Proved): ordinary degree-one injectivity with a coefficient field, in every characteristic.. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, and let $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$ be an excellent normal strictly henselian local $k$-algebra whose residue map restricts to the identity on the specified coefficient field $k$. Assume $N=\dim R\ge3$. Put \[ X=\operatorname{Spec}R\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}, \qquad Y=X\cap V(f),\qquad 0\ne f\in\mathfrak m, \] and assume $X$ and $Y$ regular. Ordinary algebraic equivalence is defined by actual line bundles on the fixed $k$-scheme times a smooth connected $k$-curve. Then \begin{equation} \ker\bigl(\operatorname{Pic}(X)_{\mathrm{alg}} \longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(Y)_{\mathrm{alg}}\bigr) \begin{cases} =0,&\operatorname{char}k=0,\\ \text{is $p$-primary torsion},&\operatorname{char}k=p>0. \end{cases} \end{equation} In particular $J^1(X)\to J^1(Y)$ is injective with rational coefficients in every characteristic; in characteristic $p$ the integral map also becomes injective after tensoring with $\mathbb Z[1/p]$. Neither algebraizability nor a resolution of singularities is assumed. The coefficient-field hypothesis is retained explicitly; this statement does not reinterpret ordinary algebraic equivalence over an unspecified mixed-characteristic base.

Assume $N=\dim R\ge3$. Put \[ X=\operatorname{Spec}R\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}, \qquad Y=X\cap V(f),\qquad 0\ne f\in\mathfrak m, \] and assume $X$ and $Y$ regular. Ordinary algebraic equivalence is defined by actual line bundles on the fixed $k$-scheme times a smooth connected $k$-curve. Then \begin{equation} \ker\bigl(\operatorname{Pic}(X)_{\mathrm{alg}} \longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(Y)_{\mathrm{alg}}\bigr) \begin{cases} =0,&\operatorname{char}k=0,\\ \text{is $p$-primary torsion},&\operatorname{char}k=p>0. \end{cases} \end{equation} In particular $J^1(X)\to J^1(Y)$ is injective with rational coefficients in every characteristic; in characteristic $p$ the integral map also becomes injective after tensoring with $\mathbb Z[1/p]$. Neither algebraizability nor a resolution of singularities is assumed. The coefficient-field hypothesis is retained explicitly; this statement does not reinterpret ordinary algebraic equivalence over an unspecified mixed-characteristic base.

statement: C.3p (Known with derivation): local etale Lefschetz, Picard torsion, and completion.. Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be an excellent normal strictly henselian local ring, let $0\ne f\in\mathfrak m$, and write \[ X=\operatorname{Spec}R\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}, \qquad Y=X\cap V(f),\qquad N=\dim R. \] Assume $X$ regular. Restriction of finite etale covers is fully faithful for $N\ge3$ and is an equivalence for $N\ge4$: \begin{equation} \operatorname{FEt}(X)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{FEt}(Y)\qquad(N\ge4). \end{equation} If also $Y$ is regular, then, for every positive integer $n$ invertible in $R$, \begin{equation} \operatorname{Pic}(X)[n]\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[n]\qquad(N\ge4). \end{equation} This assertion includes mixed characteristic and has no coefficient-field or algebraizability hypothesis. Separately, in the coefficient-field setting of C.3n, completion induces a canonical isomorphism of the represented local Picard functors \begin{equation} \mathbf{Pic}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{R/k} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathbf{Pic}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{\widehat R/k} \qquad(N\ge3). \end{equation} The functors in this last assertion use henselized tensor products as defined in C.3n. It does not identify their arbitrary parameter families with line bundles on the fixed product $X\times T$.

statement: C.3q (Proved under the stated geometric hypotheses): lifting abelian subgroups of the local Picard functor in characteristic $p$.. Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $p>0$. Let $R$ be the strict henselization at a $k$-rational point of a normal local scheme essentially of finite type over $k$. Suppose $N=\dim R\ge4$ and that \[ X=\operatorname{Spec}R\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}, \qquad Y=X\cap V(f),\qquad0\ne f\in\mathfrak m, \] are regular. Put \[ G=\mathbf{Pic}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{R/k},\qquad H=\prod_a\mathbf{Pic}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{C_a/k}, \qquad r:G\longrightarrow H, \] where $\prod_a C_a$ is the finite normalization of $R/(f)$ and $r$ is the restriction morphism of local Picard group schemes. These group schemes are locally of finite type, since $\dim C_a=N-1\ge3$; as in C.3n, $G(k)=\operatorname{Pic}(X)$ and $H(k)=\operatorname{Pic}(Y)$. For every closed abelian subvariety $B\subset H$ there exist a closed abelian subvariety $A\subset G$, an integer $e\ge0$, and isogenies of abelian varieties over $k$ \begin{equation} s:B\longrightarrow A,\qquad r_A:A\longrightarrow B,\qquad r_A\circ s=[p^e]_B, \end{equation} where $r_A$ is induced by $r$. Both isogenies have $p$-primary kernels. Thus every target abelian subgroup lifts up to a power-of-$p$ isogeny at the level of the specified local Picard functors.

statement: C.3s (Refuted in every available positive codimension): universal local Chow and ordinary-$J$ finiteness.. Let $N\ge2$ and $1\le r\le N-1$ be arbitrary integers. There exists an explicitly specified excellent normal strictly henselian local $\mathbb C$-algebra of dimension $N$, with regular puncture $U$, such that \[ \mathrm{CH}^r(U)_{\mathrm{alg}}\otimes\mathbb Q\ne0. \] Consequently neither $\mathrm{CH}^r(U)$ nor its ordinary algebraically trivial subgroup is universally finite in any available positive codimension. For $r\ge N$ these groups are zero for every such puncture, since it has no point of codimension $r$. Thus this is the exact universal finiteness/vanishing range for these two groups over $\mathbb C$. The groups modulo algebraic equivalence remain separately governed by C.3g and its stated ranges.

statement: C.3t (Refuted in every odd critical dimension): ordinary local Gysin vanishing.. Let $r\ge2$ and \[ r+1\le N\le2r-1. \] We construct an excellent normal strictly henselian local complex ring of dimension $N$, a nonzero element $f$ of its maximal ideal, and regular punctures $X$ and $Y=X\cap V(f)$, such that the Gysin map \[ J^{r-1}(Y)\longrightarrow J^r(X) \] has a non-torsion integral image. statement: C.3u (Proved under the stated cone hypotheses): ordinary degree-one surjectivity in every characteristic.. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of arbitrary characteristic. Let $V$ be a smooth projective integral $k$-variety of dimension $d\ge3$, and let $L$ be a very ample invertible sheaf such that its full section ring \[ S=\bigoplus_{a\ge0}H^0(V,L^a) \] is generated in degree one. Write $\mathfrak v=S_{>0}$, and form the normal strictly henselian cone local ring and its puncture \[ R=(S_{\mathfrak v})^{\mathrm{sh}},\qquad X=\operatorname{Spec}R\setminus\{\mathfrak m\}, \qquad N=d+1\ge4. \] The geometric residue field in this strict henselization is the given field $k$. Let $0\ne f\in\mathfrak m$, and suppose $Y=X\cap V(f)$ is regular. The element $f$ need not be homogeneous. Let $\rho:X\to V$ be the cone projection, and put $A=(\operatorname{Pic}^0_{V/k})_{\mathrm{red}}$. For ordinary algebraic equivalence defined by actual line bundles on products with smooth connected $k$-curves, the following statements hold: \begin{align} A(k)&\xrightarrow[\rho^*]{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Pic}(X)_{\mathrm{alg}}, \\ \operatorname{Pic}(X)_{\mathrm{alg}} &\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(Y)_{\mathrm{alg}} \quad\text{is surjective}. \end{align} In characteristic zero the map in \eqref{eq:C3-cone-ordinary-surjectivity} is an isomorphism. In characteristic $p>0$ its kernel is a finite $p$-primary group. Consequently \[ J^1(X)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }J^1(Y) \] with rational coefficients in every characteristic. These are statements about the specified smooth cone source and arbitrary regular divisor punctures inside it; they do not impose a cone structure on the divisor or assert the same conclusion for a deformation of the source cone.

statement: C.3v (Refuted already in dimension two): finiteness of the ordinary divisor quotient.. For every $N\ge2$, there is an explicitly specified excellent normal strictly henselian local $\mathbb C$-algebra $R_N$ of dimension $N$, with regular puncture $X_N$, for which \begin{equation} B^1(X_N):=\frac{\operatorname{Pic}(X_N)} {\operatorname{Pic}(X_N)_{\mathrm{alg}}} \simeq \begin{cases} (\mathbb C,+)\oplus\mathbb Z/4,&N=2,\\ (\mathbb C,+)^{N-1}\oplus\mathbb Z,&N\ge3. \end{cases} \end{equation} Here algebraic equivalence is ordinary algebraic equivalence through line bundles on the fixed product with a smooth connected curve. Thus a finiteness assertion for the degree-one quotient on 14:107 is false on this reading. The quotient using the connected local Picard functor is a different relation and is not refuted by this calculation.

statement: C.3z (Proved): removing the algebraizability restriction for the ordinary degree-one theorem.. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $(R,\mathfrak m,k)$ be an excellent henselian normal noetherian local $k$-algebra whose specified coefficient map induces the identity on the residue field. statement: C.4aa. A countermodel to an unrestricted graph-transfer principle (Proved).. Let $\Lambda=\mathbb Z_{(2)}$, let $U=\mathbb Z^2$, and consider \[ q_1=x^2,\qquad q_2=y^2,\qquad q_3=(2x+y)^2. \] There is no finite three-coloured graph $G$ and no positive integer $d$ admitting a common $\Lambda$-orthogonal direct-sum decomposition \[ H_1(G,\Lambda)=\iota(U_\Lambda)\oplus\ker\beta, \qquad \beta\iota=1, \] for which the restriction of the colour-$s$ graph form is $dq_s$ for all three colours. Nevertheless, these three forms are the monodromy forms of an algebraic family of principally polarized abelian surfaces, every geometric fibre of which has an algebraic minimal curve class. Thus a graph-transfer conclusion of this form cannot follow from algebraicity alone for arbitrary integral monodromy cones.

The Hodge-endomorphism assumptions therefore make $t,s,n$ integers: each scalar preserves a nonzero free lattice, and $\ell$ is primitive. There are no rational Hodge homomorphisms between $T(A)_{\mathbb Q}$ and $\mathbb Q\ell$. Indeed a map in one direction would give a rational Hodge class in $T(A)$, and duality gives the same conclusion in the other direction. The lattice $H^2(A,\mathbb Z)$ is unimodular, and $\ell^2=4$. Choose $w$ in this lattice with $(w,\ell)=1$. The decomposition of $Z^*$ into its two rational eigenspaces gives \[ Z^*w-sw=\frac{n-s}{4}\ell. \] The left side is integral, and $\ell$ is primitive. Consequently \[ n-s\in4\mathbb Z. \tag{PF.2} \] Write $\Delta_{22}$ for the $(2,2)$ component of the diagonal. This follows from the leading-degree part of Grothendieck--Riemann--Roch; the cycle pushforward has coefficient one because each resolution is birational onto $Z_i$. Indeed, such a projector has $t=1,s=0$, so the forward construction applies. Conversely the normalized divisor $D_i$ above has only the component $H^1(A)\otimes H^1(C_i)$. Its pushforward therefore has only component $(1,3)$, and the sum acts as the identity on $H^1$. Thus its cohomology class is exactly $\delta_1$. Assume that $\gamma$ is finite and generically separable. The cycle of its fibre product is \[ [S\times_Y S]=[\Delta_S]+[W], \] where $W$ is the residual correspondence, with its natural cycle multiplicities. statement: C.4b (Proved corrected integral form of 2.4--2.5).. Let $X,Y$ be smooth projective connected varieties over $k$ and let $Z\in\mathrm{CH}_1(X\times Y)$ be integral. It defines $u_Z:B_X\to A_Y$ and, for $n=\dim X$, \[ a(Z):H^1(Y,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^{2n-1}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell)(n-1). \] This is an isomorphism if and only if $u_Z$ is an isogeny. In that case its inverse is induced by the unique class corresponding to $u_Z^{-1}\in\operatorname{Hom}(A_Y,B_X)_{\mathbb Q}$. It is represented by an integral normalized divisor correspondence if and only if $u_Z$ is an isomorphism. More precisely, for a positive integer $m$, \begin{equation} m u_Z^{-1}\in\operatorname{Hom}(A_Y,B_X) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad [m]|_{\ker u_Z}=0 \end{equation} as a morphism of finite group schemes. If the right side holds, $[m]:B_X\to B_X$ factors through the fppf quotient $B_X/\ker u_Z=A_Y$, yielding the left side. Conversely, $(m u_Z^{-1})u_Z=[m]$ kills the kernel. Thus the least positive denominator is the \emph{exponent} of $\ker u_Z$, not generally its order. For $u=[2]$ on a $g$-dimensional abelian variety, it is $2$, whereas the kernel order is $2^{2g}$, including in characteristic $2$ when its scheme structure must be retained. This refutes the strongest literal ``best denominator'' reading of 14:64 while preserving its assertion about the set of possible prime divisors. The induced map \[ H^1(Y,\mathbb Z_\ell)\longrightarrow H^{2n-1}(X,\mathbb Z_\ell)(n-1)/\mathrm{tors} \] is an isomorphism precisely when $u_Z$ is an isogeny of degree prime to $\ell$. Indeed it is the corresponding map of free Tate-module lattices; its index has $\ell$-adic valuation $v_\ell(\deg u_Z)$. An isomorphism before dividing out torsion also requires the target to be torsion free. This is the exact distinction made by the insertions in Corollary 2.5.

statement: C.4e (Proved equivalence for principal polarizations; known counterexamples).. For a principally polarized complex abelian variety $(A,\theta)$ of dimension $g$, Question 2 is equivalent to algebraicity, with \emph{integral} coefficients, of \[ \gamma_\theta=\frac{\theta^{g-1}}{(g-1)!} \in H^{2g-2}(A,\mathbb Z). \] One direction can be read directly from a curve decomposition of $\gamma_\theta$: the induced map $\widehat A\to A$ is the inverse principal polarization, as is checked in a symplectic basis; composing with that polarization gives the identity factorization in C.4d. For the other direction, a direct summand of a product of Jacobians satisfies the integral Hodge conjecture for curves. Indeed the theorem for the product is \citet[Theorem 1.2]{cyBeckmannFortman2023}; pushing an integral Hodge homology class along the inclusion and then pushing an algebraic representative back along the retraction proves the claim for the summand. Apply it to $\gamma_\theta$. This agrees with \citet[Theorem 1.4, Proposition 2.1, Corollary 2.5]{cyVoisin2024}; the published theorem number is 1.4, although an earlier revision labels it 1.3. Over arbitrary algebraically closed fields, the relevant extension is \citet[Theorem 1.2]{cyScaviaSuzuki2025}: it retains the integral $\ell$-adic conditions for every $\ell\ne p$ and the crystalline condition at $p$. Thus a single prime-to-$p$ assertion must not be silently promoted to an integral assertion including $p$. For a principal polarization the polarization itself is already algebraic. The modern universal integral assertion is false. \citet[Theorem 1.1]{cyEngelFortmanSchreieder2026} proves that on a very general complex principally polarized abelian variety of dimension $g\ge4$, a curve class is an even multiple of $\gamma_\theta$. Question 2 therefore fails there. Their Corollary 1.2 identifies the cycle-class image in dimensions $4$ and $5$ as exactly $2\mathbb Z\gamma_\theta$. We have checked the theorem and corollary in version 3 of the primary source, and do not substitute a historical claim of openness for this newer result.

statement: C.4f (Proved cases and the precise outstanding small-dimensional case).. Question 2 holds for a curve: the Abel map identifies its $H^1$ with that of its Jacobian and its graph gives the needed one-cycle. It holds for Jacobians and products of Jacobians, in every characteristic, by the splitting in C.4d; this includes all products of elliptic curves. It holds for principally polarized abelian varieties of dimension at most three: over an algebraically closed field these are Jacobians of compact-type curves, hence products of Jacobians \citep[Theorem 4]{cyOortUeno1973}. These statements do not decide Question 2 for every \emph{non-principally-polarized} abelian surface or threefold. Knowing the integral Hodge conjecture for curves on $A$ alone is insufficient for that inference; the general criterion over $\mathbb C$ uses $A\times\widehat A$, equivalently the actual splitting in C.4d. Passing to an isogenous principally polarized variety is not an integral splitting. This is a remaining gate in the precise scope of C.4.

statement: C.4h (Proved: the ideal of scalar factorizations).. Let $A$ be an abelian variety of positive dimension $g$ over an algebraically closed field $k$, in arbitrary characteristic. We define \[ I_J(A)=\{n\in\mathbb Z:\ [n]_A=v\circ u \text{ for some }A\xrightarrow{u}\prod_jJ(C_j) \xrightarrow{v}A\}, \] where each $C_j$ is a smooth projective connected curve over $k$. This is an ideal of $\mathbb Z$. Indeed, multiplication of $v$ by an integer realizes integer multiples; the product of two intermediate products of Jacobians realizes the sum of their two composites. We will prove below that $I_J(A)\ne0$, and write $I_J(A)=s_J(A)\mathbb Z$ with $s_J(A)>0$. Then \begin{equation} A\text{ is an actual direct summand of a product of Jacobians} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad s_J(A)=1. \end{equation} For completeness, if $v u=1_A$, the maps \[ A\times\ker v\longrightarrow J,\quad(a,b)\longmapsto u(a)+b, \qquad J\longrightarrow A\times\ker v,\quad x\longmapsto(v(x),x-u v(x)) \] are mutually inverse as group schemes. The kernel is a connected smooth proper group: smoothness follows from the splitting of the differential of $v$, and connectedness from the displayed product decomposition. It is consequently an abelian variety. The definition also gives \[ s_J(\widehat A)=s_J(A),\qquad s_J(A\times B)=\operatorname{lcm}(s_J(A),s_J(B)). \] For the first assertion we dualize a factorization and use the canonical principal polarizations of the Jacobians. For the second we restrict and project a factorization to each factor, and conversely combine two factorizations of the same integer. Here is the exact isogeny calculation needed later. If $f:A\to B$ is an isogeny and the \emph{group scheme} $\ker f$ is killed by $e>0$, the quotient property gives a homomorphism $h:B\to A$ with $h f=[e]_A$; surjectivity of $f$ also gives $f h=[e]_B$. Thus \begin{equation} eI_J(B)\subset I_J(A),\qquad eI_J(A)\subset I_J(B). \end{equation} In particular an isogeny whose kernel is killed by an integer prime to $\ell$ preserves the $\ell$-adic valuation of $s_J$. We may always take $e=\deg f$; this remains true for inseparable isogenies \citep[Section 8, paragraph after Proposition 8.1, p.~12 of the corrected text]{frC4Milne1986}. None of these statements replaces an integral retraction by a rational inverse to an isogeny.
