statement: C.4i (Proved: a uniform factorial bound in every characteristic).. For every $A$ as above, \begin{equation} s_J(A)\mid(2g-1)!. \end{equation} We spell out the algebraic construction, including the integer in the composite. This is a quantitative application of the proof of \citet[Proposition 3.4, equations (3.1)--(3.3)]{cyScaviaSuzuki2025}, not an inference from rational cohomology alone. We first record its useful form. Suppose $X$ has dimension $d$, $\theta=c_1(L)\in\mathrm{NS}(X)$, and an integral curve cycle $\alpha$ has numerical class \[ \alpha=n\,\frac{\theta^{d-1}}{(d-1)!}. \] Write $\alpha=\sum_j m_j(f_j)_*[C_j]$ using normalizations of its integral curve components. Such normalizations are smooth over the algebraically closed field, including in characteristics $2$ and $3$. Choose base points and let $\bar f_j:J(C_j)\to X$ be the induced homomorphisms. Set $J=\prod_jJ(C_j)$, let $\lambda_j:J(C_j)\xrightarrow{\sim}\widehat{J(C_j)}$ be its canonical polarization, and define \[ U:X\longrightarrow J,\quad U=(\lambda_j^{-1}\widehat{\bar f_j}\,\varphi_\theta)_j, \qquad V:J\longrightarrow X,\quad V=\sum_jm_j\bar f_j. \] Matsusaka's identity gives the equality of homomorphisms \begin{equation} VU=[\,n\chi(L)\,]_X,\qquad \chi(L)=\deg\frac{\theta^d}{d!}. \end{equation} The sign is the positive sign in equation (3.1) of the cited proof: its two occurrences of Matsusaka's $\delta$ have the same negative sign and cancel. statement: C.4j (Proved: a simultaneous polarization criterion in dimensions at most three).. Define the positive integer \[ \delta(A)=\gcd\{\chi(L):L\in\mathrm{Pic}(A)\}. \] Equivalently, we may take the gcd only over ample $L$. To see this, fix an ample $H$ and any line bundle $L$. The function $t\mapsto\chi(L\otimes H^t)$ is a polynomial of degree at most $g$ with integer values. For all sufficiently large consecutive integers $t$, the line bundles are ample. Integral finite differences, or interpolation in the binomial basis shifted to these integers, express its value at $0$ as an integral linear combination of these values. Hence their common divisor divides $\chi(L)$. If $1\le g\le3$, then \begin{equation} \boxed{\quad s_J(A)\mid \gcd\bigl((2g-1)!,\delta(A)\bigr).\quad} \end{equation} Indeed, let $L$ be ample. The group-scheme form of the polarization descent theorem gives a maximal isotropic subgroup scheme $H\subset K(L)$, a quotient isogeny $f:A\to B=A/H$, and a principal polarization $M$ on $B$ with $f^*M\simeq L$. This is \citet[Section 23, Theorem 4 and Corollary 1, pp.~233--234]{frC4Mumford1970}; its proof explicitly includes $\mu_p$ and $\alpha_p$, so it has no separability restriction. Riemann--Roch gives \[ \deg f=\chi(L). \] By \citet[Theorem 4, p.~2 of the opened preprint]{cyOortUeno1973}, the principally polarized variety $B$, in these dimensions and over any algebraically closed field, is the Jacobian of a compact-type curve, and therefore the product of the Jacobians of its smooth irreducible components. Thus $\chi(L)\in I_J(A)$ by \eqref{eq:c4-isogeny-divisibility}. Taking the gcd and using \eqref{eq:c4-factorial-bound} proves the claim. Consequently it suffices that, for \emph{each} prime $\ell\mid(2g-1)!$, there exist an ample line bundle $L_\ell$ on $A$ with $\ell\nmid\chi(L_\ell)$. The choices of $L_\ell$ may be different. We take the finitely many resulting factorizations, together with the factorial factorization, and integers $a_j$ with $\sum_j a_j n_j=1$. If $v_j u_j=[n_j]_A$, then \[ u=(u_j)_j,\qquad v=\sum_j a_jv_j \quad\text{satisfy}\quad vu=1_A. \] This constructs a single actual retraction. In particular: \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c} \dim A & \text{universal bound for }s_J(A) &\text{sufficient local polarization checks}\\ \hline 2 & 6 & \ell=2,3\\ 3 & 120 & \ell=2,3,5. \end{array} \] If $k$ has characteristic $2$ or $3$, the check at that very prime is retained. The construction uses finite subgroup schemes rather than their sets of geometric points. The kernel exponent can improve the quantitative divisibility: if a principalization has kernel killed by $e$, we obtain $s_J(A)\mid\gcd((2g-1)!,e)$. For a separable polarization of type $(d_1,\ldots,d_g)$, its kernel has exponent $d_g$, so we may use $e=d_g$. For an inseparable polarization we use its actual group-scheme kernel exponent, or the always valid bound $e=\chi(L)$; a prime-to-characteristic elementary-divisor description must not be substituted for the full kernel.

statement: C.4k (Proved: what the N\'eron--Severi calculation establishes).. For an abelian surface, choose a basis $D_1,\ldots,D_\rho$ of $\mathrm{NS}(A)$, and write $q_i=D_i^2/2$ and $b_{ij}=D_iD_j$. Then \begin{equation} \delta(A)=\gcd\bigl(\{q_i\}_i,\{b_{ij}\}_{i<j}\bigr). \end{equation} Indeed, $\chi(\sum n_iD_i)=\sum_iq_in_i^2+\sum_{i<j}b_{ij}n_in_j$; the reverse divisibility follows by evaluating at $D_i$ and $D_i+D_j$. Thus this particular sufficient test is a finite integral lattice calculation. In dimension three we may compute the analogous gcd from the Euler polynomial on the finite grid $0\le n_i\le3$: its successive finite differences are integral, and the binomial-basis interpolation expresses every other integer value as an integral combination of these grid values. If $\mathrm{NS}(A)=\mathbb Z[L]$ for a primitive ample $L$, then $\delta(A)=\chi(L)$, since $\chi(L^n)=n^g\chi(L)$. In particular a complex surface with primitive polarization type $(1,d)$ is settled whenever $\gcd(d,6)=1$; a complex threefold with primitive polarization type $(1,d_2,d_3)$ is settled whenever $\gcd(d_2d_3,30)=1$. These are sufficient conditions and give no counterexample when the gcd is larger than one. There is a precise limitation on the proposed coprime-isogeny method. An isogeny $A\to B$ of degree prime to $\ell$, with $B$ principally polarized, pulls a principal line bundle back to an ample $L$ with $\ell\nmid\chi(L)$. The converse follows from Mumford's principalization. Therefore, when $\ell\mid\delta(A)$, there is \emph{no} such prime-to-$\ell$ principalization in the same dimension, even if we allow all possible quotient polarizations. This rules out that particular proof strategy in the residual Picard-rank-one cases; it does not rule out a retraction through Jacobians of higher dimension.

statement: C.4l (Proved limitation of divisor products; no geometric counterexample asserted).. We can make the residual surface calculation more explicit. Let $A/\mathbb C$ have $\mathrm{End}(A)=\mathbb Z$ and $\mathrm{NS}(A)=\mathbb Z[L]$, with $L$ of type $(1,d)$. Let $\widehat L$ be the primitive dual polarization, normalized by $\varphi_{\widehat L}\varphi_L=[d]$. On $A\times\widehat A$ put $D=\operatorname{pr}_1^*c_1(L)$, $\widehat D=\operatorname{pr}_2^*c_1(\widehat L)$ and $P=c_1(\mathcal P_A)$. The N\'eron--Severi group is generated by $D,\widehat D,P$: the cross summand is $\operatorname{Hom}(A,\widehat{\widehat A})=\operatorname{End}(A)$. The endomorphisms induced on $\widehat A$ by integral curve cycles that are integer combinations of products of three divisors form exactly \begin{equation} \gcd(6,d)\,\mathbb Z\,1_{\widehat A}. \end{equation} Here is a direct calculation, avoiding an assumption that all integral curve classes are generated by divisors. Choose an integral symplectic basis $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ for $H^1(A,\mathbb Z)$ and the dual basis $y_1,\ldots,y_4$ for $H^1(\widehat A,\mathbb Z)$ so that \[ D=x_1x_2+d\,x_3x_4,\quad \widehat D=d\,y_1y_2+y_3y_4,\quad P=\sum_{a=1}^{4}x_ay_a. \] Products here mean exterior products. The normalized class $P^3/6$ has the cross component inducing $1_{\widehat A}$, and expansion gives \begin{equation} D\widehat D P=-d\,P^3/6. \end{equation} The only degree-three monomials in these divisor classes with K\"unneth bidegree $(3,3)$ are $P^3$ and $D\widehat D P$; the other monomials have no component inducing a map $\widehat A\to\widehat A$. They therefore give precisely the integers generated by $6$ and $d$. The identification of the cross component follows either from the curve-factorization formula in C.4a or from \eqref{eq:c4-matsusaka-integer} for $P$. The script \texttt{verify\_c4\_exterior.py} checks the exterior identity symbolically, together with its factorial normalization. Thus for $d=2$, $3$, or $6$ the divisor-product calculation itself cannot produce the desired identity. This is a proved statement about that subring of algebraic cycles, not a statement about all of $\mathrm{CH}_1(A\times\widehat A)$. The rational Hodge group calculation does not justify replacing the latter integral group by the former.

statement: C.4q (Proved: the exact contribution of curves in proper abelian subvarieties).. Put $e=d_g$, and write \[ e=u v^2\quad(u\text{ square-free}),\qquad \kappa(e)=uv=\prod_{\ell\mid e}\ell^{\lceil v_\ell(e)/2\rceil}. \] Let $X=A\times\widehat A$, and let $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{prop}}(X)$ be the subgroup of $H^{4g-2}(X,\mathbb Z)$ generated by the classes of integral curves contained in translates of proper abelian subvarieties of $X$. We use the integral cohomological Fourier transform, followed by the canonical interchange of the factors of $\widehat X=\widehat A\times A$, to identify $H^{4g-2}(X,\mathbb Z)$ with $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$. If $D$ and $\widehat D$ are the pullbacks of the primitive ample classes on the two factors and $P=c_1(\mathcal P_A)$, then \begin{equation} \boxed{\quad \mathcal F_X\bigl(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{prop}}(X)\bigr) =\mathbb ZD\oplus\kappa(e)\mathbb ZP \oplus\mathbb Z\widehat D. \quad} \end{equation} Here the factor interchange is understood in the notation $\mathcal F_X$. Consequently the smallest positive multiple of \[ \mathcal R_A=\frac{P^{2g-1}}{(2g-1)!} \] that belongs to $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{prop}}(X)$ is exactly $\kappa(e)$. In particular, this restricted source of curves cannot remove any prime dividing $e$ from the direct-summand problem. This is a statement about a specified subgroup of curve classes, not a counterexample to algebraicity of $\mathcal R_A$.

statement: C.4r (Proved: a single integral numerical surface class detects the remaining cases).. Let $A$ be an abelian variety of dimension $g\in\{2,3\}$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ of arbitrary characteristic. Put $X=A\times\widehat A$, write $P=c_1(\mathcal P_A)$, and set \[ N^r(X)=\mathrm{CH}^r(X)/{\equiv_{\mathrm{num}}}, \qquad r=2g-2, \] with integral coefficients. We regard this torsion-free group as a subgroup of $N^r(X)_{\mathbb Q}$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $A$ is an actual direct summand of a product of Jacobians; \item the rational numerical class \[ \gamma_A=\frac{P^{2g-2}}{(2g-2)!} \in N^{2g-2}(X)_{\mathbb Q} \] belongs to the integral numerical lattice $N^{2g-2}(X)$. \end{enumerate} Thus we require an integral dimension-two cycle numerically equivalent to $P^2/2$ for a surface, or to $P^4/24$ for a threefold. Over $\mathbb C$ the same conditions are also equivalent to integral algebraicity of the corresponding integral Hodge class.

statement: C.4s (Known consequence: every supersingular surface is affirmative).. Every supersingular abelian surface over an algebraically closed field of positive characteristic is an actual direct summand of a product of Jacobians, including in characteristic two. Indeed, \citet[Lemma 6.2, p.~185]{frC4FuLi2021} prove that it admits a principal polarization. Their Proposition 6.1, p.~184, explicitly includes characteristic two in the N\'eron--Severi lattice calculation used by the proof. The principally polarized surface case C.4f then applies. This does not settle arbitrary nonsupersingular surfaces whose polarization Euler characteristics are all even.

statement: C.4t (Known exclusion, with the generic strengthening proved: the natural principally polarized product is not a genus-four Jacobian).. Let $(A,L)$ be a complex abelian surface of polarization type $(1,2)$. Write $\lambda=\lambda_L:A\to\widehat A$, and let $\widehat\lambda:\widehat A\to A$ be its dual polarization, normalized by $\widehat\lambda\lambda=[2]_A$ and $\lambda\widehat\lambda=[2]_{\widehat A}$. On $X=A\times\widehat A$, the symmetric homomorphism \[ \Lambda= \begin{pmatrix}\lambda&1\\1&\widehat\lambda\end{pmatrix} :X\longrightarrow\widehat X \] is a principal polarization. The principally polarized variety $(X,\Lambda)$ is not the Jacobian of any smooth connected genus-four curve. If, in addition, \[ \operatorname{End}(A)=\mathbb Z,\qquad \operatorname{NS}(A)=\mathbb Z[L], \] then every principal polarization on $X$ is carried to $\Lambda$ by an automorphism of $X$. In that case the unpolarized abelian variety $X$ is not isomorphic to a genus-four Jacobian.

statement: C.4u (Proved: all supersingular threefolds in characteristic at least five).. Every supersingular abelian threefold over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p\ge5\) is an actual direct summand of a product of Jacobians. In characteristics two and three we obtain, respectively, \[ s_J(A)\mid2\quad(p=2),\qquad s_J(A)\mid3\quad(p=3); \] these two divisibilities do not by themselves prove a retraction. More generally, for a supersingular abelian variety \(A\) of dimension \(g\ge1\), \begin{equation} s_J(A)\mid p^{\,v_p((2g-1)!)}. \end{equation} In particular every such \(A\) is a direct summand if \(p>2g-1\).

statement: C.4v (Proved: full real multiplication removes every polarization gcd obstruction in characteristic zero).. Let \(A\) be an abelian variety of dimension \(g\) over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Suppose that there is an action \[ \mathcal O_F\hookrightarrow\operatorname{End}(A) \] of the full ring of integers of a totally real field \(F\) of degree \(g\), and a polarization whose Rosati involution fixes \(F\) pointwise. Then \[ \delta(A)=1. \] In particular, if \(g\le3\), \(A\) is an actual direct summand of a product of Jacobians. This includes a simple abelian surface or threefold with \(\operatorname{End}(A)=\mathcal O_K\) for a CM field \(K\) of degree \(2g\). No principal polarization on \(A\) is assumed. There is a useful local refinement. Suppose an order \(\mathcal O\subset F\), rather than the full integer ring, acts with the same Rosati property, and put \(c=[\mathcal O_F:\mathcal O]\). Then every prime divisor of \(\delta(A)\) divides \(c\). Consequently an abelian surface with \(c\) odd, or an abelian threefold with \(\gcd(c,6)=1\), is still an actual direct summand of a product of Jacobians. These conclusions require local maximality only at two, or at two and three, respectively.

statement: C.4w (Proved: ordinary full-real-multiplication varieties in every characteristic).. Let \(k\) be algebraically closed of characteristic \(p>0\), including \(p=2\), and let \(A/k\) be ordinary of dimension \(g\). Suppose that the full ring of integers of a totally real field \(F\) of degree \(g\) acts on \(A\), and that a polarization has Rosati involution fixing \(F\) pointwise. Then \(\delta(A)=1\). In dimensions at most three, \(A\) is therefore an actual direct summand of a product of Jacobians. statement: C.4x (Proved: full real multiplication in arbitrary positive characteristic).. Let \(k\) be algebraically closed of characteristic \(p>0\), and let \(A/k\) have dimension \(g\). Suppose that the full integer ring of a totally real field of degree \(g\) acts: \[ \mathcal O_F\hookrightarrow\operatorname{End}(A), \qquad [F:\mathbb Q]=g. \] We assume that \(A\) has a polarization whose Rosati involution fixes \(F\) pointwise, equivalently an \(\mathcal O_F\)-linear polarization. Then the integer \(\delta(A)\) of C.4j is a power of \(p\), with exponent possibly zero. If, in addition, \begin{equation} [\operatorname{Lie}(A)] =[\mathcal O_F\otimes_{\mathbb Z} k] \quad\text{in }G_0(\mathcal O_F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k), \end{equation} where \(G_0\) is the Grothendieck group of finite modules, then \[ \delta(A)=1. \] Condition \eqref{eq:c4-hb-lie-condition} is automatic if \(p\) is totally ramified in \(F\). There is no ordinarity or supersingularity hypothesis, and \(p=2\) and \(p=3\) are included. Consequently, in dimensions two and three respectively, \begin{equation} s_J(A)\mid p^{v_p(2)} \quad(g=2),\qquad s_J(A)\mid p^{v_p(6)} \quad(g=3). \end{equation} Every such surface in characteristic different from two, and every such threefold in characteristic at least five, is an actual direct summand of a product of Jacobians. In every characteristic, including the remaining two small primes, \eqref{eq:c4-hb-lie-condition} gives the same affirmative conclusion for \(g\le3\). In particular this holds when the characteristic is totally ramified in the acting real field.

statement: C.4y (Proved): a parity obstruction for semihomogeneous Chern constructions.. Let $A/\mathbb C$ be an abelian surface with $\operatorname{End}(A)=\mathbb Z$ and a primitive polarization $L$ of type $(1,2)$. Put $X=A\times\widehat A$, and write \[ \ell_1=p_A^*c_1(L),\qquad \ell_2=p_{\widehat A}^*c_1(\widehat L),\qquad P=c_1(\mathcal P_A), \] where $\widehat L$ is the dual polarization, so that $\lambda_{\widehat L}\lambda_L=[2]$. Let $R_{\rm sh}$ be the integral graded subring of numerical cycle classes on $X$ generated by the Chern classes of all semihomogeneous vector bundles on $X$. Then \[ P^2/2\notin R_{\rm sh}^{2}. \] Moreover, the mixed Matsusaka coefficient of every class in $R_{\rm sh}^{3}$ is even. Here we normalize the mixed coefficient to take the value $1$ on $P^3/6$; an overall change of Poincar\'e sign does not change the parity assertion. These statements rule out this construction of the missing class in C.4r. They assert nothing about arbitrary algebraic cycles or arbitrary vector bundles on $X$.

statement: C.5a (Proved: products over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$ vanish integrally).. Let $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_p$. For every smooth projective $X/k$, the group $\mathrm{CH}^r(X)_{\mathrm{alg}}$ is both torsion and divisible. Algebraic equivalence is generated by pushforwards of degree-zero divisor classes on smooth projective curves under correspondences. Each such Jacobian point is defined over a finite field and is therefore torsion. Multiplication by any positive integer, including $p$, is surjective on the $k$-points of a Jacobian: the corresponding isogeny is surjective as a morphism of varieties over an algebraically closed field. Its images, and sums of these images, are divisible. This proves both assertions. If $\alpha,\beta$ are algebraically trivial cycle classes, choose $m>0$ with $m\alpha=0$, and choose $\gamma$ with $\beta=m\gamma$. Bilinearity gives \[ \alpha\cdot\beta=\alpha\cdot(m\gamma)=(m\alpha)\cdot\gamma=0. \] The identical argument applies to external products on two varieties. There are no inverted primes in this proof. In particular the assertions $1^\circ$ and $1^\circ\mathrm{bis}$ of 14:126 hold integrally modulo rational equivalence over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$.

statement: C.5b (Known theorem and proved deductions: the Albanese kernel over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$).. For a smooth projective connected $X/k$ as above, \[ \operatorname{alb}_X:\mathrm{CH}_0(X)^0\xrightarrow{\sim}A_X(k) \] is an integral isomorphism. The precise opened input is \citet[Theorem 1.2]{cySpiessSzamuely2003}: it applies to a smooth variety admitting a smooth compactification over an algebraic closure of a finite field, and gives the full Albanese isomorphism on degree-zero Suslin homology. For proper $X$ that homology is $\mathrm{CH}_0(X)^0$, and $X$ is its own compactification. This includes the $p$-primary part. The prime-to-$p$ assertion of their Theorem 1.1, or prime-to-$p$ Rojtman alone, would not suffice. For an abelian variety the inverse is $x\mapsto[x]-[0]$, so this map is additive and the assertions $4^\circ$, $4^\circ\mathrm{bis}$ hold. Assertion $5^\circ$ is precisely the displayed theorem. The canonical identity $\operatorname{Alb}(X\times Y)=A_X\times A_Y$ gives $6^\circ$. The kernel generators in $2^\circ$ and the rectangle relations in $3^\circ$, $3^\circ\mathrm{bis}$ vanish by C.5a. Thus all members of the chain hold over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$, integrally. We make no assertion that $\mathrm{CH}_0(X/\mathbb F_q)^0=A_X(\mathbb F_q)$ for an arbitrary finite-field model: the theorem just used is over its algebraic closure.

statement: D.0a (Proved under the Tate identification): audit of the part of R3 used here.. Let $M$ be the full group of Weil $q$-numbers which are units away from $p$, modulo roots of unity, and let $M_0=\ker w$. The class $t=[\sqrt q]$ is Galois invariant, has weight $1$, and satisfies $e=2t$. Consequently \[ M=\mathbb Zt\oplus M_0,\qquad M/\mathbb Ze\simeq\mathbb Z/2\oplus M_0. \] The weight-zero group $M_0$ is uniquely divisible: every root of a weight-zero Weil number is again such a number, while the ambiguity between roots is killed in the quotient by roots of unity. Conjugation acts as $-1$ on $M_0$. Thus duality of multiplicative-type groups gives $U\simeq\mu_2\times D(M_0)$, with the second factor an inverse limit of compact real tori. This verifies the band calculation from the assumed Tate classification; it is not an unconditional proof of that classification. The relevant classification and endomorphism statements are \citet[Proposition 2.6 and Theorem 2.19]{Milne1994}. At $\ell\ne p$, the \'etale realization with the specified Artin identification and a Tate basis gives a point of the relative gerbe over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, so its class there is zero. For the $\mu_2$ component at $p$ and at infinity, take a supersingular elliptic curve over $\mathbb F_{q^2}$ with Frobenius $q$. Honda--Tate gives its quaternion endomorphism algebra with invariants $1/2$ at $p$ and infinity and zero elsewhere. The same Artin-descent construction written out in D.3b evaluates the character $t$ of $U$ on this algebra. Since $t$ is precisely the generator of the $\mathbb Z/2$ summand, both local $\mu_2$ components are nonzero. This checks the local assertion used from R3; it says nothing about the order of the remaining component.

statement: D.0b (Proved): audit of the real-torus step in R8.. For a compact real torus $V\simeq (R^1_{\mathbb C/\mathbb R}\mathbb G_m)^d$, the norm exact sequence gives \[ H^1(\mathbb R,V)\simeq(\mathbb Z/2)^d\simeq V(\mathbb R)[2], \qquad H^2(\mathbb R,V)=0. \] Indeed the relevant terms of the norm sequence are \[ \begin{aligned} H^1(\mathbb R,R^1\mathbb G_m) &=\mathbb R^\times/N\mathbb C^\times=\{\pm1\},\\ H^1(\mathbb R,\mathbb G_m)&=0,\qquad H^2(\mathbb R,R_{\mathbb C/\mathbb R}\mathbb G_m) =\operatorname{Br}(\mathbb C)=0 . \end{aligned} \] Exactness forces $H^2(\mathbb R,R^1\mathbb G_m)=0$. These identities also appear in the proof of \citet[Proposition 2.42]{Milne1994}. For a finite free character lattice with $w(e)=2$, the divisibility of $e$ can only be $1$ or $2$. Its kernel torus is connected in the first case. In the second, $e=2t$ with $w(t)=1$ splits the kernel as a compact torus times $\mu_2$; the nonzero quaternion component above obstructs a real fibre in the finite-field motivic setting. In the connected-kernel case, relative real fibre functors form a torsor under the displayed $H^1$. The parity homomorphisms $a:M\to\mathbb F_2$ with $a(e)=1$ form a torsor under $\operatorname{Hom}(M/\mathbb Ze,\mathbb F_2)=V(\mathbb R)[2]$. This verifies the group calculation behind the fibre/polarization correspondence used below, with its commutativity and finite-rank hypotheses explicit.

statement: D.1a (Proved): exact criterion for a rational slope to restrict to $\mu _2$.. Let $M$ be any subgroup of the group of Weil $q$-numbers, or any subgroup of its quotient by roots of unity, containing $e=q$. A prime $\mathfrak p$ over $p$ gives the additive map \[ s_{\mathfrak p}:M\longrightarrow\mathbb Q, \qquad s_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)= \frac{v_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)}{v_{\mathfrak p}(q)}. \] It satisfies $s_{\mathfrak p}(e)=1$ and $s_{\mathfrak p}(m)+s_{\mathfrak p}(cm)=w(m)$. statement: D.1e (Proved): the full category versus a finite subcategory.. In the full Weil-number group, $e=q$ is twice $\sqrt q$; its class modulo roots of unity is still twice that class. Hence $a(e)=1$ is impossible on the full connected group. In the conditional motivic setting of R3 there is no unmodified real fibre functor on the full category, for any $q$. On the full even-weight subgroup modulo roots of unity there is, in contrast, a canonical parity $a=w/2\bmod2$. It is the only parity with $a(e)=1$: its weight-zero subgroup is divisible, since all roots of a weight-zero Weil number are again weight-zero Weil numbers, and every homomorphism from a divisible group to $\mathbb F _2$ vanishes. These statements do not depend on a choice of slope. They are consistent with the uniqueness statement for parity-one polarizations on weight-zero motives in \citet[Lemma 2.46]{Milne1994}. Thus a request for a ``privileged packet'' without specifying slope compatibility has no unique mathematical meaning; with the compatibility of 15:123 it has the exact obstruction D.1a. There is nevertheless a useful alternative that works for every $q$ on every finite-type even-weight subcategory. Namely $a_0=w/2\bmod2$ is defined there, is Galois invariant, and is preserved by every automorphism respecting $w$ and $e$. The splitting $M=\mathbb Ze\oplus\ker(w/2)$ makes the kernel of $\varepsilon$ a compact real torus. By D.0b the real gerbe is neutral, and the R8 correspondence selects the fibre-functor class belonging to $a_0$. This gives a canonical singleton packet from the even grading alone. In D.1d it is $(a(e),a(f))=(1,0)$. It is not slope-compatible: it takes $2f$ to zero, whereas the admissible slope packet takes $2f$ to one. Thus the existence of an alternative Galois-invariant selection does not repair the undefined restriction of the original slope.

statement: D.2b (Refuted, with an exact finite invariant): rational transitivity.. Real transitivity does not imply rational transitivity, even in the odd-weight case. If $T$ is defined over $\mathbb Q$, let $\Delta$ be the finite image of Galois in $\operatorname{Aut}(M)$. Its rational orbits are precisely the orbits on (D.4) of the finite group \[ \overline{\mathcal A}_{\mathbb Q} =\operatorname{im}\bigl(\{A\in\operatorname{GL}(M):Ae=e,\ wA=w, \ A\delta=\delta A\ (\delta\in\Delta)\} \longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(M/2M)\bigr). \tag{D.5} \] For a possibly disconnected group of multiplicative type with character module $N$, the corresponding answer uses the image in $\operatorname{GL}(M/2M)$ of Galois-equivariant automorphisms of $N$ preserving $e,w$, where $M=N/N_{\mathrm{tors}}$. This image can be smaller than (D.5). These formulas specify the exact finite orbit invariant for a supplied character module; we do not claim a classification of all such integral Galois modules. For an explicit example arising from Weil numbers take $q=17$, \[ \alpha=1+4i,\qquad \beta=3+2\sqrt{-2},\qquad M=\langle\alpha,\overline\alpha,\beta/\overline\beta\rangle. \] Both norms are $17$. Independent conjugations of the two quadratic fields show that the displayed generators are multiplicatively independent: a relation first forces the exponent of $\beta/\bar\beta$ to vanish, then the valuations at the two primes over $17$ in $\mathbb Q(i)$ force the other two exponents to vanish. In the resulting basis $(x,y,t)$, $e=x+y$, $w=(1,1,0)$; one Galois involution exchanges $x,y$ and fixes $t$, while another fixes $x,y$ and negates $t$. A rational automorphism must preserve the three distinct rational Galois eigenspaces. Preservation of $e$ forces the invariant eigenline to be fixed, and integral invertibility forces multiplication by $\pm1$ on the other two lines. Thus the only changes on polarizations are the exchange of $a(x)$ and $a(y)$; $a(t)$ is fixed. The four polarizations form exactly two rational orbits, \[ \{(0,1,0),(1,0,0)\},\qquad \{(0,1,1),(1,0,1)\}. \] The torus is connected, so this also refutes transitivity for $\operatorname{Aut}(G,\varepsilon,j)$. Honda--Tate realizes the two weight-one numbers, and the weight-zero ratio belongs to the generated abelian-motive category. No assertion about higher Tate classes is needed to verify the lattice example. The even-weight example in D.1d has two singleton orbits even over $\mathbb R$. For the full connected Weil-number group of D.1e, the set (D.4) is empty; for its full even-weight quotient it is a singleton, fixed by all three automorphism groups. The finite-lattice classification above concerns finite-type groups, as in the dimension statements on 15:119. For a general infinite-rank character module the same automorphism action on $\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb F_2)$ gives the exact orbit relation, but we do not assert the finite-rank transitivity theorem without that hypothesis.

statement: D.3a (Proved): inversion and a coherent order-two lift.. For an abelian band $U$ over a field $k$, in a Galois-cocycle presentation of a $U$-gerbe of class $h\in H^2(k,U)$, an equivalence inducing inversion on $U$ exists if and only if $2h=0$. Whenever it exists it can be chosen to square to the identity, coherently. Thus in this particular inversion problem there is no additional order-two obstruction after $2h=0$.

statement: D.3b (Proved under the R3 band identification): the fundamental class has infinite order.. For every prime $p$ and every $q=p^n$, the class of the gerbe of fibre functors on all finite-field motives, rigidified on Artin motives and the Tate object as in R3, has infinite order. Consequently its canonical band involution, which is inversion on $U$, does not lift to any gerbe equivalence, and in particular not to an involution. The obstruction is already visible using abelian varieties and their endomorphisms.

statement: D.4b (Proved as an equivalence; finite-field conclusion conditional): the effectivity claim.. For a fixed tensor category and its specialization maps $u(s')$, define the spectral cone to consist of characters having nonnegative pairing with every conjugate of every normalized valuation of the specialized Frobenius. An algebraic number which is a unit away from its residue characteristic is integral exactly when these valuations are nonnegative. Therefore recovery of the actual effective cone from those maps is exactly the assertion that simultaneous integrality of all specialized eigenvalues implies effectivity; the reverse implication is the usual integrality property of the effective realizations. The statement is an equivalence of two descriptions of the same missing implication, not a proof of that implication. Over $\mathbb F_q$, assume the Tate classification of simple pure motives and semisimplicity. If a simple motive has integral Weil eigenvalue $\lambda$ of weight $i\geq1$, choose an $i$th root $\alpha$ of $\lambda$. Every conjugate of $\alpha$ has absolute value $q^{1/2}$ and $\alpha$ is integral. Honda--Tate gives $A/\mathbb F_q$ with $\alpha$ on $H^1(A)$; then $\lambda$ occurs on $H^i(A^i)$ by K\"unneth. A simple factor of this effective motive has the same Weil number, so Tate classification identifies it with the given simple motive. Weight zero is handled by a finite \'etale scheme, since an integral weight-zero Weil number is a root of unity. An integral nonzero number cannot have negative weight, because its nonzero integral norm would have absolute value less than $1$. Taking sums proves the finite-field assertion under the stated hypotheses. Without full faithfulness/classification, equality of Frobenius spectra alone does not identify the given motive with that effective factor.

statement: D.4c (Proved): a test for specialization to preserve a polarization.. Let $(\mathcal C,w,\mathbb T)$ be a real Tate triple with polarization $\Pi$, and let $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal Q$ be a quotient by a closed subgroup $H\subset\pi(\mathcal C)$ containing the weight torus. Assume that $\mathcal Q$ is semisimple. A sufficient condition for a polarization $\Pi_{\mathcal Q}$ with $F\Pi=\Pi_{\mathcal Q}$ is the following concrete positivity test: \[ \text{for every }Y\in\mathcal C^H \text{ and }\psi\in\Pi(Y),\qquad F(\psi)\text{ is positive definite on }F(Y). \tag{D.9} \] Here $F(Y)$ is regarded as an ordinary real vector space because the fundamental group of $\mathcal Q$ acts trivially on it. Moreover, for any tensor functor to a semisimple target in which every object is a direct summand of an image, preservation of a polarization is equivalent to every image $F(\psi)$ being a Weil form. This gives an actual test, rather than assuming the desired compatibility in different notation.

statement: D.4d (Known with derivation, and with the stated 2026 input): geometric cases of the distribution condition.. Fix a prime of $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ over $p$ and write $\mathbb F=\overline{\mathbb F}_p$. On the categories of Lefschetz motives, with rational correspondences generated by divisor classes modulo numerical equivalence, the reduction functor \[ R_{\rm L}:\operatorname{LCM}(\overline{\mathbb Q}) \longrightarrow\operatorname{LMot}(\mathbb F) \] preserves the canonical polarizations. For motives with all algebraic correspondences, the same assertion holds for reduction of CM abelian motives if the rational Hodge conjecture holds for every complex CM abelian variety. Thus D.4a applies to these reductions wherever the slope parity used to select the real fibres is defined. In particular, it applies to the even subcategories generated by a CM abelian scheme over an open subscheme of a number ring, with its extending correspondences and relatively ample polarizations, at its admissible closed points. The equality concerns the polarization structures after transport to a common real fibre; representing homomorphisms have the conjugacy ambiguity already stated on 15:183.

statement: D.4f (Proved under the stated standard framework): the all-motives effectivity criterion detects the Tate conjecture.. The remaining classification input in D.4b can be characterized precisely. Fix $q$ and suppose that the category $\mathcal N_q$ of pure numerical motives over $\mathbb F_q$ has the usual algebraic Kunneth decomposition, is semisimple with finite-dimensional rational morphism spaces, and has a faithful $\ell$-adic realization factoring through numerical equivalence, for some $\ell\ne p$. The last condition is essential: without it the phrase \emph{eigenvalues of a numerical motive} has not been justified by this realization. Use the usual effective subcategory of direct summands of finite sums of motives of smooth projective varieties. In this framework the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item every motive whose Frobenius eigenvalues are algebraic integers is effective; \item every motive on which Frobenius is the identity is effective; \item for every smooth projective $X/\mathbb F_q$ and every $r$, the cycle map is onto the Frobenius-fixed subspace of $H^{2r}(X_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell(r))$. \end{enumerate} Here (3) is the cycle-class form of the Tate conjecture on all varieties over the fixed field; the framework already supplies semisimplicity of the Frobenius actions used below.

statement: D.4g (Proved under the cited 2026 theorem): a common geometric polarization for arbitrary abelian families.. The geometric preservation case can be enlarged beyond CM families. Let $S$ be integral and of finite type over $\mathbb Z$, and let $A_1,\ldots,A_t$ be abelian schemes over $S$ equipped with relatively ample polarizations. Thus cycles and projectors are assumed to extend in the given family; a generic correspondence with no specified specialization is not being used. Assume Theorem I of \citet{D_VanHoftenSempliner2026}. There is a common polarization $\Pi_{\mathcal C}$ such that every $F_s$ preserves it. It is the unique polarization containing the specified geometric forms on the generating degree-one motives and the Tate object. On the even subcategory, the distribution assertion D.4a therefore holds with these geometric polarizations and the fibre/polarization identification specified there, whenever the chosen slope parities exist.

statement: E.1b (Proved lattice form).. For a torus with character lattice $M$ and cocharacter lattice $N=\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb Z)$, assume $C\subset N$ is Galois stable. Then \[ C^\vee=\{m\in M:\langle m,c\rangle\ge0\quad\forall c\in C\}, \qquad \operatorname{Sat}(C)= \{v\in N:\langle m,v\rangle\ge0\quad\forall m\in C^\vee\}. \] To check that rational representations detect every listed character, we take the representation whose weights are the finite Galois orbit of $m$. Galois stability of $C$ makes the whole orbit effective exactly when $m$ is in $C^\vee$. For a split connected reductive group, the same formula works on a maximal torus for a Weyl-stable cone: move $m$ into a dominant chamber; the irreducible representation of highest weight $m$ has all its weights in the convex hull of its Weyl orbit. The Weyl-stable polar therefore makes that whole representation effective. Over $\mathbb Q$ we use a rational representation containing the finite Galois orbit, with multiplicity if descent requires it; multiplicities do not change inequalities.

statement: E.1c (Refuted automaticity for additive cones).. We give complete data compatible with the normalization $\langle\varepsilon,j\rangle=2$. Let \[ T=\mathbb G_m\times R^1_{\mathbb Q(i)/\mathbb Q}\mathbb G_m, \qquad N=\mathbb Z^2, \qquad \overline{(a,b)}=(a,-b), \quad \varepsilon=(1,0)\in M, \quad j=(2,0)\in N. \] Set \[ C=\mathbb N(1,1)+\mathbb N(1,-1) =\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^2:a\ge |b|, a\equiv b\pmod2\}. \] It is an additive Galois-stable cone, contains $j$, and has $\varepsilon$ strictly positive away from the origin. The character $\varepsilon$ is in the interior of its real polar. Its integral polar is $C^\vee=\{(u,v):u\ge|v|\}$, because the two generator inequalities are $u+v\ge0$ and $u-v\ge0$. Therefore \[ \operatorname{Sat}(C)=\{(a,b):a\ge|b|\}\supsetneqq C; \qquad (1,0)\in\operatorname{Sat}(C)\setminus C. \] The two cones define exactly the same effectivity structure. This is a counterexample to automatic saturation under the additive-cone requirements alone. Even imposing root saturation is not enough. The monoid \[ C_{\mathrm{open}}=\{0\}\cup \{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^2:a>|b|\} \] is root saturated: $nv\in C_{\mathrm{open}}$ for an integer $n>0$ implies $v\in C_{\mathrm{open}}$. It has the same integral polar and the same bipolar as $C$, but omits $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$. Thus the required saturation includes closure as detected by integral half-spaces, not merely divisibility in the cocharacter lattice.

Suppose ``cone'' is defined in advance to mean $C=K\cap N$, where $K\subset N_{\mathbb R}$ is a closed convex cone and $\varepsilon$ lies in the interior of $K^\vee$. Then $C$ is saturated as above, in particular when $K$ is rational polyhedral. The conclusion holds without rational polyhedrality: a separating normal for a lattice point outside $K$ can be perturbed into the interior of $K^\vee$ while keeping its value negative at that point, then approximated by a rational normal and scaled to an integral character. This character is nonnegative on $K\cap N$ and excludes the point from the integral bipolar. For completeness, the perturbation uses $m_t=m+t\varepsilon$ for sufficiently small $t>0$, where $m\in K^\vee$ satisfies $\langle m,v\rangle<0$. statement: E.1e (Audit of the portion of R13 used here).. The closure of $P(\nu)$ under sums, subobjects and tensor products follows by taking weights, and a positive $\langle\varepsilon,\nu\rangle$ makes sufficiently many Tate twists of every fixed representation effective. For a cone with the strict interior condition, the same twist works uniformly on that cone: normalize $\langle\varepsilon,c\rangle=1$, use compactness of the closed section, and bound each of the finitely many weights of the representation on it. This verifies the step of R13 needed in E.1. We do not use E.1 as a proof of the motivic conjecture that every cohomologically effective motive is effective. Lead E1, concerning the Galois orbit and Frobenius slopes, belongs to E.2 and is not decided by these purely representation-theoretic statements.

statement: E.2a. The slope description (Proved for Weil characters; proved for numerical motives under the Tate conjecture).. Let $L/\mathbb Q$ be a finite Galois CM field and let $M=M(q,L)$ consist of $p$-units $\lambda\in L^\times$ with $\lambda\bar\lambda=q^{w(\lambda)}$, $w(\lambda)\in\mathbb Z$. For a prime $\mathfrak p$ over $p$ put \[ i_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)= \frac{\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)} {\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak p}(q)}\in\mathbb Q. \] These are rational cocharacters of $D(M)^0$, satisfying $i_{\mathfrak p}+i_{\tau\mathfrak p}=w$ and $i_{\mathfrak p}(q)=1$. With $M^+=M\cap\mathcal O_L$, \[ M^+=\bigcap_{\mathfrak p\mid p} \{\lambda\in M:i_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)\geq0\}. \] Thus arithmetic effectivity is the intersection of the halfspaces of the Galois conjugate rational slope cocharacter. For a rational representation, the condition is imposed on all its geometric characters. At that level this is the assertion denoted by the intersection of the $P(\sigma i)$ in the question; $i$ must be allowed to be rational.

statement: E.2c. Finite subcategories and an integral criterion (Proved).. For a Galois-stable finitely generated character group $N\subset M(q,L)$ containing $q$, the distinguished slope at $\mathfrak p$ is integral exactly when \[ \operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak p}(N) \subset\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak p}(q)\mathbb Z. \] This follows immediately from its definition as a homomorphism $N\to\mathbb Q$; its values must lie in $\mathbb Z$ to be a cocharacter. It is a criterion for this specified slope, not a claim that all normalized integral cocharacters have been classified. The example from R8 is confirmed exactly: \[ L=\mathbb Q(i),\quad q=25,\quad \lambda=15+20i=(2+i)^3(2-i). \] At the two primes above $5$ its normalized slopes are $3/2$ and $1/2$ although its weight is $2$. Thus even weights alone do not make the slope integral. The supplied program verifies the factorization and norm with exact Gaussian arithmetic.

statement: E.2e. The finiteness axiom (Refuted globally; finite-lattice version proved).. The marginal proposal on 14:3, ``un nb fini de types de motifs effectifs de poids $i$'', is false for the full category over every $\mathbb F_q$, even when ``types'' means simple isomorphism classes. Already in weight zero, for every $r\geq1$ the cyclotomic direct summand of $h^0(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^r})$ has Frobenius minimal polynomial $\Phi_r(T)$. The rational cyclic group algebra is semisimple and its cyclotomic factor $\mathbb Q(\zeta_r)$ is a simple rational representation, so these give pairwise nonisomorphic simple effective Artin motives. This proof involves no conjecture on cycles. There are also infinitely many simple effective weight-one types. The numbers $\sqrt q\,\zeta_r$ are Weil $q$-integers, and their degrees are unbounded: the field generated by one of them together with $\sqrt q$ contains $\zeta_r$, hence its degree is at least $\varphi(r)/2$. Honda--Tate assigns distinct simple isogeny classes along a subsequence of unbounded degrees. The same construction in each positive weight, using B.1a and the spectral factor, gives infinitely many eigenvalue types. The simple-motive classification in all weights is not needed to refute the axiom. For a fixed finite Galois CM field $L$ and a fixed weight $i$, however, there are only finitely many effective characters in $M(q,L)$: each valuation lies between $0$ and $i\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak p}(q)$ and there are finitely many prime valuations. A specified divisor and weight determine the element up to an ordinary norm-one unit, which is a root of unity of the fixed finite group $\mu(L)$. This proves the sharp finite-lattice statement behind R13 while explaining why it cannot be passed to the full protorus.

statement: E.3d (Proved endpoint cases; exact remaining gates).. For $i=1$ and $i=n$, both directions follow in every characteristic from $P^1=\operatorname{Pic}^0(k)$ and $P^n=\operatorname{Alb}(k)$: the family map is an actual homomorphism of abelian varieties, and its rational Tate-module action is zero if and only if the homomorphism is zero. For an abelian variety $A/k$ and a normalized cycle $Z\in\mathrm{CH}^i(A	imes X)$, we have \[ u_Z=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a({}^tZ):H^{2(n-i)+1}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell(n-i)) \longrightarrow H^1(A,\mathbb Q_\ell) 	ext{ is zero}. \] For integral $Z$ the corresponding map with $\mathbb Z_\ell$ coefficients is also zero, since its target $H^1(A,\mathbb Z_\ell)$ is torsion free. Thus the characteristic-$p$ implication requested on 14:38 is true. The proof does not require an algebraic adjoint in the middle cohomology of $X$. \emph{The torsion lemma.} Bloch's map \[ \lambda_X^i:\mathrm{CH}^i(X)[\ell^\infty] \longrightarrow H^{2i-1}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell/\mathbb Z_\ell(i)) \] vanishes on $N^i(X)\cap\mathrm{CH}^i(X)[\ell^\infty]$. We prove this carefully, without requiring the individual Albanese-equivalence generators to be torsion. Take $z$ in that intersection. We choose an expression $z=\sum_j (W_j)_*
u_j$, where $T_j$ are smooth projective, $
u_j$ are degree-zero zero-cycles on $T_j$, and $\operatorname{alb}_{T_j}(
u_j)=0$. We also choose rational equivalences expressing this equality and $\ell^r z=0$ for some $r$. All cycles, functions, morphisms and points in these finite data descend to a field $K$ finitely generated over $\mathbb F_p$. We include the Albanese varieties $B_j$ of the geometric $T_j$ and their pointed Albanese maps $b_j:T_j	o B_j$ in the descended data. After enlarging $K$ and shrinking an integral finite-type model over $\mathbb F_p$, these extend to smooth projective families, abelian schemes, cycles, and morphisms. We shrink further so that the supports and rational functions used in the finite Chow relations spread and the fibrewise relations remain valid. In particular, we preserve the chosen relation $\ell^r z=0$. The equality $b_{j*}
u_j=0$ holds as an equality of sections of $B_j$. Choose a closed point of this model in the good locus. The specialization can be taken along a valuation with geometric generic field $\overline K$ and residue field $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$: at a smooth closed point, a full flag of local parameters gives an iterated discrete valuation, and we extend it to $\overline K$. Equivalently we specialize along that flag one step at a time. Proper specialization of Chow classes commutes with the proper pushforwards and refined pullbacks defining $(W_j)_*
u_j$. We therefore obtain \[ z_s=\sum_j(W_{j,s})_*
u_{j,s}, \qquad \ell^r z_s=0,\qquad b_{j,s*}
u_{j,s}=0. \] We must justify that specialization does not silently change the needed Albanese kernel. The map $b_j^*:H^1(B_j,\mathbb Z_\ell)	o H^1(T_j,\mathbb Z_\ell)$ is an isomorphism on the geometric generic fibre, integrally: it is the usual identification with the dual of the Albanese Tate module. This is a morphism of lisse $\mathbb Z_\ell$ sheaves on our connected good model. Smooth proper base change therefore makes it an isomorphism at $s$ as well. Thus the induced homomorphism $\operatorname{Alb}(T_{j,s})	o B_{j,s}$ is an isogeny with degree prime to $\ell$. The Albanese class of $
u_{j,s}$ lies in its finite kernel and hence has order prime to $\ell$. Every degree-zero Chow class over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$ is torsion, as proved in C.5a by curve parameterization. Roitman's prime-to-$p$ torsion theorem, in the proved form \citet[Theorem 4.2]{cyBloch1979}, identifies its $\ell$-primary torsion with that of the Albanese. Consequently $
u_{j,s}$ has no $\ell$-primary part: it has finite order prime to $\ell$. So $z_s$ has order prime to $\ell$ while also being killed by $\ell^r$, and therefore $z_s=0$. The Bloch map commutes with specialization \citep[Proposition 3.8]{cyBloch1979}, and smooth proper base change identifies the corresponding cohomology groups with $\mathbb Q_\ell/\mathbb Z_\ell$ coefficients. Hence $\lambda_X^i(z)=0$. Extension from $\overline K$ back to $k$ preserves this conclusion by the same base-change compatibility. This proves the torsion lemma. \emph{Application to an abelian family.} Put $g=\dim A$ and view $Z$ as a correspondence from $A$ to $X$. statement: E.3j (Proved: the family converse for one-cycles when zero-cycles are supported on a curve).. Let $X/\mathbb C$ be a smooth projective connected $n$-fold, $n\ge2$, and suppose that a closed subvariety $C\subset X$ of dimension at most one supports $\mathrm{CH}_0(X)$; that is, $\mathrm{CH}_0(C)\to\mathrm{CH}_0(X)$ is surjective. Then for every abelian variety $A$ and every normalized $Z\in\mathrm{CH}^{n-1}(A\times X)$, \[ a({}^tZ)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u_Z=0 \quad\text{in }\operatorname{Hom}\bigl(A(\mathbb C),P^{n-1}(X)\bigr). \] This is an integral conclusion about $u_Z$, although the cohomological vanishing can be tested with rational coefficients. \emph{The decomposition and its precise cycle action.} We give the decomposition-of-the-diagonal argument needed here. Choose a countable algebraically closed subfield $k_0\subset\mathbb C$ over which $X$ and $C$ are defined. Embed $K=k_0(X)$ in $\mathbb C$ over $k_0$. The corresponding geometric generic point $\eta$, viewed as a complex point of $X$, is rationally equivalent to a zero-cycle supported on $C$. The finitely many cycles and rational functions in this relation spread over a finite-type integral $\overline K$-scheme. A closed $\overline K$-point in a good open specializes the relation to $\overline K$, preserving $\eta$ and the support on $C$. The resulting finite data descend to a finite extension $K'/K$. Taking the norm therefore gives \[ M[\eta]=z_C\quad\text{in }\mathrm{CH}_0(X_K), \qquad M>0,\quad\operatorname{supp}(z_C)\subset C_K. \] Closing $z_C$ in $X\times C$ and applying localization to the generic point of the first factor yields \begin{equation} M\Delta_X=\Gamma_C+\Gamma_D\quad\text{in }\mathrm{CH}^n(X\times X), \end{equation} where $\Gamma_C$ is supported on $X\times C$ and $\Gamma_D$ on $D\times X$ for a divisor $D\subset X$. We have proved the needed decomposition from the stated complex support hypothesis; we have not assumed universal support over every field extension. Normalize the curve components of $C$. Their contribution lifts to divisor correspondences on $X\times\widetilde C$; components over isolated points have the same, or simpler, factorization. They act on $\mathrm{CH}^{n-1}(X)$ through $\mathrm{CH}^{0}(\widetilde C)$, since the lifted correspondence has codimension one and the source has dimension $n$. As $\mathrm{CH}^{0}(\widetilde C)$ has no algebraically trivial part, $\Gamma_C$ annihilates $\mathrm{CH}^{n-1}(X)_{\mathrm{alg}}$. statement: E.3m (Proved: the exact integral Walker reformulation of the general family converse).. Fix a smooth projective complex variety $X$ and a codimension $i$. The following assertions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item For every abelian variety $A$ and every normalized $Z\in\mathrm{CH}^i(A\times X)$, the vanishing $a({}^tZ)=0$ implies $u_Z=0$ integrally. \item The natural surjection $P^i(X)\to J_W^i(X)(\mathbb C)$ is an isomorphism. \item $N^i(X)=\ker\psi_W$ in $\mathrm{CH}^i(X)_{\mathrm{alg}}$. \end{enumerate} These equivalent fixed-target conditions are refuted universally by E.3u below. Their exact common condition is the Walker-kernel equality, which differs from the false integral ordinary Abel--Jacobi equality in Lead E4. We write $J=J_W^i(X)$, $P=P^i(X)$, and $\overline\psi:P\twoheadrightarrow J(\mathbb C)$. The equivalence of (2) and (3) follows from surjectivity of $\psi_W$ and E.3g's inclusion $N^i\subset\ker\psi_W$. Condition (2) implies (1) by E.3i. We prove the other direction. \emph{Choose one family covering the Walker Jacobian.} Assume (1). Every algebraically trivial cycle is an integral point of an abelian family by E.3g. The corresponding regular Walker maps have abelian-subvariety images which generate $J$. A finite sum of these images is all of $J$: otherwise one can successively enlarge their dimensions, which is impossible after $\dim J$ strict enlargements. Thus a product of finitely many such parameter varieties gives an abelian family \[ u_B:B(\mathbb C)\longrightarrow P,\qquad \phi_B=\overline\psi\,u_B:B\twoheadrightarrow J. \] If $J=0$, (1) immediately kills every family and hence $P$; we may therefore assume $\dim J>0$. Let $B_0=(\ker\phi_B)^0$. The restricted family on $B_0$ has zero Walker map and therefore zero cohomological action by E.3b--i. Condition (1) gives $u_B(B_0(\mathbb C))=0$. Consequently $u_B$ factors through $D=B/B_0$, and $D\to J$ is an isogeny. Its abstract kernel on $P$ is a subgroup of the finite group $\ker(D\to J)(\mathbb C)$. Over $\mathbb C$ this subgroup is the point group of a finite subgroup scheme $H\subset D$. Put $E=D/H$. We obtain \[ u_E:E(\mathbb C)\hookrightarrow P, \qquad \lambda:E\twoheadrightarrow J, \qquad \overline\psi\,u_E=\lambda, \] where $\lambda$ is an isogeny and $u_E$ is injective. At this point $u_E$ is a homomorphism of groups; we have not assumed that a universal integral cycle exists on $E\times X$. \emph{Every abelian-family image is already this one.} For any other abelian family $u_A:A(\mathbb C)\to P$, take the sum family on $B\times A$ and repeat the preceding construction. Its Walker map is still surjective. We get an abelian variety $E'$ isogenous to $J$ and an injection $u_{E'}:E'(\mathbb C)\hookrightarrow P$ whose image is $u_B(B(\mathbb C))+u_A(A(\mathbb C))$. The inclusion $B\to B\times A$ induces an algebraic homomorphism $B\to E'$. It kills the kernel of $B\to E$, because its composition with the injective map $u_{E'}$ is $u_B$. Quotient descent therefore gives an algebraic homomorphism $E\to E'$. It is injective on complex points, again by the injections into $P$. Both abelian varieties have dimension $\dim J$, so this homomorphism is an isomorphism. It follows that $u_A(A(\mathbb C))\subset u_E(E(\mathbb C))$. Using E.3g once more gives \[ P=u_E(E(\mathbb C)). \] Moreover, the preceding quotient construction shows that every composite $u_E^{-1}u_A:A\to E$ is an algebraic homomorphism, not merely an abstract homomorphism on points. The kernel of $\overline\psi$ is now the finite group $\ker\lambda(\mathbb C)$. But it is also $\ker\psi_W/N^i(X)$, a divisible group by \citet[Theorem 2.3, author p.~12]{cyACMVWalker2022}. A finite divisible group is zero. Hence $\lambda$ is an isomorphism and (2) follows. This already completes the equivalence; no universality assumption on the Walker map has entered the argument. \emph{Regularity of the resulting quotient, also checked directly.} Let \[ q:\mathrm{CH}^i(X)_{\mathrm{alg}}\longrightarrow P \xrightarrow{u_E^{-1}}E(\mathbb C). \] For a pointed smooth projective parameter variety $(T,t_0)$ and a correspondence $W$, its point-to-cycle map modulo $N$ factors integrally through $\operatorname{Alb}(T)(\mathbb C)$, because $W_*$ kills the Albanese kernel by the definition of $N$. In characteristic zero this means that $f$ kills the whole finite group scheme $\operatorname{Alb}(T)[m]$. Hence $f$ factors algebraically through $[m]$ as $f=g\circ[m]$ for a homomorphism $g:\operatorname{Alb}(T)\to E$. The difference $v-g$ takes values in $E[m](\mathbb C)$; its source is divisible, so this finite-valued homomorphism is zero. Therefore $v=g$. Composing with the pointed Albanese map proves regularity for projective parameter varieties. For a smooth quasi-projective parameter variety, choose a smooth projective compactification and close the correspondence; the refined fibres on the original open are unchanged. This reduces regularity to the preceding case. General smooth finite-type parameter schemes can be covered by such opens, and the resulting morphisms agree because their complex-point maps agree and the target is separated. Thus $q$ is a regular homomorphism in the usual sense. We have, in particular, \[ \psi_W=\lambda\circ q. \] The direct regularity check is consistent with the alternative isogeny-initiality proof from the same Theorem 2.3, but that alternative is unnecessary after the finite-divisible-kernel argument. The assertion that the original family converse holds for every $X,i$ remains unproved here.

statement: E.3n (Proved: a torsion-valued abelian-family map to $P$ over $\mathbb C$ is zero).. Let $X/\mathbb C$ be smooth projective, let $A$ be an abelian variety, and let $Z\in\mathrm{CH}^i(A\times X)$ be normalized. Then \[ u_Z\otimes\mathbb Q=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u_Z=0. \] The hypothesis means that every value of $u_Z$ is torsion; it does not assume a uniform exponent. We prove the required uniformity from finite-type parameter spaces for the defining Albanese relations. Uncountability of $\mathbb C$ is essential to this proof, as the example E.3f over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$ also shows. \emph{Moving the points before parameterizing the relations.} For a smooth projective connected $T$ and a nonempty open $T^\circ\subset T$, every class in $\mathrm{CH}_0(T)$ has a zero-cycle representative supported in $T^\circ$; equivalently, the map $Z_0(T^\circ)\to\mathrm{CH}_0(T)$ from the group of cycles is surjective. We are not using a covariant Chow-group map for an open immersion. Indeed, for each excluded point choose an integral curve through it whose generic point lies in $T^\circ$, normalize the curve, and use Riemann--Roch to express that point as a difference of effective divisors avoiding the finitely many points outside $T^\circ$. Pushing to $T$ proves the assertion. For dimension zero it is immediate. Represent a correspondence $W\in\mathrm{CH}^i(T\times X)$ by a finite signed sum of integral subvarieties. Those which do not dominate $T$ act trivially on $\mathrm{CH}_0(T)$: move the zero-cycle away from their images. Each dominating component is flat over a common nonempty open $T^\circ$ after generic flatness. We can therefore replace any Albanese-kernel zero-cycle $\nu$ by a rationally equivalent zero-cycle supported in $T^\circ$. Its Albanese class remains zero. Now $W_*\nu$ is represented by the actual signed sum of flat fibres $W_t$ at its finitely many support points. Thus every generator of $N^i(X)$ has this form; we need not parameterize arbitrary refined intersections at bad fibres. \emph{Countably many finite-type spaces parameterize these generators.} Embed $X$ once in projective space. We describe all data as the projective embedding dimension, Hilbert polynomials, finite lengths, and integer coefficients vary. There are only countably many such choices. Throughout we replace the parameter bases by their reductions and use finite locally closed stratifications when required for Hilbert--Chow, constant fibre dimension, or multiplicity. This does not lose any complex-point datum; allowing all the strata preserves countability and constructibility. First use Hilbert schemes to parameterize closed embedded smooth projective geometrically connected varieties $T$. The locus with these fibre properties is open in the appropriate Hilbert scheme; allowing the finitely many components and locally closed strata gives finite-type bases. Pass to the universal $T$ itself as a base to mark an origin $t_0$. The pulled-back family has a section. Its relative Albanese is an abelian scheme, with its pointed map, compatible with base change. The precise characteristic-zero existence and base-change statement is \citet[Theorem 2.2]{cyJavanpeykarMathur2022}; the marked section turns their Albanese torsor into the pointed group scheme. Relative Hilbert schemes for $T\times X$ parameterize the finitely many components of $W$. Restrict to the locus where the marked evaluation points lie in the fibre-flat locus. This is an algebraic constructible condition. More explicitly, the universal subschemes are flat over their Hilbert base; the local criterion for flatness identifies fibrewise flatness over $T$ with flatness of their projections over the universal $T$, and the bad locus has closed image because these projections are projective. Finite stratification also fixes the dimensions and multiplicities of the resulting fibre cycles. Mark the finitely many points $t_1,\ldots,t_s$ by the relative power $T^s$. For fixed integer weights $e_j$ with $\sum_j e_j=0$, the condition \[ \sum_j e_j\operatorname{alb}_{T}(t_j)=0 \] is closed: it is the inverse image of the zero section under an algebraic morphism to the relative Albanese. On this finite-type locus, the signed flat-fibre cycle $\sum_j e_jW_{t_j}$ is an algebraic family of cycles on $X$. statement: E.3t (Proved: the full morphic obstruction to Albanese equivalence).. Let $X/\mathbb C$ be smooth projective of dimension $n$, let $0\le i\le n$, and put $r=n-i$. Here $L_rH_m$ is Lawson homology with the inductive mixed Hodge structure of \citet[Sections 3--5]{cyWalker2007Morphic}; the convention already incorporates the twist making the relevant pure part have weight $-1$. There are canonical surjections \[ P^i(X)\longrightarrow J^{\mathrm{mor}}_r(X) \longrightarrow J_W^i(X)(\mathbb C) \longrightarrow J_a^i(X)(\mathbb C). \] The last map is an isogeny of abelian varieties. Then the composite of $u_Z$ with $P^i(X)\to J^{\mathrm{mor}}_r(X)$ is zero if and only if $\lambda_Z=0$. Consequently \begin{equation} u_Z=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda_Z=0 \ \Longrightarrow\ a({}^tZ)=0. \end{equation} The same first implication holds if $u_Z\otimes\mathbb Q=0$. E.4g (Proved): every rational twist over the compactified number ring.. The rational answer extends beyond twists zero and one. With the compactified convention of E.4b, for all integers $i,n$ we have \[ H_W^i(\overline{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z},\mathbb Q(n)) \simeq  egin{cases} \mathbb Q,&(n,i)=(0,0)	ext{ or }(1,3),\ \mathbb Q,&n\geq3	ext{ odd and }i=1,\ \mathbb Q,&n\leq-2	ext{ even and }i=2,\ 0,&	ext{otherwise}. \end{cases} 	ag{E.4.7} \] We specify the argument, since the negative twists distinguish ordinary rational motivic cohomology from the duality-completed Weil complex. For $n>1$, the number-ring computation of \citet[\S5.8.3, pp.~1503--1504]{D_FlachMorin2018} identifies degree one with the rationalization of $H^1_{\mathrm{et}}(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z, \mathbb Z(n))$; the degree-two group is finite and the other displayed groups are $2$-torsion. The regulator in that same computation identifies the realification of degree one with $H^0(\mathbb R,(2\pi i)^{n-1}\mathbb R)$. Complex conjugation acts here by $(-1)^{n-1}$, so this space has dimension one precisely for odd $n$. Finite generation then gives the claimed rational dimensions. The underlying rank theorem is \citet[Proposition 12.2, p.~271]{D_Borel1974}: for $j\geq2$, $K_j(\mathbb Z)\otimes\mathbb Q$ has rank one when $j\equiv1\pmod4$ and rank zero otherwise. The motivic degree-one piece has $j=2n-1$, giving exactly odd $n\geq3$. The perfect duality of \citet[Theorem 3.22]{D_FlachMorin2018}, after rationalization, gives \[ H_W^i(\overline X,\mathbb Q(n)) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}  igl(H_W^{3-i}(\overline X,\mathbb Q(1-n)),\mathbb Q igr). \] For $n<0$, the positive twist $1-n>1$ has rank one exactly when $1-n$ is odd, which is exactly negative even $n$; its degree one becomes degree two. E.4b supplies $n=0,1$. This proves every case of (E.4.7). Thus the question whether all other rational groups vanish has answer no, already in twist three, and also in negative even twists. The rank theorem used here is the published 1974 theorem. The separately opened regulator paper \citep{D_Borel1977}, received in November 1976, was published in 1977; its 1980 erratum \citep{D_Borel1980} concerns discriminant and complex-sign normalizations, not the rank formula. There is also a coherent rational extension to all opens with the real place retained. For $n
e1$ set $C_{S,\mathbb Q}^n=C_X^n\otimes\mathbb Q$, with identity restriction maps; for $n=1$ rationalize (E.4.3). Since $C_p^{n-1}\otimes\mathbb Q=0$ for $n
e1$ by E.4a, these assignments satisfy every finite-prime localization triangle and their iterated compatibilities. Moreover any extension satisfying those triangles has the same restriction isomorphisms for $n
e1$. For $n=1$ and $S
e\varnothing$, its only groups are $\mathbb Q^S$ in degree one and the sum-zero subspace of $\mathbb Q^S$ in degree two. This settles the entire rational table and the rational restriction calculation. E.4l--p below construct a compatible integral extension on this specified family of opens, with all finite-coefficient comparisons and the necessary wild support. E.4h (Proved, with the characteristic-prime restriction): the continuous tables in R15.. Let $\Gamma=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb F}_q/\mathbb F_q) \simeq\widehat{\mathbb Z}$, with arithmetic generator $f$, and let $M$ be a finitely generated $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module with continuous $\Gamma$-action. Continuous cohomology here means the derived inverse limit of the discrete cohomology of $M/\ell^rM$. Then \[ R\Gamma_{\mathrm{cts}}(\Gamma,M) \simeq[\,M\xrightarrow{1-f}M\,] \quad	ext{in degrees }0,1. 	ag{E.4.8} \] Indeed a continuous cocycle into a finite module is determined by its value at $f$; every value extends continuously after taking a finite cyclic quotient whose order is divisible by the action order and the module exponent. Coboundaries give $(f-1)M$. The usual cyclic resolution, followed by inflation through larger cyclic quotients, has zero cohomology in degrees at least two: the periodic classes in degrees at least two are killed after multiplying the quotient order by a sufficiently large power of $\ell$. This proves the two-term calculation for each finite quotient. Their cohomology groups are finite, so the inverse systems satisfy the Mittag--Leffler condition and have zero $\varprojlim^1$. Taking the derived inverse limit proves (E.4.8). For a finite-dimensional continuous $\mathbb Q_\ell$-representation, compactness of $\Gamma$ gives an invariant lattice. Continuous cochains have bounded image, so passage from that lattice to its rationalization commutes with the cochain complex and gives the same formula over $\mathbb Q_\ell$. For $\ell
e p$ we may apply this to the genuine cyclotomic lattice $M=\mathbb Z_\ell(n)$, where $f$ acts as the unit $q^n$. If $n=0$, degrees zero and one are both $\mathbb Z_\ell$; if $n
e0$, degree zero is zero and degree one is $\mathbb Z_\ell/(1-q^n)$. Higher degrees vanish. With $\mathbb Q_\ell(n)$ coefficients, both degrees are $\mathbb Q_\ell$ for $n=0$ and all groups vanish for $n
e0$. These are precisely the continuous tables after stating their topology. The characteristic prime cannot be inserted into this rank-one cyclotomic formula. For $n
e0$, multiplication by $q^n$ is not an automorphism of $\mathbb Z_p$: it is a nonunit for $n>0$ and is not even an integral endomorphism for $n<0$. Nor can it give a continuous one-dimensional $\mathbb Q_p$-representation of $\Gamma$, since the valuation of a compact subgroup of $\mathbb Q_p^	imes$ is zero. In characteristic $p$ the positive-degree logarithmic de Rham--Witt term at a finite field is zero, as used in E.4a, and the negative-twist convention excludes the $p$-part. A crystalline Frobenius with nonunit eigenvalue belongs to a different coefficient category. Thus R15's prime-to-$p$ continuous table is confirmed, while an unqualified extension of that table to a free $p$-adic cyclotomic lattice is false.

statement: E.4i (Proved): the Brauer injectivity and local descent used in R15.. We also check the separate Brauer-draft assertion rather than importing it from the earlier reading. Let $X$ be an integral noetherian scheme whose strict local rings are factorial, let $K$ be its function field, and let $j:\operatorname{Spec}K\to X$ be the generic-point morphism. Then \[ H^2_{\mathrm{et}}(X,\mathbb G_m) \longrightarrow H^2_{\mathrm{et}}(K,\mathbb G_m) =\operatorname{Br}(K) \quad\text{is injective}. \tag{E.4.9} \] In particular $\operatorname{Br}(X)\to\operatorname{Br}(K)$ is injective for the Azumaya Brauer group. These are \citet[Corollaries 1.8 and 1.10, p.~293]{D_Grothendieck1966BrauerII} in the opened Bourbaki version; its numbering is not the draft's Proposition 5.4 and Corollary 5.5. Here is the proof in the stated setting. On $X_{\mathrm{et}}$, factoriality of strict local rings gives the exact divisor sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow\mathbb G_m\longrightarrow j_*\mathbb G_{m,K} \longrightarrow \bigoplus_{x\in X^{(1)}}(i_x)_*\mathbb Z\longrightarrow0. \] The last description is the equality of Cartier and Weil divisors on strict localizations. For each $x$ the Leray edge map embeds $H^1(X,(i_x)_*\mathbb Z)$ into $H^1(k(x),\mathbb Z)= \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cts}}(\Gamma_{k(x)},\mathbb Z)=0$; compactness and torsion-freeness prove the last equality. Cohomology on the noetherian small \'etale site commutes with the filtered union of finite subsums. Thus the divisor sheaf has zero $H^1$, and the displayed sequence injects $H^2(X,\mathbb G_m)$ into $H^2(X,j_*\mathbb G_{m,K})$. Moreover $R^1j_*\mathbb G_{m,K}=0$: its stalks are limits of Picard groups of finite products of separable field extensions of $K$, which vanish by Hilbert 90. The Leray sequence now injects the latter $H^2$ into $H^2(K,\mathbb G_m)$, proving (E.4.9). The usual boundary from the exact sequence $1\to\mathbb G_m\to\mathrm{GL}_r\to\mathrm{PGL}_r\to1$ embeds Azumaya Brauer classes into $H^2(X,\mathbb G_m)$: a zero boundary means the algebra is an endomorphism algebra of a vector bundle and hence Brauer-trivial. This proves the Azumaya assertion. For a local ring $R$, a class $\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{et}}(\operatorname{Spec}R,\mathbb G_m)$ comes from an Azumaya algebra if and only if it vanishes after a finite \'etale faithfully flat extension. This is \citet[Proposition 2.4, p.~298]{D_Grothendieck1966BrauerII}. For clarity, the descent direction has an explicit construction. Refine such an extension to a finite \'etale Galois torsor $B/R$ with group $G$. The ring $B$ is semilocal, so $\operatorname{Pic}(B)=0$. The Hochschild--Serre sequence therefore represents $\xi$ by a cocycle $c\in Z^2(G,B^\times)$. The crossed product \[ A_c=\bigoplus_{g\in G}B u_g, \qquad (b u_g)(b'u_h)=b\,g(b')c(g,h)u_{gh}, \] is an $R$-algebra; the cocycle equation is exactly associativity. After the faithfully flat base change to $B$, the regular crossed product representation identifies it with a matrix algebra of degree $|G|$. Hence it is Azumaya, and its descent cocycle gives $\xi$ (replace $c$ by its inverse if the opposite boundary convention is chosen). Conversely an Azumaya algebra over a local ring has a finite \'etale maximal subalgebra which splits it: choose a separable maximal subalgebra in the residue central simple algebra, lift a generator with separable reduced characteristic polynomial, and use its unit discriminant. This proves the criterion. It does not assert that every arbitrary \'etale splitting cover admits a finite \'etale refinement; the finite condition is the actual hypothesis in this equivalence.

statement: E.5d (Proved as a classification of the indicated structures): what the crystalline moduli mean.. Let $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_p$, $W=W(k)$, $K_0=\operatorname{Frac}W$, and let $\sigma$ be Witt Frobenius. For an unramified reductive group with fixed smooth model $\mathcal G/\mathbb Z_p$, an isocrystal with a chosen trivial underlying $G$-torsor is represented by $b\in G(K_0)$; $F=b\sigma$. A change of trivialization $g$ changes $b$ to $g^{-1}b\sigma(g)$. Isomorphism classes are therefore the corresponding $\sigma$-conjugacy classes $B(G)$. This is the convention underlying \citet[Introduction and \S\S3--4]{D_Kottwitz1985}. If a dominant Hodge type $\mu$ is fixed, lattices in this fixed isocrystal are the points \[ X_\mu(b)=\{g\mathcal G(W): g^{-1}b\sigma(g)\in\mathcal G(W)\mu(p)\mathcal G(W)\}. \tag{E.6} \] Here a coset represents the lattice $gW^d$ in a faithful representation with its tensors. Applying $F$ to the lattice gives exactly the double-coset condition displayed, so (E.6) follows directly by changing a basis. This is the set defined in \citet[\S1.2.9, author-PDF p.~14]{Kisin2017}. Isomorphism classes after forgetting the embedding in the fixed isocrystal require also quotienting on the left by \[ J_b(\mathbb Q_p)=\{h\in G(K_0):h^{-1}b\sigma(h)=b\}; \] compare \citet[\S1.2.12, author-PDF p.~14]{Kisin2017}. Lead E3 captures one possible source of variation inside a Newton stratum, but cannot explain all variation on 15:193: (E.5) varies the Newton stratum itself. statement: E.5e (Proved): unstructured integral fibre functors under a smooth model.. Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $p$, let $W=W(k)$, and let $\mathcal G/W$ be a smooth affine group scheme of finite presentation. Then $H^1_{\rm fpqc}(W,\mathcal G)=1$. Indeed a $\mathcal G$-torsor $P$ is affine, smooth and of finite presentation over $W$. Its special fibre is nonempty, because the torsor map is faithfully flat, and has a $k$-point because $k$ is algebraically closed. Smoothness lifts that point successively to compatible points over $W/p^m$; the completeness of $W$ and finite presentation of the affine scheme $P$ identify their inverse limit with a $W$-point. A torsor with a point is trivial. Consequently two existing $W$-valued fibre functors whose isomorphism torsor has this group are isomorphic after forgetting $F,V$ and any additional filtration. This proves precisely why ordinary smooth torsor cohomology cannot explain nonisomorphism in that case. The crystalline nonisomorphism in E.5c is a statement about $F$-crystals, not a statement about those unstructured torsors. If the proposed integral motivic group has no such smooth model, or if the isomorphisms are required to commute with Frobenius, this vanishing argument has different hypotheses and does not apply. More generally, let $k$ be perfect of cohomological dimension at most one, and assume in addition that the special fibre $\mathcal G_k$ is connected. Then \citet[Theorem 1.9, p.~51]{D_Steinberg1965} gives $H^1(k,\mathcal G_k)=1$. The same lifting argument proves $H^1(W(k),\mathcal G)=1$. This applies in particular when $k$ is finite, and also to a smooth affine group over $\mathbb Z_\ell$ with connected special fibre. It verifies the finite-stage uniqueness assertion of R16 with its actual hypotheses. It gives no such conclusion from perfection alone, as E.5b shows. Even these finite-stage hypotheses do not alone justify a passage to a pro-group, as the following example shows.

statement: E.5g (Proved): conditions that do permit the passage to the limit.. Let $(G_n,P_n)$ be a countable inverse system of affine groups and equivariant torsors of finite type over a perfect field $k$ with $\operatorname{cd}(k)\leq1$. Suppose each $G_n$ and every kernel of $G_{n+1}\to G_n$ are smooth and connected, and the group transitions are faithfully flat. Then each $P_n(k)$ is nonempty by \citet[Theorem 1.9]{D_Steinberg1965}; the fibre over any point of $P_n(k)$ is a torsor under the indicated kernel and so has a $k$-point by the same theorem. Thus $P_{n+1}(k)\to P_n(k)$ is surjective. Inductively choosing compatible points proves $(\varprojlim P_n)(k)\ne\varnothing$. The counterexample (E.5.1) has disconnected transition kernels $\mu_2$, so it does not satisfy this sufficient condition. There is also a compactness criterion, requiring no connectedness condition on the transition kernels. For any directed inverse system, if each $P_i(k)$ is a nonempty compact Hausdorff space and the transition maps are continuous, the product of these spaces is compact. The equations defining compatible points are closed and have the finite intersection property: for finitely many equations choose a common upper index and any point there. Their intersection is nonempty. This applies to finite-type torsors over a finite field once their finite-stage rational points exist, since these point sets are finite. It also applies to affine finite-presentation torsors over $\mathbb Z_\ell$ once their integral points exist: each such point set is closed in some $\mathbb Z_\ell^N$ and hence compact. Together with E.5e this proves pro-level uniqueness over $\mathbb Z_\ell$ for an inverse presentation whose finite-stage isomorphism torsors have smooth models with connected special fibres. It supplies the missing compatibility argument in exactly those cases, while (E.5f) proves that perfection and cohomological dimension alone do not supply it.

statement: E.6a (Proved): the class over $\mathbb Q_\ell$.. Let $k$ be a number field and let $\mathcal{AT}(k)$ be the semisimple pure $\mathbb Q$-linear category generated by finite Artin motives and $\mathbb Q(1)$, not a category of mixed Tate extensions. Let $\Gamma_k$ be the absolute Galois group, regarded as the constant profinite group scheme through its finite quotients. After fixing a geometric fibre functor its Tannaka group is \[ G=\Gamma_k\times\mathbb G_m. \tag{E.7} \] For $k=\mathbb Q$, the right comparison torsor $\operatorname{Isom}^{\otimes}(\omega_\ell, \omega_{\mathrm{dR}}\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell)$ has class \[ [\iota_\ell,1]\in H^1(\mathbb Q_\ell,\Gamma_{\mathbb Q}\times\mathbb G_m), \tag{E.8} \] where $\iota_\ell:\Gamma_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\to\Gamma_{\mathbb Q}$ is a local decomposition embedding, defined up to conjugacy. The convention for (E.8) is that the descent cocycle of an Artin representation $V$ is $\rho\circ\iota_\ell$. Reversing the orientation of the isomorphism torsor reverses the cocycle convention; it does not change triviality. Its Tate component is always trivial. Thus within this category a nonzero class cannot occur independently of the Artin part.

statement: F.2a (Proved correction): two normalizations in the supplied Tate survey.. In the notation of \citet[Theorem 1.6 and its proof, p.~3]{rootMilneTate2007}, the sufficient hypothesis is $S^d(X\times X,\ell)$ for $\dim X=d$. The printed $S^{2d}$ does not match the cohomology group in that proof: $S^r$ is defined using $H^{2r}(-,\mathbb Q_\ell(r))$. To check the corrected implication, extend coefficients to split Frobenius. Poincar\'e duality and K\"unneth identify the tensor of a generalized eigenvalue-$a$ block $V_a$ and its reciprocal block with $\operatorname{End}(V_a)$ in $H^{2d}(X\times X,\mathbb Q_\ell(d))$. Frobenius acts on this endomorphism space by conjugation. If its unipotent Jordan factor $U$ were nontrivial, conjugation by $U$ would be a nontrivial unipotent operator: an endomorphism commuting with every endomorphism is scalar, and a scalar unipotent operator is the identity. The corrected $S^d$ hypothesis rules this out, and all Frobenius blocks are semisimple. We do not extract an unconditional semisimplicity theorem from the printed top-degree index. For a $p^{n_1}$-Frobenius $\pi_1$ and a $p^{n_2}$-Frobenius $\pi_2$, common finite-field extension gives the crossed relation \[ \pi_1^{n_2N}=\pi_2^{n_1N}. \] The survey's preceding discussion on p.~2 has these powers; its definition on p.~4 interchanges them incorrectly. For example, on $H^2(\mathbb P^1)$ the Frobenius scalars over $\mathbb F_p$ and $\mathbb F_{p^2}$ are $p$ and $p^2$. Crossed powers agree, whereas the uncrossed equality would say $p^N=p^{4N}$ for $N>0$, which is impossible. These are normalization checks, not assertions that the survey's correctly normalized inputs fail.
